provisions.heading: Admit the System Identity on Every System-Run Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `system-access-missing` for a reaction or job that runs, commands, or queries a use case whose access admits no system identity, and `record-invalid` for `runsAs` beside a `system` or `anonymous` grant.
provisions.statement: A use case that a reaction or a job runs, commands, or queries MUST admit the system identity: its grant is `system` or `anonymous`, or it states `runsAs: system` beside its grant for person callers.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or a job runs with no person behind it. The call it sends carries the system identity, and a permission, self, or signed-in grant admits people alone. Each system run of such a use case is refused at runtime without `runsAs`, so stating it beside the person grant admits the system identity too.
provisions.example: Claimwick erase-personal-data grants `permission/remove-personal-data` to finance staff and states `runsAs: system`. The nightly erase job runs it beside the staff, and without `runsAs` each nightly run is refused.

provisions.heading: Authenticate Every Caller Through a Declared Authentication Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an `authentication` kind outside session, token, device, link, app, and none.
provisions.statement: Each entry point MUST name its authentication kinds from session, token, device, link, app, and none.
provisions.rationale: The authentication kind says how the caller proved identity before the grant check. A session marks a signed-in person, a device marks a managed scanner, and `none` marks open calls. Without a declared kind, open calls and authenticated calls look alike.
provisions.example: An expense submission names `session`. A library self-checkout kiosk names `device`, and a public catalog names `none`.

provisions.heading: Authorize Every Use Case Through a Declared Grant
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a grant outside permission, self, signed-in, anonymous, and system, and `reference-unknown` for a permission no record defines.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its grant as a permission, a self grant, signed-in, anonymous, or system.
provisions.rationale: The grant is the check the call passes. Five forms cover the ground: a permission for role-held action, a self grant for action on owned records, signed-in for an authenticated caller with no permission, anonymous for open calls, and system for work an internal trigger runs. A grant outside these five leaves the checker with no stated check to enforce.
provisions.example: `permission/manage-copies` guards staff work, and `self(permission/read-loans)` lets a reader read owned loans. `signed-in` opens a workspace to any signed-in person with no permission, while `anonymous` opens a public catalog and `system` covers an archive use case only its retention job runs.

provisions.heading: Declare Access on Every Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use case without `access`, `grant`, or `tenant`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its grant and its tenant scope in `access`.
provisions.rationale: The grant and the tenant scope answer the two access questions together: what check the call passes, and which tenant data it touches. A use case missing one part leaves that question to code. The entry point the call arrives through declares how the caller proved identity.

provisions.heading: Declare Erasure for Every External System
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an external system without `erasure` and `reference-unknown` for an unsupported, manual or not-applicable erasure without an Intent decision.
provisions.statement: An external system MUST declare how personal data it holds is erased in `erasure`.
provisions.rationale: Personal data sent outside stays outside unless some operation or event removes it. The erasure declaration states the call, the forwarding event, or the reason removal is absent. An unsupported, manual, or not-applicable erasure cites the Intent decision accepting the limit.
provisions.example: A payout archive declares an unsupported erasure with the accepting decision. The declaration carries the reason settled payouts belong to the bank, plus the sentence employees see.

provisions.heading: Define Each Scope Level in the Glossary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scope-term-missing` for a role scope with no glossary term titled with the level and Scope.
provisions.statement: Each scope level a role names MUST have a glossary term titled with the level and Scope, stating what the level covers in this product.
provisions.rationale: A bare level such as `platform` reads the same in each product, and each product means a different reach by it. The glossary term states that reach once for the product. A reviewer reads what `platform` covers here instead of guessing from the word. This follows decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once.
provisions.example: Claimwick `platform` scope has a glossary term, Platform Scope. The term states coverage of each expense in the Claimwick installation.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Served Content Entry with Its Serving Fields
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a served content entry without path, contentType, cacheControl, versioning, or fulfills.
provisions.statement: Each served content entry on a browser entry point MUST carry path, contentType, cacheControl, versioning, and fulfills.
provisions.rationale: Served content is a file the product hands out rather than behavior it runs. The five serving fields are the whole contract for it. Without them, a legal text or a static script ships as an unreviewed file with no stated requirement or freshness.
provisions.example: A terms text carries its path with `text/html`. It states its cache window, its version rule, and the requirement it fulfills.

provisions.heading: Evaluate Access in One Order
provisions.evidence: Does every call evaluate principal, assignments, permission, tenant scope, ownership, and delegation in that order? Walk one allowed and one refused call through the steps.
provisions.statement: Access MUST be evaluated in one order: the authenticated principal, then the role assignments whose bound scope instance matches the target, then the permission, then the use case tenant scope, then the self-ownership restriction, then delegation validity, with several assignments combining as a union.
provisions.rationale: Each step narrows what the next step checks. Identity comes before assignments, assignments before the permission they carry, the permission before the reach of its use, and ownership and delegation last as restrictions on an otherwise allowed call. One order gives two implementations the same allowed and refused calls. Settled by decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order.
provisions.example: A Claimwick approver holds the approver role for one cost center. A call evaluates the session principal, then the approver assignment matching the expense cost center, then the permission, then the own tenant scope, with an assignment for another cost center ending in the derived forbidden result.

provisions.heading: Grant Across Tenants Only Through Declared Delegation
provisions.evidence: Does every cross-tenant delegation grant declare its grant on both sides? Check the delegation grants the tenancy extension declares.
provisions.statement: A grant that acts across tenants through delegation MUST declare its delegation grant on both sides.
provisions.rationale: Delegation lets one actor act for another. A grant on one side alone leaves the other side unreviewed. Declaring the grant on both sides shows who delegates and who is acted for, with the tenancy extension stating the fields each side carries.
provisions.example: An assistant acts for a manager only where both delegation grants name the pairing. The manager side names who is acted for, and the assistant side names who acts.

provisions.heading: Grant Permissions Through Roles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a permission with no `grantedTo` entry or a role with no `excludes`, `permission-unused` for a permission no role grants, and `role-unused` for a role no permission names.
provisions.statement: Each permission MUST name the roles that grant it in `grantedTo`, with each role's `excludes` stating what the grant does not cover.
provisions.rationale: The grant is the middle of the chain. It joins the actors holding the role to the use cases citing its permissions in their grants. Each permission in Behavior names its Intent roles in `grantedTo`, so the book gathers each role set from the permissions naming it.
provisions.example: `permission/request-expense` names `role/employee` in `grantedTo`. The submit use case cites that permission in its grant, closing the chain.

provisions.heading: Limit the Age of a Sign-In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a `recentSignInWindow` that is neither an ISO 8601 duration nor a `setting/` identifier, or that names a setting of another value type, and `reference-unknown` for a setting no record defines.
provisions.statement: A use case that requires a recent sign-in MUST state the window in `recentSignInWindow` as an ISO 8601 duration or a `setting/` identifier.
provisions.rationale: Some operations need a fresh sign-in. Approving a large payout on a week-old session differs from approving it just after signing in. A window one use case needs sits beside it as a duration, while a window several use cases share lives in a setting. Settled by decision/0074-declare-access-settings-and-deadlines.
provisions.example: Claimwick reimbursement states `recentSignInWindow: PT15M`. A session older than fifteen minutes ends in the derived sign-in-too-old result, and a shared product window lives in a setting each use case names.

provisions.heading: Model a Hosted Sign-In as Use Cases
provisions.evidence: Does every hosted sign-in run as start and complete use cases against the provider external system, with anonymous grants and declared provider calls? Check the sign-in use cases beside the provider system.
provisions.statement: A sign-in through a hosted identity provider MUST be modeled as use cases that start and complete the sign-in, with the provider as an external system.
provisions.rationale: The product signs people in through a hosted provider with OpenID Connect and PKCE through its backend for frontend. The browser holds no provider tokens at any point. The start use case builds the redirect with its challenge, and the complete use case exchanges the code, validates the tokens, finds or creates the person, and starts the session. This follows decision/0103-dotnet-stack-binding.
provisions.example: Claimwick signs employees in through its hosted provider. `use-case/identity.start-sign-in` builds the redirect, `use-case/identity.complete-sign-in` exchanges the code and starts the session, and `external-system/identity-provider` declares the authorize, token, and logout operations.

provisions.heading: Name Each Permission by a Use-Case Verb
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `permission-verb-unknown` (level G) for a permission name whose opening verb is neither in the table, nor a glossary verb of kind command or either, nor `manage`.
provisions.statement: Each permission name SHOULD open with a verb from the use-case verb table, a glossary verb of kind command or either, or with `manage`.
provisions.rationale: The first word of a permission name tells a reader whether the grant reads or changes, and which kind of use case it covers. The verb table gives each opening word one meaning across the product. A name opening with an unlisted word says nothing about what it includes.
provisions.example: `permission/approve-expense` opens with `approve` and `permission/manage-policy` opens with `manage`, so both pass. `permission/handle-documents` opens with an unlisted word, so it is reported.

provisions.heading: Name Every Actor with Its Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an actor without `kind` and `record-invalid` for a kind outside person, organization, and system.
provisions.statement: An actor MUST name its kind in `kind`.
provisions.rationale: The kind says who stands behind the actor: a person answering directly, an organization answering as one party, or an outside system standing in a flow step. A reviewer assigns responsibility from that statement. The system kind pairs with the external-system record naming the actor in `represents`.
provisions.example: An employee actor carries `person`. The library as a lending party carries `organization`, and the text gateway standing in a flow step carries `system`.

provisions.heading: Name Every Authorization Precondition
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a precondition of another rule kind or one the use case cites nowhere in its steps, inputs, or results, and `reference-unknown` for a precondition no rule holds.
provisions.statement: Each `preconditions` entry MUST name a rule of kind `precondition` that the use case also cites.
provisions.rationale: An authorization condition the behavior leaves unstated lives in prose beside the definition. Each definition restates it, and the copies drift from the behavior they guard. Naming a precondition rule the use case already cites keeps one rule with one refusal.
provisions.example: Claimwick approve-expense names `rule/expense.approver-is-not-submitter` in `preconditions`. The rule is kind `precondition`, the use case cites it in its steps, and a refused call ends in the rule refusal.

provisions.heading: Name the Caller Identity of a Self Scope
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for `scope` without `identityInput` or `identityInput` without `scope`, for an identity input naming no input or carrying another origin, and for an identity input identifying no actor, and `reference-unknown` for an identity input whose `identifies` names no record.
provisions.statement: A use case declaring `scope: self` MUST name its caller-identity input in `identityInput`, with `origin: verified-claim` identifying an actor.
provisions.rationale: A scope without its identity input leaves the guard guessing which value is the caller. Handlers then compare their own field with the verified identity, and each comparison is authorization logic sitting in a handler. Naming the verified input beside the scope gives the guard the one value to compare the target with.
provisions.example: Claimwick list-expenses declares `scope: self` with `identityInput: employee`. The employee input carries `origin: verified-claim`, and a call lists that employee owned expenses alone.

provisions.heading: Record Every Role an Actor Holds
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `role-unused` for a role held by no actor, and `record-invalid` for a hold that is not a role identifier, such as a hold carrying a scope.
provisions.statement: An actor that acts through a role MUST list the role's identifier in `holds`.
provisions.rationale: The hold joins the actor to its grant. Without it, the actor and the role sit on separate pages with no stated connection, and no reviewer tells what the actor is allowed to do. The hold names the role alone, and the reach comes from the role scope. This follows decision/0055-state-each-access-scope-once and decision/0083-evaluate-access-in-one-order.
provisions.example:
```json
"holds": ["role/employee"]
```

provisions.heading: Scope Every Grant to Its Tenant Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a tenant scope outside own, cross, public, and none.
provisions.statement: Each access declaration MUST name its tenant scope as own, cross, public, or none.
provisions.rationale: The tenant scope bounds which tenant data the call touches. `own` stays inside the caller tenant, `cross` reaches across tenants, `public` works beyond tenant boundaries, and `none` touches no tenant data. Without the scope, a read inside one tenant and a read across all tenants look the same.
provisions.example: An expense report names `own`, and a staff search across tenants names `cross`. A public catalog names `public`, and a health check names `none`.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Role to Its One Reach
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a role without `scope` and `record-invalid` for a scope outside kebab-case form. A `scope` on a permission entry or on a hold fails the schema as an unknown property.
provisions.statement: A role MUST name its one scope in `scope`.
provisions.rationale: The same permission allows product-wide action in one grant and own-record action in another. The role scope decides what each grant reaches. Stating the reach on each hold or each permission as well keeps three copies of one value, and the copies drift apart.
provisions.example: A scope of `team` bounds the role to one team. A scope of `platform` bounds it to the whole product.

provisions.heading: State Every Permission with Its Meaning
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a permission without `meaning`.
provisions.statement: A permission MUST state what it allows in `meaning`.
provisions.rationale: The `meaning` is the one sentence a reviewer reads to judge the fit of a grant. A name alone carries no boundary. Two grants with the same name pattern and no meanings drift into overlapping grants no audit separates.
provisions.example: `permission/request-expense` carries the sentence on submitting an expense for reimbursement. The sentence draws the boundary the short name leaves open.

provisions.heading: Apply Guidance Precedence
provisions.evidence: Does the design apply the project waiver, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order? Check the design beside the overlapping guidance.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply the project waiver, the extension, the deeper page, and the shallower page in that order.
provisions.rationale: Overlapping guidance is normal: a project waiver narrows a shared provision, an extension replaces a baseline default, and a stack page refines its area page. Without a fixed order, two agents resolve the same overlap differently and the workspace drifts. The order puts the most local decision first, so the broader baseline fills the gaps it leaves.

provisions.heading: Check Your Own Change Before Handing It Back
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name the build, model check and analyzers run for the changed paths, each result, and the behavior the agent exercised? Check the report beside the changed paths and the commands it names.
provisions.statement: Before reporting done, an agent, including a worker under another agent, MUST run the narrowest build and model check for the paths it changed, let the configured analyzers run in that build, exercise each behavior change once as `litespec/core/agent#exercise-changed-use-cases-through-the-running-stack` states, and report each command with its result.
provisions.rationale: A worker handing back code without running its own narrow gates returns compile errors and failing checks for the caller to find. The caller then spends its review on mechanical failures instead of the change. Running the gates on the changed paths catches those failures where the context is freshest, and naming each command and result lets the caller see what actually ran.
provisions.example: After changing one Claimwick command handler, an agent builds the backend project, runs `litespec model check`, submits an expense through the seeded stack, and lists each command with its result in the completion report.

provisions.heading: Exercise Changed Use Cases Through the Running Stack
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name the seed, walker or direct call for each changed use case and what it showed, and does it call a build-only change unexercised? Look at the report beside the changed use cases.
provisions.statement: Before reporting done, an agent MUST exercise each use case the change affects through the running stack, by the seed, the API walker or a direct call, and state in the completion report what it ran and what it saw, reporting a change verified only by build as unexercised.
provisions.rationale: A build and a passing test show that code compiles and a chosen case passes, not that the endpoint, the handler and the screen agree at runtime. A change leaves an event with no handler, a command needing an id no read returns, or a screen reading less than it shows, and none of those fails a build. Running the changed use case on the seeded stack puts the whole path under the report evidence, and saying what ran and what was seen lets the owner tell an exercised change from a build-only one.
provisions.example: After changing Claimwick's submit-expense use case, an agent seeds the client-visit scenario, calls the endpoint with Ava's 48.90 EUR fare and reads the approval list back, then reports the request and the returned expense in its completion report. An agent running only `dotnet build` reports the change as unexercised.

provisions.heading: Follow the Record, Not the Neighbour
provisions.evidence: Does each new code shape trace to a record and its provisions, with the neighbour used only for style and each contradiction reported? Check the change beside the cited records and the neighbours it read.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST shape new code from the record and the provisions, use a neighbouring file only for style, and follow the record and report the neighbour when the two contradict.
provisions.rationale: A neighbouring file shows the names and idioms this project chose, but it carries an older or local rule. Copying it spreads one rule into several homes, and the copies drift from the record. The neighbour is not authority: the record is decided Intent, and a contradiction is a defect for the owner to see.
provisions.example: A Claimwick handler's neighbour reads a rate from configuration while the rule record cites dated reference data. The agent reads the rate from the cited reference data and reports the neighbour as out of date.

provisions.heading: Inspect Existing Work Before Editing
provisions.evidence: Does `git status` output precede the edits, with user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output untouched? Check the session log beside the working tree.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST read `git status` before editing and preserve user changes, untracked files, and unrelated generated output.
provisions.rationale: A working tree carries the user's own uncommitted edits, untracked files, and generated output from an unrelated task. An agent editing without looking overwrites or deletes work outside its scope. Reading `git status` first marks that work as untouchable.

provisions.heading: Inspect Local Examples After Standards
provisions.evidence: Does the change name the neighboring files shaping it after the standards? Check the change beside its neighbors.
provisions.statement: Inspect neighboring consumer files after loading applicable standards.
provisions.rationale: Standards state the needed shape, while neighboring files show the names, folders, and idioms this project chose for it. An agent skipping them writes compliant but foreign-looking code that the next edit rewrites.

provisions.heading: Keep Agent Working Files Under Agents
provisions.evidence: Does every agent working file sit under `.agents/` or the path the working-files convention names? Check the working files beside the convention.
provisions.statement: Keep agent working files under `.agents/`, with tracked `skills/` and `records/` folders and ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.rationale: Agent work with no agreed home lands beside authored records, where it pollutes review, or vanishes with the session, where nobody audits it. The split keeps durable work in `skills/` and `records/` and machine-local work in the ignored `scratch/` and `delegate/` folders.
provisions.example:
```text
.agents/
  skills/
  records/
  delegate/
  scratch/
```

provisions.heading: Keep the Agent Protocol Current
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `agent-protocol-drift` (level S) when the region differs from what `render` would write, `agent-protocol-missing` (level S) when `AGENTS.md` holds no region, and `skill-drift` (level S) when a project-scope skill copy differs from what the carried release generates.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep its agent protocol region and its project-scope skill copies equal to what its LiteSpec release generates.
provisions.rationale: The region carries the commands and rules every session loads first. A stale region points agents at an old release, an old selection, or commands that changed, while the tool output stays current. The project-scope skill copies carry the same procedure to tools loading skills on demand, and a stale copy points at the same old release. Settled by decision/0037-generate-the-agent-protocol and decision/0039-ship-a-litespec-skill.
provisions.example: Claimwick upgrades its LiteSpec release and runs `litespec model render`. The region in its `AGENTS.md` and its project-scope skill copies match what the new release generates.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Extensions
provisions.evidence: Does the change name each extension loaded before editing inside its boundary? Check the change record beside the extensions the project selects.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST load selected project extensions and selected applicable local extensions before editing code or prose inside the extension's boundary.
provisions.rationale: An extension replaces baseline guidance inside its boundary. An agent editing there without loading the extension follows the baseline the extension replaced, and the change contradicts the project's own selection.
provisions.example: A change to the cached catalog reads the selected caching extension before touching the code its boundary covers.

provisions.heading: Load Applicable Provisions Before Editing
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report answer every judgment provision `litespec rules --since <base>` listed? Compare the rules output with the report.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST run `litespec rules <path>` before editing a file and answer each judgment provision `litespec rules --since <base>` lists before reporting done.
provisions.rationale: Provisions stay usable only where retrieved by situation: the query prints the record's contract card first, then what governs the change, grouped by strength, with project conventions and waivers merged in. Checked provisions collapse into one summary line that `litespec rules <...> --all` expands, and `litespec rules <...> --full` adds rationale and example where a statement is short for the reader. Settled by decision/0125-deliver-standards-through-five-agent-layers.
provisions.example: `litespec rules use-case/spending.submit-expense` prints the use case's contract card first, then the provisions governing the change, grouped by strength.

provisions.heading: Make Coherent Scoped Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every changed artifact trace to the authorized request? Check the changed files beside the task text.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST make the smallest coherent change that satisfies the authorized request.
provisions.rationale: A change stopping at code and skipping its records, tests, or operating evidence leaves the workspace claiming behavior nothing proves. A change sprawling past the request drags unrelated files into review. The smallest coherent change keeps the records, code, tests, and evidence belonging together in one reviewable unit.

provisions.heading: Name Judged Provisions in the Completion Report
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name every judged provision with its judgment? Check the report beside the provisions the query returned.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name each provision the agent judged and how it judged it.
provisions.rationale: The report shows which binding provisions, defaults, and advisory provisions the change met and the judgment for each, so the owner checks the reasoning without re-reading the change. A provision the query returned but the report skips is a judgment nobody checks.
provisions.example: The report names each returned provision with its judgment: followed, replaced by a named convention, or parked by a waiver.

provisions.heading: Protect Proofs from Implementation Edits
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check --since <ref>` reports `proof-hash-drift` (level S) for each scenario whose proving test method changed since the base while the scenario did not.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST NOT delete, skip, or weaken a test that proves a scenario, or change its expected values, unless the scenario changed in the same change; it reports a test it believes is wrong instead of editing it.
provisions.rationale: A proof changing with the implementation stops proving the decided behavior and starts restating the code. The proof ledger records each scenario's hash and the hash of each test proving it, so `model check --since` reports, as a blocking finding, each scenario whose proving test changed while the scenario stayed put. Settled by decision/0033-agents-never-weaken-proving-tests.
provisions.example: A handler change makes a proving test fail. The agent reports the failing test and the mismatch instead of changing the expected value to fit the new result.

provisions.heading: Raise a Spec Gap Instead of Bending the Code
provisions.evidence: Does each forced shape the agent met have a named concept and an owner question with a recommendation or a backlog item, with no code written around it? Check the completion report beside the gap and the code.
provisions.statement: When a check, a record type, or a provision forces a shape the domain does not have, an agent MUST stop, name the missing concept, and raise it as an owner question with a recommendation or a backlog item instead of writing code around it.
provisions.rationale: A check accepting a rate table only as an external system, or a refusal with no record to hold it, pushes the agent to a substitute shape. The substitute compiles and passes the check while the real concept stays unmodelled, so the next agent copies it and the gap spreads. A missing concept is an open need: it travels up as a question to the owner with a recommendation or as a backlog item, and the agent writes no code around it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's checks accept the per-diem rate table only as an external system, but the rates are figures the business changes while the system runs. The agent stops, names the missing concept of dated reference data, and raises a question to the owner with a recommendation instead of adding an external port the domain lacks.

provisions.heading: Read the Full Record Before Changing a Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does each file generation or boundary change cite the full record it matched? Check the change beside the cited records.
provisions.statement: Read the full record, the record file with its explanation file, before generating a file, changing a public boundary, or choosing between patterns.
provisions.rationale: Generating a file or changing a public boundary from a summary risks baking a paraphrase into a contract. The full record carries the exact fields, links, and wording the new surface matches. A small edit following an existing local pattern leans on neighboring code instead.

provisions.heading: Replace Only Declared Conventions
provisions.evidence: Does each convention replacement resolve to a recorded local convention? Check the replacements beside the project documentation.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST apply a replacement for a convention only when the project documentation records that replacement.
provisions.rationale: Conventions exist to be replaced, but only through a recorded decision. An undocumented local preference silently replacing a baseline default reads exactly like a mistake, so the next agent fixes it back. The recorded convention keeps the replacement visible and reviewable.

provisions.heading: Restrict Unapproved Side Effects
provisions.evidence: Does an explicit task instruction naming the action and its bounds cover each consequential action beyond the task, or does the project's `AGENTS.md` grant the wider authority? Check the task text beside the actions taken.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stay inside its authorized task and take no consequential action beyond it without an explicit task instruction that names the action and its bounds.
provisions.rationale: Inside the task, the agent applies an approved standard or decision, drafts records and proposed decisions, implements the change, and reports findings, including a failed check or a conflict between provisions. It approves no product-policy proposal of its own, widens no scope, invents no business value, and takes no consequential outside action beyond the task. Packages, migrations, authentication, a public API, production data, releases, spending, and outside calls changing state each need an explicit task instruction naming the action and its bounds, because none of them follows from the task text alone. Settled by decision/0086-set-one-agent-authority-boundary.
provisions.example: A task naming the migration and its scope approves it. A task silent on releases leaves a release unmade.

provisions.heading: Review Changed Use Cases from an Independent Packet
provisions.evidence: `litespec audit semantic` writes the packet of each changed use case and reports `code-unimplemented` for a changed line outside the tests that still holds a stub marker.
provisions.statement: A change to a use case SHOULD get a semantic review by a reader other than its author, working from the use case packet that holds the record, its judgment provisions, its neighbours and the changed code.
provisions.rationale: The author of a change checks it against what the author meant, so a rule that never fires, a wrong unit, or a screen that skips a permission passes the author's own review. A second reader working from the record and the changed code alone sees the change as the specification states it.
provisions.example: After a change to Claimwick's submit-expense handler, `litespec audit semantic --since main` writes the submit-expense packet, and a second agent reads it and reports that the receipt threshold rule is never consulted for foreign-currency expenses.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Convention to Files It Governs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `convention-unreached` (level G) for a project convention whose Applies to matches no file in the project tree and no record.
provisions.statement: A project convention MUST state an Applies to that matches at least one file in the project tree or one record the project writes.
provisions.rationale: `rules` returns a convention only where its Applies to meets the queried path or record. A convention meeting nothing reaches no agent, so its rule stays unread while the project believes it is stated. One match keeps every stated convention live.
provisions.example: Claimwick records that every command handler logs its outcome, with `stack: dotnet; artifact: command-handler`. The convention meets each handler file, so `rules` returns it before an agent edits one.

provisions.heading: Search the Provisions Before Recording a Decision
provisions.evidence: Does any technical decision restate a choice a provision already makes? Compare each decision with the `rules` output for its subject.
provisions.statement: Query `litespec rules` for the decision's subject, and where a provision makes the choice, follow that provision instead of recording a decision.
provisions.rationale: Many technical choices are already decided: a provision names the shape, the baseline, or the boundary the code follows. A decision restating such a choice splits authority between the provision and the record, and the two drift. Searching first keeps one home for each decided choice.
provisions.example: An agent about to record how Claimwick declares integration edges queries `litespec rules` for the subject. The provision declares every edge in a record, so the code follows it and no decision is recorded.

provisions.heading: Select Task Context
provisions.evidence: Does the completion report name the model query that selected the cited records, or the prose-only correction and the record it read? Check the report beside the cited records.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST query the project model for the records that cover the request, and read the query output, before changing behavior, access, a contract, or a trace link; a prose-only correction of an existing record needs only the record and its explanation file.
provisions.rationale: Without the query, an agent reads too little and invents the missing rules, or reads half the repository and buries the task in unrelated guidance. The query returns the smallest record set covering the request, with the links the builder joined between records, so the agent starts from decided Intent. A prose-only correction of an existing record needs no joined links: the record and its explanation file show the decided shape, and a query slows ordinary work without adding information. Settled by decision/0086-set-one-agent-authority-boundary.
provisions.example: `litespec model query use-case/spending.submit-expense` returns the use case with its rules, results, and scenarios. A spelling fix in a setting record reads the record and its explanation file, then edits without querying the model.

provisions.heading: Stop on Unresolved Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does the stopped work quote the conflict with both provision IDs and paths? Check the handoff beside the disagreeing provisions.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST stop when applicable provisions disagree without declared precedence and quote both provision IDs and paths.
provisions.rationale: Where two provisions disagree and no precedence decides, any continuation invents a compromise neither provision states. Stopping with both provision identifiers and paths hands the decision to a person with exactly the evidence the decision needs.

provisions.heading: Write Only Rules You Have Seen Hold
provisions.evidence: Does every rule the agent added to the agent file name the run or observation that showed it hold, with none written from assumption? Look at the added lines beside the session log.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST write a rule into the project's agent file only after seeing that rule hold, and a rule about a library's behavior only after running the library.
provisions.rationale: A rule in the agent file reads as decided guidance on every later task, so a guess about how a library behaves turns into an instruction every later agent follows. Running the behavior first gives the rule the evidence the agent names, and leaving an unverified rule out keeps the file to what the project knows.
provisions.example: Before adding a line to Claimwick's `AGENTS.md` about how its orchestrator starts the stack, an agent runs the start command and sees the hosts come up. It leaves out a line about a library's behavior until it has run that library and seen the result.

provisions.heading: Audit Only Selected Commands
provisions.evidence: Does every audited category carry a recorded selection reason? Check the declared selection.
provisions.statement: A project MUST NOT audit every Command without a recorded selection.
provisions.rationale: Volume defeats review. A trail recording every command buries the sensitive action among routine traffic, and the reviewer stops reading. A recorded selection keeps the trail small enough to read.

provisions.heading: Commit a Success Record with Its Business Change
provisions.evidence: Does every succeeded record commit inside its business transaction? Check the success write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `succeeded` outcome MUST commit in the same database transaction as the change it describes.
provisions.rationale: One transaction makes the action and its evidence inseparable. The change commits with its record or neither commits. Separate writes admit both an unrecorded action and a record of a rolled-back action.

provisions.heading: Correct Mistakes with a New Record
provisions.evidence: Is every correction a new record that points at the earlier one? Check the correction records.
provisions.statement: A correction to the trail MUST be a new record that references the earlier one.
provisions.rationale: An edited history carries no evidential value. A reviewer tells a correction from a cover-up only when both stay visible. The new record keeps the mistake and the fix side by side.

provisions.heading: Declare Which Commands Are Audited
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `audit-missing` for a command with neither an audit position nor an exemption, `record-invalid` for an audited command without its category, `audit-target-missing` for an audited command changing a record with no target, `audit-target-unknown` for a target naming no input, an input with no `identifies`, or no output field, and `audit-target-kind-drift` for a target kind differing from what a single target input identifies.
provisions.statement: Every command use case MUST declare its audit position in its `audit` field, or declare an exemption with its justification.
provisions.rationale: A selection living in code stays invisible. The `audit` field turns each omission into a visible statement, so a reader tells an unaudited command from an audited one with a missing call. The target ties the record to the data the command changes.
provisions.example: A Claimwick command listing public help pages carries an exemption with its justification. Reading public text is outside the sensitive set, and the exemption says so on the record.

provisions.heading: Delete Expired Records Through a Separate Operator Account
provisions.evidence: Does all retention deletion and tenant data erasure run through the operator process under its own account? Check the deletion job and the granted store privileges.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST run retention deletion and tenant data erasure through a separate audited operator process under its own account.
provisions.rationale: The application account holds no deletion privilege, so retention deletion needs a second account. The operator process holds `DELETE` under its own account and writes one deletion record per deleted segment. Tenant data erasure runs through the same process, so no application path deletes audit data. This follows decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps sign-in denials for two years and expense records for seven. A nightly operator job deletes the closed segments past retention and writes one deletion record per deleted segment, while the application account keeps `INSERT` and `SELECT` alone.

provisions.heading: Enforce Append-Only Through Storage Privilege
provisions.evidence: Does any account except the operator deletion account hold update or delete on the audit store? Check the granted store privileges.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST refuse update and delete through the privileges granted to every account except the operator account that deletes expired records.
provisions.rationale: Absent code paths stay absent until someone writes them. Revoked privileges refuse the write no matter what the code tries. A reviewer verifies a privilege in the database instead of auditing each line for a write that is absent.
provisions.example: The application account holds `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the audit table, with neither `UPDATE` nor `DELETE`. The operator account holds `INSERT` and `DELETE` on the same table and writes through the deletion job alone.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets and Payment Data from the Trail
provisions.evidence: Does any stored record contain a secret or a payment instrument value? Check the stored audit rows.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST NOT contain a secret, as `litespec/quality/security#keep-secrets-out-of-tracked-and-observable-data` states, or a payment instrument value.
provisions.rationale: The trail is retained, widely readable, and append-only. That combination extends exposure and removes repair: a credential written once stays readable for the whole retention period. Secrets and payment values travel in the systems built to hold them.

provisions.heading: Record Each Segment Deletion in the Following Segment
provisions.evidence: Does every deleted segment have its deletion record in the following segment? Check the deletion records against the retention schedule.
provisions.statement: An audit deployment MUST record each deleted chain segment as an audit record in the following segment of the same category.
provisions.rationale: A deleted segment leaves no rows. The deletion record in the following segment states which segment went with its count and final checkpoint. The following year segment is still live, so it holds the record. This follows decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year.
provisions.example: Deleting the 2026 sign-in denial segment writes one record into the 2027 denial segment. The record names the deleted segment with its count and final checkpoint.

provisions.heading: Record Every Attempt Outcome
provisions.evidence: Does every record carry a `succeeded`, `denied`, or `failed` outcome? Check the outcome column.
provisions.statement: An audit record MUST carry an outcome of `succeeded`, `denied`, or `failed`.
provisions.rationale: Successes alone show a change history. Refusals carry the security signal and failures carry the operating signal, and three outcomes hold both beside the successes. A validation refusal records `failed` with its refusal code, while `denied` stays for refused authorization.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, an expense refused for a missing receipt records `failed` with the receipt refusal code. An approval by someone lacking the permission records `denied` with the forbidden code.

provisions.heading: Record Refused Authorization
provisions.evidence: Does every refused authorization produce a denied record? Check the refusal paths beside the trail.
provisions.statement: An authorization decision that refuses an audited action MUST produce an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Repeated refusal is the first indicator of a compromised or probing account. Nothing else holds it: the change went nowhere, so nothing else was written. Each refusal writes its own record, so the trail shows an attacker who failed.

provisions.heading: Record the Audit Adoption Decision
provisions.evidence: Does the adoption decision behind the audited Commands name its categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, and records entry? Check that decision record.
provisions.statement: An audit adoption decision MUST record its audited categories, threshold, access model, integrity method, and records entry.
provisions.rationale: Policy choices belong in one declared place. A reviewer reads the declared policy and then reads the implementation against it, so two reviewers start from the same statement. The records entry fixes where the evidence lives, including the split between the tenant trail and the global trail.

provisions.heading: Scope Every Record to Its Tenant
provisions.evidence: Is every record scoped to the right trail, with tenant data carrying its tenant identity and authentication events in the global trail? Check the tenant column and the global trail.
provisions.statement: Every audit record MUST carry the scope it belongs to: an action inside tenant-owned data carries the identity of that tenant, and an authentication event that belongs to no tenant lives in the global trail apart from tenant activity.
provisions.rationale: The tenant is the filter for each read of the trail. Scoping each record at write time keeps that filter exact. Authentication events belong to no tenant, so the global trail holds sign-in evidence apart from tenant data.

provisions.heading: Segment the Audit Chain by Category and Calendar Year
provisions.evidence: Does every audit record sit in the segment of its category and year, with its own genesis and checkpoints? Check the stored chain values.
provisions.statement: An audit store MUST hold one hash chain segment per audited category and calendar year, each with its own genesis record and checkpoints.
provisions.rationale: Deleting one category from a shared chain breaks each later link. One segment per category and year lets the deployment delete a whole closed segment while the rest still verify from their own anchors. The segment closes with a final checkpoint before deletion. This follows decision/0097-one-audit-chain-segment-per-category-and-year.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds its 2026 sign-in denials in one segment. When the two years end, the deployment deletes that segment whole, and the expense segments verify from their own genesis records.

provisions.heading: Write an Unsuccessful Record Outside the Failed Transaction
provisions.evidence: Does any denied or failed record roll back with its transaction? Check the unsuccessful write path.
provisions.statement: An audit record with a `denied` or `failed` outcome MUST be written on a connection that the failing transaction does not roll back.
provisions.rationale: A denied or failed attempt ends with its transaction rolling back. A record inside that transaction rolls back with it and vanishes. The separate connection keeps the evidence of a refusal past the rollback.

provisions.heading: Attach Examples to Their Provisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_EXAMPLE_LABEL`, `PAGE_UNKNOWN_SECTION`, or `REFERENCE_EXAMPLE_DECLARATION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An informative example MUST belong to its provision or to a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates.
provisions.rationale: An example outside its provision reads as a second rule, and readers follow the illustration instead of the obligation. Sitting inside its provision, or inside a Reference Example that names every provision it demonstrates, marks it as illustration.

provisions.heading: End Each Provision with One Verification Line
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `VERIFY_MISSING_ID`, `VERIFY_DUPLICATE_ID`, `VERIFY_ORDER`, or `VERIFY_HEADER` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST end its fields with exactly one verification line.
provisions.rationale: A provision with no verification line is a rule nobody checks. Each team assumes a tool covers it, while no tool does. One line per provision, beside the rule it checks, makes each rule reviewable by a person or a tool.

provisions.heading: Exclude Cross-Release Compatibility Work
provisions.evidence: Does any page promise migration, mapping, or alias between releases? Check the release material the change adds.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec repository MUST NOT publish a compatibility guarantee, migration path, deprecation period, or identifier alias between its own releases.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec is a pinned contract, not a running service: consumers adopt a release whole, on their own schedule. Compatibility guarantees, migration paths, deprecation periods, and identifier aliases between LiteSpec releases promise a continuity the model never offers. A consumer product keeps its own API compatibility, migration, deprecation, and rollback provisions for its own users.

provisions.heading: Exclude Historical Transition Material
provisions.evidence: Does any active file carry history-specific paths, aliases, or migration material? Check the files the change adds.
provisions.statement: Current standards material MUST NOT contain history-specific paths, IDs, terms, aliases, replacement maps, release migration material, compatibility rules, or transition checks other than the generated provision identifier list in the changelog.
provisions.rationale: A snapshot that carries aliases, maps, migration notes, or transition checks for other releases forces each reader to learn releases never pinned. The published snapshot states its own contract and nothing else. An extension's `Baseline Relationship` section names a provision it replaces inside this release, which is a current replacement rather than history. The changelog's generated list of added, removed, and renamed provision identifiers states a fact about the release it ships in; it offers no alias, mapping, or migration path, so it stands as the single exception this provision allows.

provisions.heading: Generate the Provision Diff for Each Release
provisions.evidence: Was any changelog identifier typed by hand, or does any name an identifier that comparing the two provision indexes does not produce? Check the changelog entry against the provision index at the previous tag and the provision index of the release.
provisions.statement: The changelog for each LiteSpec release MUST list the provision identifiers the release adds, removes, and renames, generated from the provision index at the previous tag and the provision index of the release.
provisions.rationale: A consumer cites provision identifiers in code marks, records, and waivers. A release that removes or renames an identifier without naming it leaves every citation pointing at nothing, with no way to find what changed. The generated list states a fact about the release it ships in and nothing more: it carries no alias, no replacement map, and no migration path, and no provision depends on an earlier release to state its own contract. The list derives from the two provision indexes, so a tool generates it; a list typed by hand goes stale with the next provision edit. This provision is the exception to `litespec/core/authoring#exclude-historical-transition-material`, and it extends to no other history material.
provisions.example: `litespec-maintain changelog --from v3.0.0` writes the list into the changelog entry for a release, with `litespec/core/scope#claim-the-record-layers-the-project-uses` under Added when that provision first ships, and a major release lists each identifier it removes or renames under Removed and Renamed in the same entry.

provisions.heading: Keep Authored Prose ASCII-Safe
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PROSE_NON_ASCII` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST contain only ASCII unless code, data, or mathematical content requires another character.
provisions.rationale: A curly quote renders in one reader and breaks in another: terminals, diffs, generated context, and plain-text tools each handle non-ASCII characters differently, and a character that is unreadable in one is a silent mismatch in another. ASCII prose renders the same everywhere the standard is read or checked.
provisions.example: Use a hyphen or a comma instead of a typographic dash.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Standard to One Obligation
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `STANDARD_LABEL_INVALID`, `STANDARD_LABEL_ORDER`, `STANDARD_LABEL_DUPLICATE`, `STANDARD_MISSING_DEVIATION`, `STANDARD_UNEXPECTED_DEVIATION`, `STANDARD_MISSING_REQUIREMENT`, `STANDARD_REQUIREMENT_COUNT`, or `STANDARD_UNLABELED_CONTENT` diagnostic, and reports `STANDARD_SENTENCE_COUNT`, `STANDARD_MODAL_COUNT`, `STANDARD_MODAL_VOCABULARY`, `STANDARD_DEVIATION_NORMATIVE`, `STANDARD_DEVIATION_SENTENCE`, and `PROVISION_RESTATES_HEADING` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST follow the Standard contract this page defines.
provisions.rationale: One provision with one obligation has one authority, one identifier, and one verification line. A provision that bundles two obligations leaves a project half-compliant, with no identifier for the half it missed.
provisions.example: `### Keep Business Invariants in Domain` owns one obligation about where invariants are enforced.

provisions.heading: Keep Identifiers Out of Provision Headings
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_IN_HEADING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision heading MUST carry no identifier text.
provisions.rationale: The page path with the heading already states the identifier. An identifier written into the heading repeats it at best; at worst, a rename touches one and misses the other, and the two contradict each other.

provisions.heading: Keep Prose Paragraphs Short and Plain
provisions.evidence: Does every prose paragraph stay at or under 120 words and avoid the LiteSpec-ese and promotional phrases the Style Card lists? Check the paragraphs of each page the change adds.
provisions.statement: A prose paragraph MUST stay at or under 120 words while using no phrase the Style Card in WRITING.md lists as LiteSpec-ese or promotional.
provisions.rationale: A wall of prose hides the obligation inside it: a scanning reader skips the paragraph and misses the rule. Short paragraphs put each fact where that reader finds it, and plain words keep a check and a reader on the same text. The Style Card lists the phrases that mark LiteSpec-ese and promotion, so the check names the same list.
provisions.example: A Claimwick guide states the three-day reminder rule in three short sentences, with the waiting claim, the day count, and the next step each in its own sentence.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Provision as Checked or Reviewed
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `VERIFY_MISSING_ID` for a provision whose verification line opens with any other label.
provisions.statement: A verification line MUST open with `Checked by` for a provision a tool checks or `Reviewed for` for one a person judges.
provisions.rationale: The label tells a reader who judges the provision: a tool (`checkable`) or a person (`guidance`). Without the label, a team automates a judgment call or hand-reviews what a command already proves.

provisions.heading: Match Strength to the Modal Word
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` confirms each Standards provision carries the modal its Strength line grades.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST use the modal word its Strength line grades.
provisions.rationale: The Strength line grades how binding a provision is. The modal in its Statement says the same thing in words: a required provision obliges with must or must not, while an advisory one advises with should, should not, or may. When the two disagree, each reader picks the reading that suits the change, and the grade means nothing. A lone permission reads as optional advice under a required label, so a permission joins the provision it relaxes or becomes an obligation of its own. Settled by [decision/0082-give-every-rule-one-home-and-one-strength](decision/0082-give-every-rule-one-home-and-one-strength).
provisions.example: A required provision states with must that a use case declares its kind, while an advisory provision suggests a naming shape with should.

provisions.heading: Name Observable Evidence in Verification Lines
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `VERIFY_COMMAND` or `CHECKED_BY_UNKNOWN` diagnostic, and reports `VERIFY_GENERIC_EVIDENCE`, `VERIFY_TEMPLATED_EVIDENCE`, and `VERIFY_DUPLICATE_EVIDENCE` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A verification line MUST name the observable evidence and where the reviewer looks.
provisions.rationale: A line that restates its Statement gives the reviewer nothing to check beyond the rule's own words. Naming the artifact and its location turns the line into an instruction the reviewer follows.

provisions.heading: Name the Owning Page in the Identifier
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_PAGE_FILENAME` or `ID_DUPLICATE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision ID's page segment MUST be its page's path under `docs/` without the `.md` extension.
provisions.rationale: The page segment is both the file a reader opens and the address the provision carries on the published site. Deriving it from the path keeps the identifier and the file from disagreeing.
provisions.example: `litespec/core/backend-architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case` and `litespec/core/backend-application#organize-application-by-use-case` are on two different pages.

provisions.heading: Open Each Page with a Lead
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `PAGE_LEAD_MISSING` for a page with no paragraph between its title and its first H2.
provisions.statement: Every documentation page MUST open with a lead of one or more paragraphs between its title and its first H2 that tells the reader what the subject is and why it matters to them.
provisions.rationale: A reader who arrives from a link reads the lead first and decides from it whether the page answers the question. A lead that states the subject helps that reader; a summary of the page's headings adds nothing, and the headings already show the outline. The lead takes no heading of its own, so the page starts with its answer.
provisions.example: The model page opens with "A LiteSpec project describes itself with records" and the problem the records solve, then goes straight to its sections.

provisions.heading: Order Glossary Groups Alphabetically
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `GLOSSARY_ORDER` diagnostic and reports `GLOSSARY_DEFINITION` as a warning.
provisions.statement: Glossary groups MUST stand in alphabetical order, each opening with one intro sentence.
provisions.rationale: A reader guesses where a term lives before reading any term. Alphabetical groups put each term where that guess expects it, and the opening sentence gives each group its shared context. An unordered group hides its terms from a reader who looks in the wrong place, and a group without its sentence opens with terms that share no stated context.
provisions.example: The code, product, and standard term groups open the glossary in that order, each with one sentence saying what its terms name.

provisions.heading: Place Each Stack Binding on Its Stack Page
provisions.evidence: Does any shared page carry a stack-specific section? Check the shared pages the change touches for stack sections.
provisions.statement: A stack-specific section MUST live on its stack page rather than on a shared page.
provisions.rationale: A reader following one stack finds its detail in one place. Each stack page carries its own bindings, and shared pages stay neutral across stacks.

provisions.heading: Place the ID Under Every Provision Heading
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_LINE_MISSING` or `ID_LINE_MISMATCH` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Every provision heading MUST be followed by an ID line holding the provision's identity.
provisions.rationale: A reader who cites a provision copies its ID from where the provision stands, instead of deriving a slug by hand or looking it up elsewhere. The ID line is the identity: a heading changes without changing it, so an ID line that reads differently from its heading still holds.
provisions.example: `### Compose Each Route from One Locked Archetype` on `docs/core/ui-ia.md` is followed by the ID line `litespec/core/ui-ia#compose-each-route-from-one-locked-archetype`.

provisions.heading: Prefer Direct Action Headings
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `HEADING_ACTION` as a warning.
provisions.statement: Start a Standard or Convention heading with a concrete action verb.

provisions.heading: Publish Each Release as a Complete Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` checks every page of the release in one run, and the manifest names one version for the whole contract.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec release MUST state every active provision without depending on an earlier release.
provisions.rationale: A consumer pins one snapshot and reads it as the whole obligation. If a release depended on another, the consumer pins and reads two contracts to know either. Stating every active provision in each release keeps one snapshot sufficient.

provisions.heading: Record the Reviewed LiteSpec Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `release-drift` when `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` names no release or a release other than the installed tool release.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record the LiteSpec release it adopts in `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` within `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: A provision gains force while keeping its ID. Without a recorded release, a waiver written against one release applies to a rule nobody reread. Recording the adopted release in `reviewedLiteSpecVersion` makes adoption an explicit act and tells each reader which contract the project reviewed.

provisions.heading: Regenerate the Provision Index
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain provisions --check` exits zero.
provisions.statement: A standards change MUST leave `docs/reference/provisions.md` equal to the output of `litespec-maintain provisions`.
provisions.rationale: One generated page resolves each identifier to its heading and page, so a reader follows a citation in one step. It also carries each provision's scope and strength, so the CLI reads one file instead of parsing every page. Regenerating it with `litespec-maintain provisions` on every standards change keeps the index and the pages from disagreeing.

provisions.heading: Restrict Normative Language to Standards and Conventions
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `PROSE_NORMATIVE_LOCATION` and `STANDARD_INFORMATIVE_NORMATIVE` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A capitalized modal MUST appear only in a Statement, a Default, or a Replacement.
provisions.rationale: When an obligation sits in Concepts, a Rationale, or an example, a project misses it because the labeled assertions never state it. One location for each modal lets readers and tools find each obligation in the same place. A prohibition written as `cannot` and a rule written as `never` belong in the same labels.

provisions.heading: Route the Reader Before Listing Pages
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `INDEX_MISSING_ROUTING` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A documentation root index MUST state which page style answers which reader question before its first navigation group.
provisions.rationale: Without a mapping from question to page, a reader guesses which page answers the question. Naming each style in the reader's terms before the first navigation group sends each question to the page that answers it.
provisions.example: A `Which Page Do You Want` section names each style in the reader's terms, one sentence each.

provisions.heading: Run Repeatable Authoring Checks
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate`, `dotnet test --solution LiteSpec.slnx` and `git diff --check` exit zero.
provisions.statement: A standards change MUST pass the repository validator, the test suite, and `git diff --check`.
provisions.rationale: Structure, behavior, and whitespace each need their own check: the repository validator, the test suite, and `git diff --check` each catch what the others miss. Passing all three on every standards change keeps the standard checkable by anyone who runs the same commands. Diagnostics that judge wording print as warnings and fail no run; every other diagnostic fails it. The tools check each schema with LiteSpec's own evaluator, so running them needs no paid license, settled by [decision/0022-own-schema-evaluator](decision/0022-own-schema-evaluator) on the evidence in [research/schema-evaluator-evidence](research/schema-evaluator-evidence). The change report lists each skipped check with its reason. The [command index](../tools/README.md) and the [maintainer index](../maintain/README.md) name each check and its command. Settled by [decision/0035-bind-docs-to-tools-and-example](decision/0035-bind-docs-to-tools-and-example), which checks each tool fact the pages cite against the tools' own data.

provisions.heading: State One Tier per Page
provisions.evidence: Does any command page mix mechanism into sections outside Underneath? Check outside the Underneath section of each command page the change touches.
provisions.statement: A page MUST NOT describe both a command and the mechanism that command runs, outside an `Underneath` section.
provisions.rationale: A reader who wanted the command reads mechanism detail as noise, and a reader who wanted the mechanism reads the command wrapper as an obstacle. One tier per page serves each reader, and the `Underneath` section holds the mechanism for the reader who asks for it.

provisions.heading: State What the Command Runs Underneath
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_MISSING_SECTION` diagnostic for a command page.
provisions.statement: A command page MUST state under `Underneath` what the command runs or the sentence `Nothing beneath this command is separately runnable.`.
provisions.rationale: When a command fails, the reader needs a command to run by hand and a tier to inspect. A command that states nothing beneath it leaves them with neither. Stating what the command runs, or that nothing beneath it is separately runnable, gives every failure a next step.
provisions.example: A command with nothing separately runnable writes `Nothing beneath this command is separately runnable.` under `Underneath`.

provisions.heading: Use Controlled Capitalization
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `PAGE_TITLE_CASE` and `PAGE_HEADING_CASE` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A page MUST use Title Case for its title and every heading.
provisions.rationale: A reader meets titles and headings in indexes, tabs, and search results, where they read as names. One casing rule keeps them uniform there. Title Case capitalizes every word except articles (`a`, `an`, `the`), coordinating conjunctions (`and`, `but`, `for`, `nor`, `or`, `so`, `yet`), and prepositions of four letters or fewer (`as`, `at`, `by`, `for`, `from`, `in`, `into`, `of`, `off`, `on`, `onto`, `over`, `per`, `to`, `up`, `upon`, `via`, `with`); the first and last words stay capitalized, and code, identifiers, and file names keep their own case.

provisions.heading: Use One Normative Vocabulary
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `STANDARD_MODAL_COUNT` and `STANDARD_MODAL_VOCABULARY` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A Standards provision MUST use exactly one listed capitalized modal and no other capitalized normative term.
provisions.rationale: A reader decides from one word whether a provision obliges or suggests. That works only when each strength word means exactly one thing, as the listed modals do under their RFC meaning. A second capitalized term adds a shade of obligation no contract defines.

provisions.heading: Use One Term for One Concept
provisions.evidence: Does every concept in the change go by one name? Check the terms the change adds against the glossary.
provisions.statement: Authored prose MUST name each concept with its one glossary term.
provisions.rationale: When one concept carries two names, each reader looks for a distinction the writer never meant. One term per concept means each term is defined once and checked once. Settled by [decision/0018-one-record-language](decision/0018-one-record-language) on the evidence in [research/naming-grammar-evidence](research/naming-grammar-evidence).

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Identifier Grammar
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` or `ID_DUPLICATE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision ID MUST be `litespec/<page>#<slug>` as its ID line states it.
provisions.rationale: The page segment names the file and the ID line states the slug, so a citation resolves with no lookup table. One grammar keeps each identifier writable by hand and checkable by tool. The ID line is the identity: a reworded heading leaves it unchanged, and no two provisions share one.
provisions.example: `litespec/core/ui-ia#compose-each-route-from-one-locked-archetype` is the ID line under its heading on the user interface information architecture page.

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Page Contract
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_MISSING_SECTION`, `PAGE_SECTION_ORDER` or `PAGE_UNKNOWN_SECTION` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An authored page MUST use the sections, in order, of its page style.
provisions.rationale: Readers learn the page shape once and tools find each section without guessing, because the authority, the context, the defaults, and the evidence sit in the same place on every page. A page that invents its own order forces readers and tools to search. A record file carries its type's fields in canonical key order instead of sections.

provisions.heading: Validate Each Template Against the Record Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `TEMPLATE_SCHEMA` diagnostic, and `litespec model check` reports `template-value-unchanged` on a scaffold that keeps a copied value.
provisions.statement: Each record template in `templates/consumer/` MUST satisfy `schemas/record.schema.yaml` with a placeholder value in every field, and a scaffold that `litespec new` writes keeps no copied text or number.
provisions.rationale: A template teaches the shape of its record type, so the record schema is its contract: a template that satisfies the schema stays teachable while the example product changes beside it. Each field shows a placeholder value, so nothing in the template reads as a decided value, and the Claimwick example beside it shows realistic values in one coherent product. `litespec model check` reports `template-value-unchanged` on a scaffold that keeps a copied value, so a copied period or a copied statement fails review as a decision. Settled by [decision/0093-check-templates-against-the-record-schema](decision/0093-check-templates-against-the-record-schema).

provisions.heading: Write Each Convention with a Default and a Replacement
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `CONVENTION_MISSING_DEFAULT` or `CONVENTION_MISSING_REPLACEMENT` diagnostic, and reports `CONVENTION_DEFAULT_SENTENCE`, `CONVENTION_REPLACEMENT_SENTENCE`, `CONVENTION_REPLACEMENT_WAIVER`, and `PROVISION_RESTATES_HEADING` as warnings.
provisions.statement: A Convention provision MUST follow the Convention contract this page defines.
provisions.rationale: A project replaces a default by citing it, which works only when each default has an identifier. Without the contract, defaults hide in prose and replacements cite paragraphs instead of identifiers.

provisions.heading: Write None in an Empty Required Section
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `PAGE_EMPTY_SECTION` or `PAGE_EMPTY_SECTION_TEXT` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A required section with nothing to say MUST contain only `None.`.
provisions.rationale: One marker reads the same on every page and gives the validator one shape to accept.

provisions.heading: Decide Current Truth in the Owning Module
provisions.evidence: Is every decision that needs current truth decided in the owning module? Check the reads beside the declared `queries` edges.
provisions.statement: A decision that needs current truth MUST be decided in the owning module, never from a read model.
provisions.rationale: A read model lags by its freshness. Revoked permissions, available funds, reservations, and period locks move after the copy was taken, so deciding from a copy accepts a stale answer where the business needs the current one. The owning module decides instead, through its public query the command sends with a declared `queries` edge, or by its own invariant. A read model serves reads the consumer reshapes and keeps locally.
provisions.example: The library refuses a hold on a lent copy by asking the lending module for current availability through its public query instead of reading a reporting copy.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Read Model Field from a Published Field
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` (level G) for a `from`, `erasedBy` or `removedBy` naming no module event or integration event, or a field the event does not carry, `read-model-key-invalid` (level G) for a `keyedBy` naming an aggregate of the read model's own module, and `read-model-unused` (level G) for a read model no use case reads.
provisions.statement: Each read model MUST name in `keyedBy` an aggregate of another module and, on each field, name in `from` the module event or integration event and the published field the field comes from.
provisions.rationale: A read model is a copy, and a copy with no stated source drifts: nobody tells which event fills a field, so a renamed published field breaks the read model without a finding. Naming the event and its field makes every crossing of the module boundary a declared edge the check reads, the same way an effect names its target. A read model keyed by its own module's aggregate copies state the module already reads directly. A use case names the read model in `reads`, and a read model no use case reads is kept current for no reader. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model) and [decision/0084-give-read-models-their-semantics](decision/0084-give-read-models-their-semantics).
provisions.example: `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense` is keyed by `aggregate/spending.expense`, and its `amount` field comes from `module-event/spending.expense-reimbursed#amount`.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Reaction and Job Edge in Effects
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction or job with no `effects` or with a top-level effect verb.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its edges in `effects`, with exactly one verb per entry.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job with no declared edge observes and acts nowhere, and an edge written outside `effects` hides behavior the checks see poorly. Declaring each edge in `effects`, with exactly one verb of `runs`, `sends`, `calls`, `queries`, or `commands`, keeps every consequence beside the trigger or schedule, in the one grammar every record with edges shares.

provisions.heading: Declare the Outcomes of Each Reaction and Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction or job without `outcomes` or with a name outside the closed set.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its run endings in `outcomes` from the closed set.
provisions.rationale: A run without declared endings leaves each reader guessing: a skipped item reads as a failure, and a suppressed send reads as a bug.
