Declaring each ending with its meaning states what a run produces: `completed` for work done, `skipped` for work set aside by its skip condition, `suppressed` for a send held by suppression, `failed` for work ending in refusal or error, `retry-scheduled` for work waiting on another attempt, and `nothing-selected` for a run finding no item. Scenarios end in one of these endings or in a run use case result, so every run has a proof. Settled by [decision/0081-own-scenarios-and-declare-outcomes](decision/0081-own-scenarios-and-declare-outcomes).
provisions.example: The send-due-notice reaction declares `completed` for a sent notice and `suppressed` for a notice held because the reader opted out.

provisions.heading: End Reaction and Job Scenarios in the Run Result
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a reaction or job scenario ending outside the run use case results and the declared outcomes.
provisions.statement: Each scenario on a reaction or job MUST end in a result of a use case its effects run or in one of its outcomes.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job scenario ending anywhere else proves another behavior story: it covers the trigger or schedule and asserts an ending no run use case declares and no outcome names. Ending in a run use case result or in a declared outcome keeps the scenario a proof of the reaction or job consequence. A send-only reaction or job ends its scenarios in outcomes, with no invented command.

provisions.heading: Erase a Read Model Personal Field with Its Owner
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `read-model-erasure-missing` (level G) for a `personal` or `sensitive` read model field with no `erasedBy`.
provisions.statement: Each `personal` or `sensitive` read model field MUST name in `erasedBy` the module event or integration event whose arrival erases it.
provisions.rationale: A read model copies data out of the module owning its erasure. A copy without an erasure trigger outlives the owner erasure and keeps personal data the product promised to remove. Naming the erasing event ties the copy to the owner erasure position, and the projection for that event clears the field. The erased key keeps a tombstone that a rebuild applies, so no rebuild restores the erased field. Settled by [decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model](decision/0065-read-another-module-through-a-read-model).
provisions.example: The `employeeId` field of `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense` is personal, so it names `module-event/spending.expense-personal-data-erased` in `erasedBy`, and the projection for that event clears it.

provisions.heading: File Every Reaction and Job with the Module It Changes
provisions.evidence: Does every reaction and job sit with the module whose own records it changes, or with the sending module when it changes another module only through that module's public command? Check the reactions and jobs beside the modules whose records they change and the public commands they send.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST live with the module whose own records it changes, with the sending module when it changes another module only by sending that module's public command, or with the module owning the notification when it only sends one.
provisions.rationale: Filing by trigger spreads one module's work across many trigger pages, so no page shows the module whole. Filing each reaction and job with the module whose records it changes keeps each module's behavior in one place. A module changes another module only through that module's public command, sent from a reaction or job. The sending module holds that fact and its reaction, so the reaction sits with the sender.

provisions.heading: Keep Failure Handling on the Reaction or Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `on-failure-placement-invalid` (level G) for a reaction or job whose effect entry carries `onFailure`.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST state its failure handling once, in `onFailure` on the record and never in an effect entry.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job runs one use case and owns the failure of the whole run. The record's `onFailure` states the mode, the retry and the dead-letter beside the trigger or schedule, where a reader looks for it. Repeating the shape on an effect entry leaves two places to change and two answers to the same failure, so the entry is no second home for it. A use case has no record-level `onFailure`. Its effect entries each carry their own.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reaction `reaction/spending.release-hold-on-rejection` states its retry and dead-letter in `onFailure` on the reaction record. Copying that object into its `runs` effect entry is reported.

provisions.heading: Keep Job Fields off Reactions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction carrying `kind`, `schedule`, `runbook`, `runsWhen`, `cursor`, `selection`, `lease`, `batchSize`, `serviceLevel`, or `evidence`.
provisions.statement: A reaction MUST NOT carry `kind`, `schedule`, `runbook`, `runsWhen`, `cursor`, `selection`, `lease`, `batchSize`, `serviceLevel`, or `evidence`.
provisions.rationale: Run fields describe work over time: the kind, the schedule, what each run selects, how many items per batch, the lock, where resume state lives, the condition it runs under, the promised service level, and the evidence the run leaves. A reaction answers one event and carries none of that. A run field on it claims a schedule the trigger states nowhere. Settled by [decision/0015-automations-and-sagas](decision/0015-automations-and-sagas).
provisions.example: The send-due-notice reaction answers its event with no `selection` and no `schedule`.

provisions.heading: Keep Validity Apart from Storage
provisions.evidence: Does every expiring credential and session refuse use from expiry, with a cleanup job removing expired records within a stated interval? Check the expiry rules beside the cleanup jobs.
provisions.statement: Each expiring credential or session MUST refuse its use from its expiry and be removed by a cleanup job within a stated interval.
provisions.rationale: An expiry only deleting leaves a window where an expired credential still works, and a check without cleanup leaves dead rows in place. Refusing the use from the expiry keeps validity at the moment of use, and a cleanup job removing expired records within a stated interval reclaims storage. The two stay separate: the check refuses, and the job removes. Settled by decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing.
provisions.example: A library session past its expiry is refused at its next use, and the expire-sessions job removes expired sessions within one day.

provisions.heading: Move a State by Time with a Timed Transition
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` (level G) for a timed transition naming a missing state or a job no record declares.
provisions.statement: Each transition that time moves MUST name its duration from entering its source state in `after` and the moving job in `movedBy`.
provisions.rationale: A deadline with no stated duration and no moving job has no defined moment to expire: holds linger, and reservations release nowhere. Naming the duration and the job states the timed move beside the lifecycle. The job selects instances past their window and runs the moving command once per instance. States, reactions, and timed transitions cover long-running work with no process record. Settled by decision/0074-declare-access-settings-and-deadlines.
provisions.example: The hold transition from Ready to Expired carries `after: P7D` and `movedBy: job/lending.expire-lapsed-holds`, and the job runs the expire-holds command once per lapsed hold.

provisions.heading: Name Each Job for the Use Case It Runs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `job-name-invalid` (level G) for a job outside `<verb>-<what>` with the verb of the use case it runs or its own verb when it runs none.
provisions.statement: Each job MUST be named `<verb>-<what>` with the verb of the use case it runs, or with its own verb when it runs no use case.
provisions.rationale: A job selects items and runs one command for each. Naming it for that command lets a reader go from the schedule to the behavior in one step. A job only sending or calling takes its own verb, since no use case verb names it.
provisions.example: `job/lending.expire-lapsed-holds` runs `use-case/lending.expire-holds`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Reaction for Its Act and Its Trigger
provisions.evidence: Does every reaction name state its act and its trigger? Check the reaction names beside their triggering events.
provisions.statement: Each reaction MUST be named `<verb>-<what>-on-<fact>` with a declared verb.
provisions.rationale: A reaction runs because something happened, and a name without its trigger hides why it runs: `send-due-notice` fires on a borrow, a hold, or a reminder run. Naming the act and the fact lets a reader find every consequence of a fact by its name.
provisions.example: `reaction/lending.send-due-notice-on-loan-borrowed` answers `domain-event/loan.loan-borrowed`.

provisions.heading: Name the Step a Compensating Reaction Undoes
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `compensation-target-invalid` (level G) for a `compensates` naming a use case that is not a command or the same use case the reaction runs, `compensation-trigger-invalid` (level G) for a compensating reaction answering an event the compensated use case lists in `raises`, and `reference-unknown` (level G) for a `compensates` naming no written record. The trigger check is a minimum: a reviewer confirms the trigger reports a later step's failure.
provisions.statement: A reaction that undoes a committed step of a multi-step process MUST name the undone use case in `compensates`, run a use case other than the one it names, and answer an event the undone use case does not raise.
provisions.rationale: A multi-step process commits each step before the next runs, so a later failure rolls the earlier steps back nowhere, and each committed step needs an undo running only where a later step fails. Without the link, a reader sees a reaction running an undoing command and tells poorly which committed step it reverses. Running the named use case again redoes the step instead of undoing it, and answering an event the undone step raises undoes every success. Naming the undone step in `compensates` states the undo beside the reaction, with its own trigger and failure handling.
provisions.example: The library reserves a copy with `use-case/lending.reserve-copy`, which commits the reservation. Where the later charge fails, `use-case/lending.record-charge-failure` raises `domain-event/charge.charge-failed`. The reaction `reaction/lending.release-copy-on-charge-failed` answers that event, runs `use-case/lending.release-copy`, and carries `compensates: use-case/lending.reserve-copy`, so a reader sees which committed step the release undoes.

provisions.heading: Publish Every Module Event from the Event It Translates
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a module event without `translates` or `fields`, `event-field-uncarried` (level G) for a field name its translated domain event does not carry, `event-publisher-invalid` for a module event with a second publishing module, and `effect-undeclared` for an event a handler, event handler or job publishes itself; `dotnet build` reports `LS2022` for an event published by user code.
provisions.statement: Each module event MUST name in `translates` the domain event of its own module it carries, and is published only from that domain event, by the pipeline step that stages raised events.
provisions.rationale: Where a handler builds a module event from whatever the aggregate carries after the act, it publishes state the act announced nowhere, and a second handler publishes the same event with different fields. Deriving the event from the one domain event it translates keeps every published field a field of the announced fact. The publishing use cases then follow from `raises`, with no second declaration to drift. A publish call in user code is an edge no record declares, so the stack reader reports it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `module-event/spending.expense-approved` translates `domain-event/expense.approved`, so `use-case/spending.approve-expense`, raising that event, publishes it, and its handler publishes nothing. The payouts module answers the module event from a reaction.

provisions.heading: Raise Completion Only When Every Module Is Done
provisions.evidence: Does spanning work raise completion only after every module reports done, with progress in a record the work does not delete? Check the completion reactions beside the module reports.
provisions.statement: Work that spans modules MUST raise its completion fact only after every module reports its part done.
provisions.rationale: A completion raised early declares done while parts remain: erased data returns, and closed work reopens. Each module's reaction erases or closes its part and reports done, and the completion is raised only where every report arrived. A report to an upstream module travels as its public command that the reporting module calls. Progress lives in a record outliving the deleted data, and the requesting state blocks new writes until completion. Settled by decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing.
provisions.example: Erasing a departed employee personal data enters Erasing, which blocks new writes. The spending reaction erases expenses and the access reaction erases sessions, each reporting done. The employee turns Erased only where both report, and the erasure record keeps the fact and date outside the erased data.

provisions.heading: Run at Most One Use Case from a Reaction or Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a reaction or job with more than one `runs` entry.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST run at most one use case, a job running it once per selected item.
provisions.rationale: A reaction or job is an entry point: it turns one fact or one selected item into one message, as an endpoint turns one request into one message. A reaction running two use cases decides their order and their joint failure in code no record states, and the second fails after the first committed. Two follow-on acts are two reactions to the same fact, each with its own failure handling. A use case named in `onRefusal` does not count, since it runs only after a refusal that committed nothing; settled by decision/0127-record-a-refused-run-on-the-reacting-side. A reaction or job only sending or calling runs no use case.
provisions.example: The erase-expired-personal-data job selects decided expenses past retention and runs `use-case/spending.erase-personal-data` once for each.

provisions.heading: Run Each Effect on Its Own
provisions.evidence: Does every effect of each reaction and job run, retry, and deduplicate on its own? Check the effects beside their failure handling and idempotency.
provisions.statement: Each effect of a reaction or job MUST run, retry and deduplicate on its own, with any order expressed by chaining facts.
provisions.rationale: Effects sharing one retry decide their joint failure in code no record states: the second send waits on the first, and a retry doubles the first while fixing the second. Running each effect on its own keeps each consequence independent, with its own idempotency and its own failure handling. An order between effects is a fact the first produces and the second answers, not an assumed sequence.
provisions.example: The loan-borrowed reaction sends the due notice and calls the statistics system as two independent effects. A retry of the call resends no notice.

provisions.heading: Run Every Job from Its Declared Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `schedule-invalid` (level G) for a schedule neither an `every` duration, a `cron` expression, nor `at: startup`, and fails a job without its `kind` or a scheduled job without `schedule`.
provisions.statement: Each job MUST declare its `kind` of `scheduled` or `one-off` with its `schedule` where scheduled.
provisions.rationale: A job without a kind has no defined moment to run. Naming the kind states when it runs. A scheduled job carries its `schedule`, with an `every` duration, a `cron` expression and timezone, or `at: startup` for a run once at deployment start. A `one-off` job runs once.
provisions.example: `job/lending.expire-lapsed-holds` runs every six hours over open holds past their window.

provisions.heading: Settle Every Async Outcome in Visible States
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `async-pending-missing` (level G) for a `settles` with a pending or done state that names no state or names one state twice, or with a pending state that no earlier transition reaches, `async-refused-unrecorded` (level G) for a run with no refused state and no declared retry, or a refused state that repeats pending or done, and `reference-unknown` (level G) for a `settles` naming no written aggregate or state. A run with no `settles` states nothing, because the model tells poorly whether a reader waits on it. A reviewer confirms each query reading the settled aggregate returns its state.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job whose outcome a reader waits on MUST name in `settles` the aggregate it writes with its pending state and its done state, and its refused state except where another attempt returns the run to pending.
provisions.rationale: A result produced after the commit arrives later: the command commits, and a reaction or job settles the outcome afterwards. A reader meeting the record meanwhile sees neither done nor refused, and reads the absence as whichever ending fits the screen. Naming the pending state the run leaves, the done state it enters, and the refused state a terminal refusal enters keeps the three endings apart on the written aggregate. Where every failure earns another attempt, the run returns to pending instead, and the declared retry states that no terminal refusal exists.
provisions.example: Claimwick's erase job runs the erase-personal-data command over decided expenses past retention. It settles the expense from pending Reimbursed to done Erased, and lists no refused state: its retry returns each failed expense to Reimbursed for the next nightly run.

provisions.heading: State the Failure Handling of Every Reaction and Job
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` fails a reaction or job with `onFailure` outside the one failure shape, and reports `record-invalid` for prose handling, a missing or malformed retry, and a malformed duration. A reaction or job that states `onFailure` in an effect entry is reported as `on-failure-placement-invalid`.
provisions.statement: Each reaction and each job MUST declare its `onFailure` in the one failure shape and its idempotency.
provisions.rationale: A failed reaction or job without handling retries without end or drops silently: notices double-send, and holds clear nowhere. Declaring `onFailure` states the failure shape beside the trigger or schedule: `mode` of `retry`, `skip-and-log`, or `discard`; `retry` with `maxAttempts`, `initialDelay`, `maxDelay`, and `backoff` of `exponential` or `fixed`; `ifExhausted` of `dead-letter`; `deadLetter` carrying `after` with the action a person takes; `surfacesIn` naming the entry point showing the failure, and `runbook` the recovery procedure. `retry` and `ifExhausted` come with `mode: retry`; `deadLetter`, `surfacesIn`, and `runbook` are optional. Delays and `after` are ISO 8601 durations, and prose handling is refused. The one shape also serves the effect entries of a use case. A reaction or job states failure handling once on the record.

provisions.heading: Subscribe to Every Module Event
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-event-unused` (level G) for a module event that no reaction in `triggeredBy`, no read model field in `from`, `erasedBy` or `removedBy`, and no other consumer names.
provisions.statement: Each module event MUST be named by a reaction, a read model projection or another consumer that answers or copies it.
provisions.rationale: A module event is a contract between modules. Publishing one nobody consumes stages an event on every commit that no work reads, and a reader tells poorly whether the fact matters or the consumer was forgotten. Naming the consumer makes the crossing complete: the reaction answers the fact, or the projection copies it into the reading module's own store.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `module-event/spending.expense-approved` is named by the payouts reaction paying the reimbursement. A second event with no reaction or read model is reported until its consumer is written or the event is removed.

provisions.heading: Trigger Every Reaction from Its Declared Events
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` (level G) for a trigger naming an unknown event, `reaction-trigger-foreign` (level G) for a trigger naming another module's domain event, and fails a reaction without a `triggeredBy` list.
provisions.statement: Each reaction MUST declare in `triggeredBy` the domain events of its own module, the module events of upstream modules of the product, or the inbound integration events it answers.
provisions.rationale: A reaction without a trigger has no defined moment to run. Naming the events states when it fires, as one id or a list. The reaction answers the domain events of its own module, upstream module events, or inbound integration events, and answers no other module domain event and no downstream module fact. Answering another module domain event couples it to state its module owns poorly. The owning module publishes a module event instead.
provisions.example: In the library, `reaction/lending.send-due-notice-on-loan-borrowed` answers `domain-event/loan.loan-borrowed` and runs the send-due-notice command.

provisions.heading: Write Every Runbook to Run or Recover
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a runbook page without `impact`, `prerequisites`, `procedure`, `verification`, `recovery`, or `escalation`.
provisions.statement: Each runbook MUST state its `impact`, `prerequisites`, `procedure`, `verification`, `recovery`, and `escalation`.
provisions.rationale: A runbook named by a job, a failure policy, or an alert is the answer a person opens under pressure. Its `impact` says what breaks, `prerequisites` say what to hold, `procedure` says each step, `verification` says how to confirm, `recovery` says how to undo, and `escalation` says who to call. A runbook missing one leaves the reader guessing at the worst moment.
provisions.example: The clear-stuck-reimbursements runbook states its impact on waiting expenses, its prerequisites, its procedure, its verification query, its recovery, and its escalation to the spending team.

provisions.heading: Authorize Every File Download Through Its Owning Use Case
provisions.evidence: Is every stored file reachable only through a download use case with its declared access? Look at the download endpoints and the storage addresses beside each owning use case.
provisions.statement: A caller MUST reach a stored file only through a download use case authorized from the access that use case declares.
provisions.rationale: A stored file carries the data of the record it belongs to. A direct storage address serves that data to anyone holding the address, past the owning grant and tenant scope. Routing each download through its owning use case keeps one authorization decision for the file and for its record.
provisions.example: A Claimwick receipt photo downloads through the use case that owns the expense, so the declared access decides who reads the photo, and no storage address serves it on its own.

provisions.heading: Bound Collection Queries
provisions.evidence: Does every collection response apply deterministic order with the declared default and maximum limits? Look at the collection responses beside their records.
provisions.statement: A collection endpoint MUST apply deterministic ordering, its record's declared default limit, and its record's declared maximum limit of 100 or lower.
provisions.rationale: One unbounded read causes unbounded database and serialization work. Deterministic ordering keeps pages stable, the declared default limit bounds the common case, and the declared maximum of 100 or lower caps the worst case. The use-case record declares its paging with order, cursor or offset, default limit, and maximum limit, and the endpoint applies exactly that.

provisions.heading: Bound Every File Upload
provisions.evidence: Does every upload operation declare its size and media-type bounds, and refuse files outside them? Look at each upload endpoint beside its use-case record.
provisions.statement: A file upload operation MUST accept no file larger than the size its use-case record declares and no media type outside the media types its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: A declared size and media-type bound tells the server what to accept before storage, and tells a reviewer the limit beside the use case that owns the file. An upload without both bounds lets one caller send work the server agreed to neither store nor inspect.
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense upload declares the size and the image media types a receipt photo carries. The server turns away a larger file or another media type before it stores anything.

provisions.heading: Declare Stable Operation Metadata in the Contract
provisions.evidence: Does every operation in the generated contract declare its operationId, authorization, request, success, failure, and summary entries? Look at the operations in the generated contract.
provisions.statement: An operation MUST declare a stable `operationId`, its authorization, request, success, and Problem Details metadata, and a summary.
provisions.rationale: Generated clients name their methods from `operationId`. An unstable name renames client code on every generation. Authorization metadata cites the enforced policies and Problem Details metadata covers each documented failure status, so the client models security and failure before its first call. Comments on handlers carry no contract documentation, so operations carry explicit summaries.

provisions.heading: Keep Numeric Transport Types Precise
provisions.evidence: Does every numeric field publish a plain schema, with the int64 union reserved for values beyond the safe range? Look at the numeric fields in the contract.
provisions.statement: Emit a plain numeric schema for an `int32` or `double` field, and reserve a string-or-number union for `int64` values beyond the JSON safe integer range.
provisions.rationale: A plain numeric schema lets consumers read `int32` and `double` directly. A broad union on every integer forces each consumer to coerce plain numbers, so the union stays reserved for `int64` values past the safe range.

provisions.heading: Keep One Name for a Use Case Across Layers
provisions.evidence: Does every message type, operation id, and audit action carry its use case name? Look at each use case's message type, operation id, and audit action beside its record.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST carry its name unchanged in its message type, operation id, and audit action.
provisions.rationale: A use case that reads one way in its record, another in its message type, and a third in its audit action forces every trace across layers through a translation table held by the author alone. The record id is the name; the message type, the endpoint operation id, and the audit action repeat it in their own casing, so a reader follows one name from the page to the wire to the audit log.
provisions.example: `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` travels as `ReimburseExpenseCommand`, operation id `ReimburseExpense`, and audit action `reimburse-expense`; an operation id of `PayExpense` is reported.

provisions.heading: Model a Monetary Value as One Object
provisions.evidence: Does every monetary value travel as one Money object with a string amount, with currency where the caller chooses it? Look at the monetary fields in the contract.
provisions.statement: Carry a monetary value as one `Money` object in a response model and in a request where the caller chooses the currency, with `amount` as an invariant decimal string and `currency` as an ISO 4217 code.
provisions.rationale: Split sibling fields pair by a server invariant no schema shows, so a report reads the two independently and mismatches them. One `Money` object holding `amount` and an ISO 4217 `currency` mirrors the Domain shape on the wire. The amount travels as a string, not as a JSON number, so no reader parses it as binary floating point.
provisions.example: `unitPrice` and `currencyCode` become `price` of type `Money`, traveling as `{ "amount": "12.50", "currency": "EUR" }`. A request that references an account with a fixed currency carries `amount` alone.

provisions.heading: Name the Use Case on Every Published Operation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `operation-use-case-drift` (level S) for an operation in the committed contract whose `x-litespec-use-case` is missing or differs from the use case its endpoint's mark names.
provisions.statement: Every operation in the generated contract MUST carry `x-litespec-use-case` naming the use case its endpoint implements.
provisions.rationale: The `operationId` names an operation for client code, cased for method names, so it carries no record identifier. The extension holds the identifier itself, which the OpenAPI specification reserves for this kind of metadata, and takes an integrator from an operation straight to its specification page. The value comes from the generated map of operation names to use cases, so it is written once, in the endpoint mark.
provisions.example: The Claimwick operation `SubmitExpense` carries `"x-litespec-use-case": "use-case/spending.submit-expense"`.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Upload Type from Its Content
provisions.evidence: Does every upload operation read the file type from the bytes rather than the claimed media type or file name? Look at the type check of each upload endpoint beside the declared media types.
provisions.statement: A file upload operation MUST determine the file type from the file content rather than the media type or file name the client claims.
provisions.rationale: A claimed media type and a file name are caller input. Either one says image while the bytes carry something else. Reading the type from the content enforces the declared media-type bound on what the server stores rather than on what the caller says it sent.
provisions.example: A Claimwick receipt photo named as an image stores as an image with the bytes reading as one of the declared image types. Bytes of another type meet a refusal, even with the name and claimed type agreeing.

provisions.heading: Require the Marker Header on Cookie-Authenticated Writes
provisions.evidence: Does every cookie-authenticated write without the marker header answer 401? Look at the write requests with cookie authentication.
provisions.statement: The API MUST refuse a cookie-authenticated write without the project's marker header.
provisions.rationale: Cookies travel with every request, including ones a malicious page triggers. A page on another site adds no custom header, so a missing header exposes a cross-site forgery. A write is any request other than GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS.
provisions.example: The header takes the form `X-<Project>-Request: 1`, with the exact name set in project configuration. The refused request answers 401, since it arrives unauthenticated.

provisions.heading: Return Stable Problem Details
provisions.evidence: Does every error response carry the stable code, the traceId, and one errors entry per field failure? Look at the error responses at the API boundary.
provisions.statement: An error response MUST use [RFC 9457](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9457) Problem Details carrying a stable application `code`, the current `traceId`, and an `errors` entry for each field failure.
provisions.rationale: A stable code lets a client branch on the failure without parsing prose, and the trace identifier ties the response to its diagnostics. One entry per field failure reports the whole request in a single answer, and one handler keeps every endpoint consistent.
provisions.example:
A validation failure returns this body:

```json
{
  "type": "https://example.test/problems/validation",
  "title": "Request validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "One or more values are invalid.",
  "instance": "/api/posts",
  "code": "validation-failed",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "errors": [
    {
      "field": "title",
      "code": "required",
      "message": "Title is required."
    }
  ]
}
```

`type` is a stable absolute URI owned by the consumer. `errors` appears with validity findings, carrying their member, code, and message. `code` carries the refusal result stable code, and `detail` carries the free-form prose explanation. WebApi maps Application member names to their public JSON field names. `traceId` carries the trace identifier from the current [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/) `traceparent`, with the request identifier as fallback. The same shape applies to authentication and authorization failures.

The global handler maps validation failures to 400 and missing targets through the operation disclosure policy. It maps forbidden failures to 403 or the declared 404. The derived `invalid-input` refusal answers 400, the derived `forbidden` refusal answers 403 or the declared 404, and the derived `conflict` and `rule-not-stated` refusals answer 409. Each written refusal answers the status its refusal record states. Unexpected failures answer 500 with code `internal-error`. It maps each known domain failure individually. It reports no cancellation from a disconnected request as an application error.

In the Claimwick product, reimbursing an expense that is not approved ends with `result/reimburse-expense.not-approved`, which carries the code `spending.not-approved` and the status 422. The global handler answers:

```json
{
  "type": "https://example.test/problems/not-approved",
  "title": "Not approved",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "The expense is not approved.",
  "instance": "/api/expenses",
  "code": "spending.not-approved",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"
}
```

The endpoint catches no failure.

![A domain failure or a validation failure reaches the global handler, which no endpoint preempts. The handler selects the HTTP status and returns a Problem Details body carrying the stable code, the trace identifier, and one entry per field failure.](../assets/diagrams/backend-error-flow.svg)

provisions.heading: Store Every Upload Through Infrastructure
provisions.evidence: Does any endpoint or handler write file bytes to a storage provider directly? Look at the upload endpoints and handlers beside the Infrastructure storage code.
provisions.statement: File storage for an upload MUST live in Infrastructure.
provisions.rationale: File storage is provider work beside aggregate storage. Infrastructure owns the storage provider, its configuration, and its errors, so a project changes where files live without touching an endpoint or a handler.
provisions.example: The Claimwick endpoint for a receipt photo converts the request to its command and dispatches it, the handler stages the expense, and Infrastructure writes the photo bytes to the configured store.

provisions.heading: Ask Another Module One Question Through a Decision Port
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` (level S) for another module's public query sent with no declared `queries` edge, `effect-unimplemented` (level S) for a declared `queries` edge no send takes, and `query-target-invalid` (level G) for a `queries` edge naming the calling module's own query.
provisions.statement: A handler whose decision needs another module's current value MUST ask for it through the owning module's public query, declaring the edge in `effects.queries`.
provisions.rationale: Some decisions reject a lagging copy: money still moving, or capacity still selling. The provider public query answers with the owner current value and nothing else, so the question stays narrow. The edge appears on both sides: the consumer `queries` edge names the public use case, and the provider record lists the consumer in `reachedThrough`.
provisions.example: A Claimwick reimbursement command asks spending for the current expense through spending public read-expense query, instead of reading a whole event profile through a general reader.

provisions.heading: Build Collaborators Through the Container
provisions.evidence: Does any handler, job, or step class create collaborators inside its body, or take more than ten constructor dependencies? Look at each constructor the change adds.
provisions.statement: Each handler needing a collaborator MUST take it through the constructor from the container, never create it inside its own body.
provisions.rationale: A step created inside a handler hides its dependencies behind a small-looking handler. Injected collaborators keep their dependencies visible in the constructor.
provisions.example: The Claimwick reimburse handler takes its expense repository through its constructor, while a step created inside the handler taking a repository is reported.

provisions.heading: Confirm Downstream Completion Through an Upstream Command
provisions.evidence: Does any module react to a downstream fact instead of learning completion through its own public command? Look at each reaction to another module's fact beside the upstream public commands.
provisions.statement: A module that needs to know downstream work finished MUST learn it through its own public command that the downstream module calls, never by reacting to a downstream fact.
provisions.rationale: An upstream module reacting to a downstream fact depends on the downstream module, breaking the one direction each module relationship keeps. Facts flow downstream alone, while completion confirmations travel upstream as commands through the upstream own pipeline.
provisions.example: When a Claimwick erasure spanning modules finishes its spending part, spending calls the owning module public confirm command naming the spending module, instead of the owner reacting to a spending fact.

provisions.heading: Declare a Port Only for What the Module Does Not Compute
provisions.evidence: Does every interface in the module `Ports/` folders reach outside the process, with no in-process logic, store read, duplicate platform interface, permission constant, domain exception, or enum among them? Look at each port beside its callers and its Infrastructure implementation.
provisions.statement: A module MUST declare a port in its `Ports/` folder only as an interface Infrastructure implements for work the module does not compute in memory: an external system, a file format it reads or writes, a platform service, or the clock.
provisions.rationale: A `Ports/` folder accepting in-process helpers turns into the place for whatever fits nowhere else, and a reader stops telling what the module depends on. Each port earns its folder by reaching outside the process: an external system, a file format, a platform service, or the clock.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the receipt PDF renderer is a port: Spending declares `IReceiptPdf` in `Ports/ReceiptPdf/` and implements it in `Infrastructure/ReceiptPdf/`. The mapping from an `Expense` to an export row runs in memory behind one implementation, so it stays in the use case folder.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Commands Edge on the Sender
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` (level S) for another module's public command sent with no declared `commands` edge, `effect-unimplemented` (level S) for a declared `commands` edge no send takes, `command-edge-invalid` (level G) for a `commands` edge a use case declares, and `command-target-invalid` (level G) for a `commands` edge naming the sending module's own command.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job that sends another module's public command MUST declare the edge as `effects.commands` naming the owner's public command use case.
provisions.rationale: A send no record declares hides a cross-boundary pair no diff shows. The `effects.commands` entry names the owner public command beside the behavior sending it, with the owner record listing the sender in `reachedThrough`.
provisions.example: Claimwick reporting close-period job declares `effects.commands` naming `use-case/spending.close-expenses`, and the spending close-expenses command lists `module/reporting` in `reachedThrough`.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Port in the Module Ports Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a port folder that does not spell its external-system record name, and for a port or adapter folder naming a declared module.
provisions.statement: Every port of a module MUST live in its own `Ports/{Port}/` folder holding the interface `I{Port}` with the types its signatures name in `Models/`, with its adapter in its `Infrastructure/{Port}/` folder holding its wire types in `Models/`, spelling for an external system the record name in PascalCase.
provisions.rationale: One folder per port shows every outside dependency in one listing, instead of scattered interfaces across use case folders. The folder name spells the external-system record name in PascalCase, and each port pairs with its adapter in Infrastructure.
provisions.example: Claimwick Spending declares `IReceiptPdf` in `Ports/ReceiptPdf/` with its adapter in `Infrastructure/ReceiptPdf/`.

provisions.heading: Declare Shared Access Conditions as Composable Policies
provisions.evidence: Does every use case whose record cites a rule governing an access condition declare the matching policy, with no use case guard of its own for it? Look at each authorization definition beside the guard implementations.
provisions.statement: An access condition shared by several use cases MUST be one composable authorization policy declared in each use case's authorization definition and evaluated by the one authorization guard.
provisions.rationale: A security rule copied per use case drifts: one copy checks before the permission and one after, and a new sensitive use case silently gets none. One policy factory beside the permission policy holds the condition, each citing use case declares it in its authorization definition, and the one guard evaluates it for all of them. This follows decision/0108-composable-access-policies, which holds shared conditions in one factory instead of copies.
provisions.example: Sensitive Claimwick spending use cases such as reimburse-expense declare `RecentSignIn(permission)` in their authorization definitions. The guard checks the sign-in presence, then its age against the window from the identity contract, then the permission.

provisions.heading: Declare the Audit Target and Reason Beside the Message
provisions.evidence: Does any command handler add an audit target or reason that the message already carries? Look at each audit call in the command handlers.
provisions.statement: Each audited command MUST declare beside the message the audit target and reason that the message carries, leaving the handler to add only the values it learns while running.
provisions.rationale: Values from the message exist before the handler runs, so the pipeline records them on every outcome, including a denial. The handler adds a generated identity or a reason composed from loaded state alone.
provisions.example: The Claimwick approve-expense command declares its expense id as the audit target with the reason the message carries, and the handler adds the approval reference it learns while running.

provisions.heading: Dispatch Only Declared Effect Edges
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` (level S) for a dispatch a handler, event handler, or job takes that its record declares no edge for, `effect-unimplemented` (level S) for a declared edge no dispatch takes, and `effect-timing-invalid` (level S) for a command use case declaring a `sends` or `calls` effect with `inline` timing, and `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a command or event mediator held outside an endpoint, event handler or job.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST change only its aggregate, leaving every declared `runs`, `sends` and `calls` edge to an event handler or job after the commit.
provisions.rationale: An undeclared edge hides behavior review leaves unseen. Each declared entry names one verb with its timing and failure handling, and the pipeline refuses timing outside its bounds: `sends` and `calls` on a command run `after-commit` or `async`, with the hosted sign-in token exchange as the one `inline` `calls` edge.
provisions.example: The Claimwick send-approver-reminders reaction sends the approval reminder through the messenger port after the submit commit. A send its record leaves undeclared fails the check.

provisions.heading: Enforce Target Authorization in the Pipeline
provisions.evidence: Does every message reach the guard with the `access` its record declares, with no handler throwing a forbidden refusal or taking the authorization guard? Look at each handler body and the `access` on each message.
provisions.statement: The authorization guard, not the handler, MUST authorize every message from the `access` its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: Per-handler authorization drifts, while one guard decides from one record for every message. The guard reads the presented kinds, the grant, the scope, and the tenant reach from the record, resolves ownership and delegation against the target through a scope owner lookup, and evaluates one composable policy per cited condition in order. Coarse authenticated, role, or scope checks stay at the endpoint and replace no decision that depends on business data. This follows decision/0108-composable-access-policies, which holds each shared condition in one factory the guard evaluates.
provisions.example: The Claimwick approve-expense message carries its `access` with the spending permission, and the guard authorizes the caller before the handler loads the expense. The handler compares no caller with any target.

provisions.heading: Implement One Outcome Path per Command
provisions.evidence: Does any command handler look up a record and then create one in the same method? Look at each command handler body for a lookup followed by a create.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST implement one use case with one success path, so a flow that finds a record or else creates it is two use cases that the boundary owning the flow chooses between.
provisions.rationale: A get-or-create command hides two use cases with different access, audit, and refusals behind one name. The boundary owning the flow runs a query first and sends the command fitting the answer, with one shared helper holding the sequence.
provisions.example: Signing in to the library with an unknown reader card runs as a query and then one of two commands: the endpoint queries `query/loans.find-reader-by-card`, then sends either `use-case/loans.register-reader` or `use-case/loans.record-reader-sign-in`.

provisions.heading: Issue Per-Record Work from a Job
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2015` for a command handler that changes records inside a loop, except when its use case record states `consistency: per-record`.
provisions.statement: Work over many records MUST run as a job that selects the records and sends one command per record, each in its own unit of work, never as a command handler that changes records or sends commands in a loop.
provisions.rationale: One command looping over many records rolls back the batch on one failing record and holds locks for its whole length. A job sending one command per record keeps each record in its own unit of work, with the batch condition moved into the erase act so a changed record refuses itself.
provisions.example: The Claimwick erase-expired-data job selects the expired expenses and sends one erase command per expense, each in its own unit of work, instead of a batch command looping over expenses.

provisions.heading: Keep Command Handlers to Load, Call and Stage
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a command or event mediator a handler, validator, step or domain type holds, and `LS2022` for an event published outside the platform.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST load or create the aggregate its use case changes, call one domain method on it, stage it through its repository, and return the result, and send no command or event.
provisions.rationale: Validation, authorization, idempotency, audit, the timestamp, holds, the commit, and fault classification each have an owner in the pipeline. A handler doing more widens the unit of work, so one failing step rolls back work with no reason to fail with it. A handler sending a command nests one use case inside another, with the inner commit surviving an outer failure, and a handler publishing an event announces state its act left undescribed.
provisions.example:
In Claimwick, the approve-expense command flows from the endpoint through validation and the guard to a handler loading the expense, calling Approve, staging it, and returning. The pipeline commits once after the handler.

![An HTTP request reaches the endpoint, which maps it to a command and dispatches it through the command mediator. Validation checks structural input, then the authorization guard checks the permission and the target. The handler loads or creates one aggregate through its repository, calls one domain method, and stages it. The repository stages the aggregate, and exactly one commit post-handler commits the session once.](../assets/diagrams/backend-command-pipeline.svg)

provisions.heading: Keep Query Handlers Free of Writes
provisions.evidence: Does any query handler stage, store, delete, or dispatch? Look at each query handler body.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST NOT stage, store, delete or dispatch anything.
provisions.rationale: A read writing state makes retries, caching, and read authorization unsafe. Audited reads belong to the pipeline, so the handler stays a pure projection.
provisions.example: The Claimwick list-expenses query projects its rows and stages nothing. A retry of the query repeats the same read with no new state.

provisions.heading: Keep Repository Reads Out of Loops
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `repository-read-invalid` (level S) for a repository read inside a loop body.
provisions.statement: Each handler and job MUST read no repository inside a loop body.
provisions.rationale: A read inside a loop turns one handling into as many round trips as there are items, with the slowdown hidden behind small test data. A batch read or a scoped query loads every item at once, costing one trip whatever the data holds.
provisions.example: The library reminder job loads due loans with one scoped query instead of reading each loan inside its loop.

provisions.heading: Keep Use Case Folders Small
provisions.evidence: Does any use case folder hold more than its message, handler, validator, definitions, result, and a few helpers, or a file over 200 lines? Look at the file counts and sizes in each use case folder.
provisions.statement: A use case folder SHOULD hold its message, handler, validator, definitions, and result with at most a few helpers, and no file over 200 lines.
provisions.rationale: A small folder reads as one act: a reader opening it sees the whole act at once. Many helpers or a long file point to work that belongs behind a port, such as file rendering, parsing, or production of a file format.

provisions.heading: Organize Application by Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every command and query own one folder named for its use case inside the plural aggregate folder of its aggregate in the `Application/` folder of its module, or directly in the `Application/` folder when its record is a module-level read, with its message, result, validator, handler, mapping, and pipeline-read values? Look at the folders under each module.
provisions.statement: Each command or query MUST own one folder named for its use case inside the plural aggregate folder of its aggregate in the `Application/` folder of its module, or directly in the `Application/` folder when its record is a module-level read, holding its message, result, validator, handler, mapping, and definition of pipeline-read values.
provisions.rationale: Scattered behavior turns one change into edits across many folders, and review misses one of them. One folder per use case keeps the message, the checks, the handling, and the mapping together, so a reviewer judges the whole behavior from that folder.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, `use-case/spending.approve-expense` keeps its command, result, validator, and handler in `Application/Expenses/ApproveExpense/`, with its endpoint in `WebApi/Expenses/ApproveExpense/`.

provisions.heading: Project Queries Directly
provisions.evidence: Does any query handler take a domain repository, load an aggregate, or send another module's public query without a declared `queries` edge? Look at each query handler's constructor and body.
provisions.statement: A query handler MUST project directly to its result from its own module's store and read models, without loading an aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A read path enforces no invariant, so loading an aggregate for presentation pays for enforcement no read needs and ties the read shape to the write model. Projecting directly keeps reads on the read boundary, with the command and query split behind it.
provisions.example: The Claimwick list-expenses query projects its rows from the store and read models and takes no domain repository. Its shape follows the result record, not the aggregate.

provisions.heading: Read Another Module's State Through a Read Model
provisions.evidence: Does every read model hold data its module reshaped and keeps locally, and does every read model have a use case naming it in `reads`? Look at each read model beside the use cases that read it.
provisions.statement: A use case that needs another module's data reshaped and kept locally MUST read it through a read model its own module keeps, named in its `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A read model is the reading module's own copy, with each field traced to the published field it comes from and projections keeping it current from the owner events. Reads through the model lag by up to the declared freshness, which fits rows the consumer shows and figures it accumulates.
provisions.example: The Claimwick reporting list-reimbursed-expenses query reads `read-model/reporting.reimbursed-expense`, filled from the spending expense-reimbursed module event. It calls no spending reader.

provisions.heading: Read Time from the Scoped Clock
provisions.evidence: Which handlers read the system clock directly, or take more than one timestamp for one message? Look at the clock reads in each handler.
provisions.statement: Each handler MUST read the message timestamp from the scoped clock the pipeline stamps once per message.
provisions.rationale: A handler reading the clock two or three times in one decision records different times for one act, sometimes with an outside call in between. One timestamp per message fixes the moment the message starts, and every decision in the handling answers to the same time.
provisions.example: The Claimwick approve handler stamps its approval with the handled clock, instead of a fresh clock read.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Lost Race as a Conflict
provisions.evidence: Does every command that loses a race at commit end with its use case conflict refusal? Look at the race outcomes beside the use case refusals.
provisions.statement: Each command that loses a race at commit MUST end with its use case's conflict refusal.
provisions.rationale: A duplicate key or a stale version reaches the commit as a store fault, and the pipeline classifies it as the use case named conflict refusal. The caller learns what happened and rereads and retries with current state, with no reservation or retry inside the handler.
provisions.example: Two library clerks register the same book barcode at once. The second commit violates the barcode unique index, and the command refuses with `book-barcode-taken`.

provisions.heading: Return Only Declared Results and Refusals
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `result-undeclared` (level S) for a code a handler produces that no declared result names; a handler returns only the results and codes its record lists.
provisions.statement: A handler MUST return only the results, refusals, and codes its use-case record declares.
provisions.rationale: An outcome no result declares hides behavior the specification left undescribed, so the stack reader fails it as `result-undeclared`. Refusals return in the precedence order the record lists with first match winning, and a success carrying codes returns those codes alone.
provisions.example: A Claimwick handler returning a code its record lists nowhere fails the check, even with correct spelling. Every result, refusal, and code on the wire traces to the use-case record.

provisions.heading: Send Cross-Module Queries and Commands Through the Mediator
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` (level S) for another module's public query or public command sent with no declared edge, and `effect-unimplemented` (level S) for a declared `queries` or `commands` edge no send takes, and `dotnet build` reports `LS2029` for another module's public query or query result named outside a handler, reaction, or job, and for another module's public command or command result named outside a reaction or job.
provisions.statement: A use case, reaction, or job MUST reach another module's public query or public command only through the mediator with a declared edge: a handler, reaction, or job sends another module's public query with a `queries` edge, and only a reaction or job sends another module's public command with a `commands` edge.
provisions.rationale: Provider result types appear in Application code, while Domain takes plain values and identifiers, so no provider shape leaks into invariants. Handlers read their own module through the repository or the read session, endpoints send their own use case command alone, and each cross-module send travels through the mediator with its declared edge.
provisions.example: A Claimwick reimbursement command sends spending public read-expense query through the query mediator with a declared `queries` edge, and a reporting reaction sends spending public command through the command mediator with a declared `commands` edge.

provisions.heading: Send Public Commands in Process
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2029` for another module's public command or command result named outside a reaction or job.
provisions.statement: A reaction or job MUST send another module's public command in process and synchronously through the command entry point.
provisions.rationale: The owner runs its ordinary handler through its own pipeline, with authorization, audit, idempotency, and validation intact. Each command keeps its own commit, since no handler sends a command.
provisions.example: Claimwick reporting close-period reaction sends spending close-expenses command through the command entry point, and the spending handler runs the change through spending own pipeline.

provisions.heading: Separate Input Validation from Invariants
provisions.evidence: Does every validator check structural input only, leaving aggregate state to Domain? Look at each validator body.
provisions.statement: A validator MUST limit its checks to structural input, leaving aggregate state decisions to Domain.
provisions.rationale: Shape problems fail fast, before Domain loads anything, while state refusals need the loaded aggregate. A validator that checks state pulls persistence into validation and judges one input in two layers.
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense validator rejects an empty expense identifier or an empty employee identifier and accepts every well-formed pair. Domain decides the receipt rule and rejects a receipt-less expense above the threshold with `result/submit-expense.receipt-missing`, carrying the stable code `spending.receipt-missing`.

provisions.heading: Stage Declared Module and Integration Events in the Commit
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2022` for an event published outside the platform, and `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for an event a handler, event handler or job publishes itself.
provisions.statement: Each module event and each outbound integration event MUST leave the commit only through the one pipeline step that stages raised domain events, built from the domain event its record `translates`, so no user code publishes an event.
provisions.rationale: User code publishing events produces two payloads for one fact and emits state the act left unannounced. One global step before the commit stages each raised Domain event for its own module reactions, each module event translating it, and each outbound integration event translating it, all committing with the business work.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense raises its reimbursed fact, and the staging step stages it, `module-event/spending.expense-reimbursed`, and the outbound `integration-event/expense-reimbursed`, each built from that fact, in the same commit. The reimburse handler publishes nothing.

provisions.heading: Use This Use-Case Layout
provisions.evidence: Does every use-case path, layer folder, trigger folder, and result part name follow the layout? Look at each path under the modules.
provisions.statement: Place each use case in one folder per layer that serves it, inside the plural aggregate folder of its aggregate, with a module-level read dropping the aggregate segment in each: `Application/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` with its message, result, handler, validator, pipeline definitions, own steps and triggers, and `WebApi/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` with its endpoint and transport models when it has an endpoint; place every port of the module in its own `Ports/{Port}/` folder with its adapter in `Infrastructure/{Port}/`.
provisions.rationale: One folder per use case inside the plural aggregate folder in each serving layer holds everything a reviewer needs in one set of folders. The module tree moves a reader from a handler to its endpoint without a map, and the `Ports/` folder lists every outside dependency with its adapter. Reactions and the job running the use case sit in its `Application/` folder, so the folder shows every way the use case starts.
provisions.example:
The layout reads as follows:

```text
{Product}/
  Application/                            product layer folder: pipeline positions and pipeline stages, and nothing else
  Posts/                                  one aggregate: every layer holds the plural aggregate folder
    Contracts/
      Posts/          PostId, OnPostPublished/PostPublishedModuleEvent, ReadPost/ (query and result)
    Domain/
      Posts/                              Post, PostState, and the post repository contract
    Application/
      Posts/
        CreateDraft/                      Command, Result, Handler, Validator, mapping
        GetPost/
        ListPosts/
          ListPostsQueryResultItem        a result part named after its result
        ArchiveStalePost/                 no WebApi folder: no endpoint reaches this use case
          ArchiveStalePostsJob            the job that runs this use case once per stale post
          ArchiveStalePostOnPostReportedHandler   a reaction that runs this use case
        ExportPosts/                      query, handler, definitions, result
      Notifications/
        NewPost/
          NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler   a reaction that only sends the new-post notification
    Ports/
      PostsArchive/                       IPostsArchive with its signature types in Models/
    Infrastructure/
      Persistence/                        module-wide store setup, with one folder per aggregate
        Posts/                            PostRepository with its stored documents and mapping
      PostsArchive/                       PostsArchiveWriter, one writer per section
    WebApi/
      Posts/
        CreateDraft/                      Endpoint, RequestModel, ResponseModel
        GetPost/
        ListPosts/
        ExportPosts/                      endpoint
  Customers/                              two aggregates: Domain holds one plural folder per aggregate
    Contracts/
      CustomerAccounts/  CustomerAccountId, one On{Fact}/ folder per fact, and the public queries and public commands of the account aggregate
      Consents/          ConsentId, one On{Fact}/ folder per fact, and the public queries and public commands of the consent aggregate
    Domain/
      CustomerAccounts/
      Consents/
    Application/
      CustomerAccounts/
        RestrictAccount/
      Consents/
        GrantConsent/
      ReadModels/
        OrderHistories/                   a read model of another module's published facts
    WebApi/
      CustomerAccounts/
        RestrictAccount/
      Consents/
        GrantConsent/
```

Module, aggregate, and use case order follows `litespec/core/backend-architecture#organize-code-by-module-aggregate-and-use-case`. A use case own models stay in its folder, and any other type sits in the layer folder owning it, as `litespec/core/backend-architecture#place-a-type-at-the-lowest-folder-that-holds-its-consumers` states. An event handler or job lives with what it runs and carries the mark naming its reaction.

provisions.heading: Validate Query Input
provisions.evidence: Does every query with paging, filters, or ranges declare a query validator? Look at each such query beside the pipeline validators.
provisions.statement: Each query carrying paging, filters, or ranges MUST declare a query validator run by the pipeline.
provisions.rationale: An unvalidated page size or range reaches the store unchecked, with each handler clamping its own input or none doing it. One query validator per query answers to the same input rule as commands.
provisions.example: The Claimwick list-expenses query validates its page size through its query validator.

provisions.heading: Write Only Aggregates the Record Names
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `write-undeclared` (level S) for a handler that takes a repository whose aggregate sits outside the aggregates its record names in `writes` and `reads`; one domain repository serves each named aggregate.
provisions.statement: A command handler MUST write only the aggregates its record's `writes` names, through one domain repository per aggregate.
provisions.rationale: A write outside `writes` hides behavior the record left undescribed, so the stack reader fails it as `write-undeclared`. One repository per named aggregate keeps the handler inside its declared boundary, with the atomic multi-aggregate case named with its invariant by a decision record.
provisions.example: The Claimwick approve-expense handler takes the expense repository and no other. Staging a second aggregate fails the check without a record declaring `consistency: atomic` over both with its decision.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case Its Own Models
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2019` for a use case folder referencing a type in another use case folder, and `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a message, result or transport-model file outside a use-case folder.
provisions.statement: A message, result, result part, transport model or mapping MUST belong to exactly one use case and sit in its folder, so two use cases that need the same shape each declare their own.
provisions.rationale: A shared shape couples two use cases that change for different reasons: one use case adds a field, and the other starts returning it. Counting consumers for shapes moves messages and results out of their use cases into module folders that hold more models than behavior. A copied shape costs a few lines and decides nothing, so it drifts into no wrong answer. A rule is different: two copies of a rule disagree, so a rule lives once in Domain where every use case reads it. Kernel values are the exception: money, typed identifiers, dates, and closed sets the Kernel owns come referenced directly from any layer the layer table allows, and copying one into a use case folder breaks the rule.
provisions.example: The submit-expense and approve-expense use cases each return the expense they acted on. Each declares its own result with the fields its caller needs, and neither result lives in `Domain/Expenses/`.

provisions.heading: Give Every Module Relationship One Direction
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-dependency-invalid` for a cycle in the module dependency graph over Contracts references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to facts.
provisions.statement: Every relationship between two modules MUST have one direction, so the module dependency graph over Contracts references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to facts holds no cycle.
provisions.rationale: A relationship with two directions says each module builds on the other, so neither has a seam to split along. One direction per relationship keeps the graph acyclic: A depends on B with A referencing B's Contracts, sending B's public queries or public commands, or reacting to B's facts, and no chain of such edges returns to its start. A cycle means a concept is split across two modules, and the fix moves the concept into one module, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#merge-modules-that-need-each-others-model`. Settled by [decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag](decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, reporting depends on spending through its declared edges to spending's public queries, and spending depends on nothing. A spending edge back to reporting closes a cycle and is reported naming both modules and the edges.

provisions.heading: Group a Folder That Holds Past Twenty Files
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `folder-ungrouped` for a folder past 20 files that holds none of its allowed groupings.
provisions.statement: A folder that holds past 20 files MUST hold the grouping folders the closed set of its place allows.
provisions.rationale: A folder past 20 files with no groupings reads as one long listing: a reader finds a file by search alone, and review misses what the folder holds. Each kind of place has a short closed list of grouping folders. A use case folder holds everything flat with no groupings: it stays small with fan-out living in a reaction or a job.
provisions.example: A `Domain/Expenses/` folder past 20 files groups each root action into its own `{Act}/` folder, so `Domain/Expenses/Submit/` mirrors `Application/Expenses/SubmitExpense/`.

provisions.heading: Merge Modules That Need Each Other's Model
provisions.evidence: Do any two modules take each other's model without merging or moving the shared concept? Look at the module pairs with edges both ways beside the module records.
provisions.statement: Two modules that need each other's model MUST merge into one module or move the shared concept into the module that owns it.
provisions.rationale: Two modules that each take the other's model have no seam between them: whatever the boundary, each side reaches across it. Merging them into one module, or moving the shared concept into the module that owns it, gives every concept one owner and every relationship one direction, under `litespec/core/backend-architecture#give-every-module-relationship-one-direction`. Sharing identifiers through the Kernel hides the cycle while the split concept stays split. Settled by [decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag](decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag).
provisions.example: Two modules passing each other's identifiers both ways merge into one module, and the shared concept lives in one aggregate with one owner.

provisions.heading: Organize Code by Module, Aggregate and Use Case
provisions.evidence: Is any module, aggregate, use case, notification, external-system, or read-model folder without a declared record, with a forbidden folder name, or with a technical-grouping name? Look at the folder paths in each module.
provisions.statement: Every module MUST organize its code as the module tree with one `Contracts/` folder, one `Domain/` folder holding one folder per declared aggregate in the plural, one `Ports/` folder holding one folder per driven port of the module, the `Application/` and `WebApi/` layer folders holding one plural aggregate folder with one folder per use case inside it plus one folder per module-level read, and one `Infrastructure/` folder holding `Persistence/` nested by aggregate, `Messaging/`, `Pipeline/`, and one adapter folder per port, using only the folder names its level allows.
provisions.rationale: One plural folder per declared aggregate under `Domain/`, one folder per driven port under `Ports/` with its adapter in `Infrastructure/`, `Messaging/` with the module's message pipeline pieces, one folder per aggregate under `Persistence/`, `Pipeline/` with the module's HTTP pipeline pieces, and one plural aggregate folder with one folder per use case inside each layer that serves it fix every type's address: a reader moves from a Domain aggregate to its handler, its repository, and its endpoint without a map. The closed folder names at each level keep that reading exact, because a folder outside the allowed set is reported and no second organization grows beside the tree. A module publishes what other modules reference in its `Contracts/` folder grouped by aggregate, every use case sits in the aggregate folder its record names or directly in the layer folders with a module-level read, and each reaction and job sits in the folder of the use case it runs. Every module keeps its plural aggregate folder in every layer, whatever its number of aggregates and even when the aggregate's name equals the module's. Settled by [decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs](decision/0063-place-each-trigger-with-what-it-runs). The module tree shape is settled by [decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module](decision/0107-kernel-platform-and-one-project-per-module). A folder named for a technical grouping rather than a module defeats the rule: the next unrelated type fits it too. `Shared`, `Common`, `Util`, `Helpers`, `Core`, and `Misc` inside a layer are the names that do this.
provisions.example:
```text
Spending/
  Contracts/
    Expenses/                 ExpenseId, OnExpenseReimbursed/ExpenseReimbursedModuleEvent, ReadExpense/ (query and result)
    Policies/                 the identifier, one On{Fact}/ folder per fact, and the public queries and public commands of the policy aggregate
  Domain/
    Expenses/                 Expense, the expense repository contract, and the act, part, fact, event, and refusal groupings
    Policies/
  Application/
    Expenses/
      SubmitExpense/
      ErasePersonalData/      the erase command, its handler, and the job that runs it
    ReadExpenseDirectory/     a module-level read: no aggregate folder
    Notifications/
      ApprovalReminder/       the reaction that only sends the approval reminder
  Ports/
    ReceiptPdf/               IReceiptPdf with its signature types in Models/
  Infrastructure/
    Persistence/              module-wide store setup, with one folder per aggregate
      Expenses/               the expense repository with its stored documents and mapping
    Messaging/                the domain-to-module event mapping, audit writers
    Pipeline/                 middleware, authorization conditions, authentication handlers
    ReceiptPdf/               the adapter implementing Ports/ReceiptPdf/, same folder name, with its wire types in Models/ and its collaborators in Parts/
  WebApi/
    Expenses/
      SubmitExpense/
```

The placement check asserts these folder names directly.

```text
fail when a type path contains Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc
```

provisions.heading: Own Each Layer's Contract Types
provisions.evidence: Is any inner layer's type reused as an outward contract, or any other module's port answer returned as-is, outside Kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers? Look at the results and transport models in each layer's folders.
provisions.statement: A layer MUST define its own outward contracts rather than reuse an inner layer's type or another module's contract type, except for Kernel values and aggregate typed identifiers.
provisions.rationale: With each layer defining its own outward contracts, a change to an inner shape stops at the boundary instead of forcing changes in every outer layer. Kernel values cross layer boundaries because the Kernel is shared by definition, and aggregate typed identifiers cross them because messages identify their targets. A provider's public query or public command answer stays inside the consumer's Application code, and a use case returns it in no result or transport model of its own. Domain takes plain values and identifiers, not a provider's result.

provisions.heading: Place a Type at the Lowest Folder That Holds Its Consumers
provisions.evidence: Is any type sitting above the lowest folder holding every consumer that references it? Look at each type beside its consumers, watching for Shared, Common, Util, Helpers, Core, or Misc folders.
provisions.statement: A type that is not a use case's own model MUST live at the lowest folder containing every consumer that names it.
provisions.rationale: Counting consumers gives each type exactly one folder, so placing a type takes no judgment. The lowest folder is the use case folder with one referencing use case, the module folder with several use cases of one module referencing it, and the product layer folder with several modules referencing it and no module between them. A domain rule several use cases of one aggregate reference lives in that aggregate's `Domain/{Aggregates}/` folder. Every port of a module lives in the module `Ports/` folder instead, whether one use case or many call it, with its adapter in `Infrastructure/`, so the consumer count places no port. A type another module references is published by its owning module in `Contracts/`; across modules a type stays unshared. A use case file's layer comes from its top folder in the module, and a type referenced from Infrastructure alone is an Infrastructure type. A type that exists to shape one contract's input or output stays with that contract, and a closed enumerated set stays whole.
