provisions.rationale: A criterion the feature cannot guarantee sets a test nobody passes: submitting an expense does not make the employee reimbursed by Friday, because the manager decides in their own time and finance runs reimbursements on its own schedule. A criterion the feature controls, such as showing the expense as waiting for approval the moment it is submitted, is built and checked. An outcome depending on people or on other features belongs to the goal the feature advances.
provisions.example: The library feature for due dates states that a reader sees the due date of every copy they hold, not that no reader pays a late fee, which depends on the reader returning the copy in time.

provisions.heading: State the Boundaries of Every Feature
provisions.evidence: Does every feature state what the feature leaves to other features, what it depends on, and its open questions? Look at `excludes` and the Boundaries section of each feature explanation file.
provisions.statement: A feature MUST state in `excludes` what it leaves to other features, which features it depends on, and each open question its owner has not decided.
provisions.rationale: A feature answering part of a problem reads as answering all of it unless its edges are written down. Builders then fill the gap with behavior nobody asked for. Naming what the feature leaves to other features, and which features it depends on, keeps each behavior in one feature. An open question written beside the feature reaches the owner as a question instead of reaching the code as a guess. Settled by [decision/0046-write-features-for-builders-and-testers](decision/0046-write-features-for-builders-and-testers).
provisions.example: The Claimwick approval feature leaves reminders for late decisions to the approval reminders feature, depends on the receipt threshold decision, and names one open question: whether a manager on leave hands decisions to a deputy.

provisions.heading: State the Brand on the Product
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a product `brand` outside the record schema.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST state the product brand in `brand`, with its reader, what the product is accountable for on every screen, three words the product is, three words it is not, and the rules every screen keeps.
provisions.rationale: The brand decides what every screen keeps, so it sits with the product every screen serves. Filed beside token values and component names in the implementation design contract, it sits outside what the records govern, and a project claiming only Intent and Behavior has nowhere to state it. Stated on the product record, the reader, the accountability, the two word lists, and the screen rules travel with the product itself. Settled by [decision/0089-specify-the-ui-as-a-blueprint](decision/0089-specify-the-ui-as-a-blueprint).
provisions.example: Claimwick states its reader as an employee submitting expenses from a phone, its accountability as showing what each expense waits for, `is` as calm, plain, and exact, `isNot` as playful, dense, and showy, and one `do` rule: every screen shows each amount with its currency code.

provisions.heading: State the Cost and Workaround of Every Problem
provisions.evidence: Does every problem state its workaround with its burden, and its cost with time, money, and risk kept apart? Look at the `workaround` and `cost` fields of each problem record beside the Current Workaround and Cost sections of its explanation file.
provisions.statement: A problem MUST state in `workaround` what the sufferer does instead today with the burden that workaround carries, and in `cost` what the pain costs them, with time, money and risk each in the sufferer's own units or the word `unknown`.
provisions.rationale: A pain with no cost and no workaround is a slogan: no reader tells a daily loss from a passing annoyance, and no feature is judged against the price of standing still. The workaround shows the pain is real enough to work around. Work done by hand is no burden on its own, so the workaround names the burden: the time it takes, what the sufferer repeats or has to remember, and what it still misses. Time, money, and risk stay apart because each is judged in its own units; a total mixing them hides which one matters. Where nobody priced the cost or named the workaround, `unknown` states the gap honestly. The explanation file restates `workaround` and `cost` in its Current Workaround and Cost sections. Settled by decision/0044-state-problems-by-failure-case.
provisions.example: A reader losing track of due dates pays late fees, an amount nobody has measured. The reader keeps a paper list of due dates, updates it at every loan and renewal, and cannot check it when the list stays at home.

provisions.heading: State the Measure on a Counted Requirement
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `requirement-measure-missing` for a requirement carrying `measure` without `check` or a passing run, and for a quality statement naming a number with no `measure`.
provisions.statement: A quality requirement whose statement names a number MUST carry `measure`.
provisions.rationale: A number nobody defines is checked in no way: the team tells what is counted in no manner. The `measure` names what is counted, so a quality statement naming a number without one is unfinished. A number in a functional or policy requirement asks for no `measure`. A requirement carrying `measure` needs a `check` and a passing run, and a quality statement naming a number with no `measure` is reported by `litespec model review` at level R.

provisions.heading: State What the Product Assumes Each Actor Knows
provisions.evidence: Does any actor `knowledge` item state a user knowledge as a fact about every user instead of an assumption of the product? Look at the `knowledge` items and the Knowledge section of each actor explanation.
provisions.statement: An actor MUST state in `knowledge` what the product assumes the actor knows, as an assumption of the product, and it states no user's knowledge as a fact about every user.
provisions.rationale: What a user knows decides what the product asks of them, so a reader needs the assumption stated where it applies. A fact such as "has no training in accounting" written in the opening paragraph reads as a claim about every user, and the product has no way to check it. Written as "Claimwick does not assume the employee knows the expense policy", it names the product assumption and the actor it applies to. The explanation file restates `knowledge` in its Knowledge section. Settled by [decision/0053-actors-by-responsibility-and-knowledge](decision/0053-actors-by-responsibility-and-knowledge).
provisions.example: The Claimwick employee actor states in its Knowledge section that Claimwick does not assume the employee knows the expense policy.

provisions.heading: State When Each Flow Finishes
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a flow record file missing `finishedWhen`.
provisions.statement: A flow MUST state its observable end in `finishedWhen`.
provisions.rationale: A flow without a stated end stops anywhere: the reader tells a finished flow from an abandoned one in no way, and serving records tell done from dropped in no way. `finishedWhen` states the observable end in one sentence, in product words.
provisions.example: `finishedWhen`: the employee holds the reimbursement.

provisions.heading: State When Each Flow Starts
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a flow record file missing `startedWhen`.
provisions.statement: A flow MUST state the observable state in which it starts in `startedWhen`, in one sentence.
provisions.rationale: A flow with its start in its summary, its Example, and its first step has three starting points, and a reader tells where the path begins in no way. `startedWhen` gives the start one home beside `finishedWhen`, which states the end, and a check reads it. The detail of one occasion belongs in the Example, not in the field. Settled by [decision/0048-state-the-start-and-branches-of-each-flow](decision/0048-state-the-start-and-branches-of-each-flow).
provisions.example: `startedWhen`: the employee has paid a work cost and has not yet submitted it.

provisions.heading: Summarize Every Flow Before Its Steps
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a flow record file missing `summary`.
provisions.statement: A flow MUST state its `summary` in up to four sentences before its steps.
provisions.rationale: Steps first teaches a cold reader the mechanics before the purpose. The summary states the flow in the actor terms: who takes the flow, what starts it, what good looks like, and the consequence at stake and for whom. The book renders it first on the page, so purpose comes before mechanics. `finishedWhen` stays the checkable end state; the summary carries the purpose no field checks. Settled by [decision/0068-call-ordered-steps-a-flow](decision/0068-call-ordered-steps-a-flow).
provisions.example: The library flow to borrow and return describes a reader holding a copy, starting at the shelf and ending with the copy back on its shelf, because a reader plans the next visit around the return.

provisions.heading: Treat Generated Research as Source Material
provisions.evidence: Does a research record or a decision stand behind every position built from generated records? Compare the change with the research and decisions it cites.
provisions.statement: An agent MUST treat records generated outside `docs/` as source material until a research record or a decision states the claim.
provisions.rationale: Records generated outside `docs/` mix verified facts, inferences, and recommendations in one confident voice. Treating them as source material with no authority keeps a recommendation from being built as if someone decided it. A research record or a decision restates the claim before anything rests on it.

provisions.heading: Write Flow Steps as Sentences with Ids
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a flow step missing `id`, `title`, or `statement`, or naming a use case; `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a step id outside the `step/<flow>.<act>` form, for a `<flow>` segment naming another flow, or for a positional act; `litespec model check` reports `identifier-title-invalid` for a step whose act is no word subsequence of its title; `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a step citation naming no step.
provisions.statement: Each flow step MUST carry its `id` as `step/<flow>.<act>`, its `title` naming its act in Title Case, its product sentence in `statement` naming one act of its performer and no use case, and in `carries` each requirement the step carries.
provisions.rationale: A step written as a product sentence reads in flow detail with no Behavior knowledge: it states what a person experiences, not which handler runs. The sentence states one act of its performer and ends with the product observable response after the act where one applies, as in "Finance reimburses the approved expense, and Claimwick pays the amount into the employee account". How the product computes that response stays in the cited requirement, and a second act of a person is a second step. Numbers, limits, and conditions stay in the cited requirement; the step states the experience only. The `id` names the step act as a verb phrase in kebab case, scoped by its flow, as `step/submit-and-reimburse.submit-expense`: use cases, reactions, and jobs point up with `serves` to that id, and the citation reads without opening the flow. The `title` names the same act in Title Case, as `Submit Expense`, and the act is the title words in kebab case. The book, the trace, and `model query` show the title, while the `statement` keeps the full sentence. A step naming its use case drags Behavior into Intent and breaks the flow detail every time Behavior renames. An act only numbering the step, such as `s3` or `step-2`, says nothing and breaks on every inserted step, so the act names what the performer does. The performer and the failure text are optional: a step names another actor only at a handoff in `actor`, or the system actor standing for the outside system when no person acts, and carries `failure` where the flow fails. Settled by [decision/0048-state-the-start-and-branches-of-each-flow](decision/0048-state-the-start-and-branches-of-each-flow).
provisions.example: The step `step/submit-and-reimburse.reimburse-expense` carries `Reimburse Expense` in `title`, states `Finance reimburses the approved expense.` in `statement`, and leaves use cases out; `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` names that id in `serves`.

provisions.heading: Allow Completion Only with a Current Fencing Value
provisions.evidence: Does any completion write succeed on a stale fencing value? Check the store write path and its fencing tests.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST mark completion only while its fencing value remains current.
provisions.rationale: A stale fencing value marks ownership that moved to another replica. The Worker marks completion while its value stays current, so one result lands per occurrence.

provisions.heading: Escape Formula-Leading Export Values
provisions.evidence: Does every exported value starting with a formula character go out escaped, outside the formula fields the team fills on purpose? Check the CSV and spreadsheet writers.
provisions.statement: A CSV or spreadsheet export MUST escape formula-leading values unless the team intentionally fills a field with a formula.
provisions.rationale: A value starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` turns into a live formula in the opener's spreadsheet, running with the opener's data. Escaping keeps data as data, except in a field the team fills with a formula on purpose.
provisions.example: The library product escapes a member note starting with `+` in its CSV export, while its total column keeps its formula.

provisions.heading: Name a Varying Time Zone by Its Source
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a schedule timezone that is neither a zone name nor a setting or field reference.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST state its time zone as a literal IANA zone or as the setting or aggregate field holding the zone.
provisions.rationale: One schedule serves tenants in many zones. A literal zone freezes one country into every run, while a setting or tenant field lets each run read its own zone.
provisions.example: Claimwick's nightly close names `setting/reporting.close-time-zone` instead of a literal zone, so the operator moves the close with one setting.

provisions.heading: Record the Schedule on the Job Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `schedule-invalid` (level G) for a job schedule that is neither an `every` duration nor a `cron` expression; each scheduled job record states its timezone.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST record its schedule in structured form with its timezone on its job record.
provisions.rationale: Tools read `every` or `cron` directly from the record, and the misfire behavior measures against the recorded time. A schedule in prose gives tools nothing to parse.

provisions.heading: Resume Batch Work from Its Cursor
provisions.evidence: Does every batch job name its resume position in its cursor, with a scenario for the remainder after a halfway failure? Check the job records and the scenario tests.
provisions.statement: A job that works through items in batches MUST name where resume state lives in its `cursor`.
provisions.rationale: A batch that fails halfway resumes instead of restarting. The cursor holds where the run stopped, so the next run continues past finished items instead of replaying them or skipping unfinished ones.

provisions.heading: Run One Command per Selected Item
provisions.evidence: Does every job run one command per item in its `selection` within its `batchSize`, each in its own unit of work? Check the job record selection and the handler code.
provisions.statement: A job MUST run one command per item in its `selection` within its `batchSize`, each in its own unit of work.
provisions.rationale: One item in its own unit of work replays alone after failure. A batch sharing one unit of work replays its finished items beside the failed one.

provisions.heading: Scope Command Idempotency by Occurrence
provisions.evidence: Does every retry of one occurrence use its occurrence identity as the idempotency key scope? Check the command idempotency keys.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job MUST use its occurrence identity as the command idempotency key scope.
provisions.rationale: Every retry of one occurrence replays the same scheduled business action. The occurrence identity scopes the key to that action, while a wider key merges separate occurrences into one.

provisions.heading: Scope Export Output to the Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every export store output under a tenant-scoped path in object storage? Check the export storage paths.
provisions.statement: An export MUST store its output under a tenant-scoped object-storage path.
provisions.rationale: Export addresses follow a pattern callers guess. A tenant-scoped path keeps each tenant's exports under its own prefix, so a guessed address stays inside the guesser's own data.
provisions.example: Claimwick stores each tenant's expense export under that tenant's prefix, so one tenant opens only its own files.

provisions.heading: State Clock Behavior for Business-Local Schedules
provisions.evidence: Does every business-local schedule record its IANA zone and the skipped and repeated local-time behavior? Check each schedule record.
provisions.statement: A business-local schedule MUST record an IANA time-zone identifier and define skipped and repeated local-time behavior.
provisions.rationale: Daylight-saving transitions omit one local hour and repeat another. The record names the zone and both behaviors, so no transition drops or doubles the local work.

provisions.heading: Tolerate Duplicate Execution
provisions.evidence: Does any job Command or side effect record more than one accepted effect after a replayed occurrence? Check the replay tests.
provisions.statement: A scheduled job Command and side effect MUST tolerate duplicate execution after lease or process failure.
provisions.rationale: A lease or process failure replays a job whose completion stayed uncertain. A command that absorbs the repeat keeps one accepted effect, while work assuming exactly-once execution breaks on the first uncertain failure.
provisions.example: Claimwick's nightly close replays the close command for the same scheduled instant after a Worker restart, and the second run records no second close.

provisions.heading: Check Shape at Compile Time and Dates at Startup
provisions.evidence: Is any date rule left to a compile-time check, or any shape rule left to a startup check? Look at the build diagnostics beside the startup validation of each set.
provisions.statement: Shape and cross-references in code MUST be checked at compile time, while overlaps, gaps, and coverage of the current period are checked at startup.
provisions.rationale: Row types, roles, and references between model types are fixed by the code, and the compiler proves them on every build. Dates depend on the rows a set ships, so only loading the set proves that its periods overlap nowhere, leave no gap, and cover today. Startup is the first moment the whole set is known, and a failure there names the row before any request uses it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's build proves that every per-diem row carries a country, an amount, dates, and a source. At startup the travel model rejects a German row overlapping another or leaving the current year uncovered, and the product stops serving until it is fixed. The rejection raises `InvalidOperationException`, as `TravelRegistry.Validate` does.

provisions.heading: Give Each Knowledge Area One Model
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `knowledge-set-missing` for a variant an area names with no set, and `knowledge-variation-undeclared` for rows that differ by variant without a declared dimension.
provisions.statement: A knowledge area MUST have one knowledge model and one knowledge set per variant of its dimension, keeping its one table in the model when it varies by nothing.
provisions.rationale: One model gives every caller the same types and lookups, and one set per variant keeps values for a country or a branch apart without copying the types into each set. An area varying by nothing needs no set. A second shape for one table leaves readers unsure which carries the values.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `travel` area has the `Claimwick.Travel` model and a set for each country its rates cover, while its approval-target table, varying by nothing, stays in the model.

provisions.heading: Keep Knowledge Sets Free of Logic
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2039` for a method or property body in a knowledge set that does more than return or construct rows; a static `Parse`, `From`, `FromCode`, `Of` or `Create` call on a named type with only literal arguments, such as a typed key built from its text, counts as constructing.
provisions.statement: A knowledge set MUST hold only rows built through its model's constructors, with any behavior a variant needs added as a case in the model's closed set of strategies.
provisions.rationale: A set deciding something splits one rule into one copy per variant, and the copies drift. Rows built through model constructors carry the model types and validation. Where a country or a branch needs a treatment data alone states poorly, a case in the model strategy set carries the rule and the set selects it, so every variant shares the same behavior.
provisions.example: Claimwick's Germany and Netherlands sets list dated per-diem rows and nothing else. Where a country needs a different rounding of a partial day, the rule becomes a case in the model rounding strategy set, selected by the set's data.

provisions.heading: Name a Role Not a Row
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-role-missing` (level G) for a required role played by no row.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table MUST list in `requiredRoles` the roles its citing rules read, with each role played by a row in `role`.
provisions.rationale: A data key names one row of one data set, so code naming the key breaks where another data set keys its rows differently or not at all. A role names what the product needs, such as the standard target, and each data set says which row plays it.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `reference-data/spending.decision-target` lists `requiredRoles: [standard]`, and both its rows play `standard`, so the approval rules read the standard target without naming a row.

provisions.heading: Read Knowledge by Role and Date
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2040` for a knowledge key built from a string literal outside a knowledge set.
provisions.artifact: knowledge-model, knowledge-set, command-handler, query-handler, reaction, job
provisions.statement: Operational code MUST read knowledge by role and date through the model's typed keys, naming no set and building no key from a string literal.
provisions.rationale: A data key names one row of one set, so code naming it breaks where another set keys its rows differently. A role states what the caller needs, and each set says which row plays it. A typed key built through the model keeps the caller from spelling a country or a date into a raw string.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense submission asks the travel model for the `FullDay` per-diem role on the travel date. It builds the key through the model and leaves country projects and row keys alone. A literal such as `new TravelKey("DE")` is reported.

provisions.heading: Read Knowledge Through Its Model
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS2038` for a module assembly referencing a knowledge set assembly: a project under `Knowledge/` named `<Product>.<Area>.<Variant>` of the same product that references its model, so another vendor's packages are out of scope. It reports `LS1001` for an outer-layer reference in a model outside the dependency-injection, logging and options libraries.
provisions.artifact: knowledge-model, knowledge-set, command-handler, query-handler, reaction, job
provisions.statement: A module MUST reach a knowledge area through its knowledge model, leaving a set to be referenced only by a host that registers it.
provisions.rationale: A module naming a set ties its code to one country or branch, so adding a variant means editing the module. The model gives modules one stable surface, and a host registers each set with that model at startup. The model owns its registry, its composition and its startup validation, so it references the dependency-injection, logging and options libraries those need.
provisions.example: Claimwick's spending module asks `Claimwick.Travel` for a per-diem role on the expense date and leaves country projects alone. The API host registers `Claimwick.Travel.Germany` and `Claimwick.Travel.Netherlands` with the model at startup.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Missing Rule with a Reason
provisions.evidence: Does any knowledge lookup return a null or a default when no row is in force, or end without naming the missing rule? Look at each lookup beside the use-case refusals.
provisions.statement: A lookup with no row in force MUST end its use case in a refusal naming the missing role, date, and variant.
provisions.rationale: A null or a default value spends a value no rule supports, with no record of why. A refusal with a reason points the operator at the missing row, and the use case records the refusal beside its other endings. The model derives that ending as `result/<use-case>.rule-not-stated`, and throws the product rule-not-stated refusal type deriving the kernel domain exception.
provisions.example: Where no German per-diem row covers a travel date, Claimwick's submission ends in a refusal naming the `FullDay` role, that date, and Germany, instead of paying zero. Claimwick's travel model throws `TravelRuleMissingException`, deriving the kernel `DomainException` and carrying the code `travel.rule-missing`.

provisions.heading: Validate Reference Data Before Serving
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-data-key-unknown`, `reference-data-value-invalid`, and `reference-data-role-missing` (level G) for a cross-reference to a missing key, a value outside `choices`, and a required role played by no row.
provisions.statement: Each reference-data table MUST hold only rows that resolve their cross-references, stay within its closed set where one is listed, and play its required roles.
provisions.rationale: A broken cross-reference, an unlisted value, or a missing role each fails at read time, far from the row causing it. Validating the whole table before serving it moves each failure to startup, naming the file and row. The host refuses to start until the tables it loads validate.
provisions.example: A Claimwick row referring to `reference-data/spending.decision-target#target-2030` is reported, naming the file and row, before the product serves the table.

provisions.heading: Cite Shared Provisions in Their Published Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A shared provision citation MUST use its published identifier.
provisions.rationale: A shared provision is cited across projects, so its identifier reads the same everywhere. The published `litespec/<page>#<slug>` form stays fixed, while project records use the type forms above.

provisions.heading: Keep Names an Outside Standard Fixes
provisions.evidence: Was any fixed name renamed to fit the grammar? Check the Gherkin fields and CloudEvents attributes the change touches.
provisions.statement: Every name an outside standard fixes MUST stay exactly as that standard spells it.
provisions.rationale: A name an outside standard fixes belongs to that standard: renaming `given` to fit the word classes breaks each Gherkin reader. The grammar stays complete by exempting exactly these names instead of adding a list of exceptions. Gherkin and CloudEvents names are the only exemptions.
provisions.example: A Claimwick scenario keeps `given`, `when`, and `then`, which the word-class table gives no class.

provisions.heading: Keep Wire Codes Stable
provisions.evidence: Does any wire code in the contract break the values deployed clients branch on? Check the wire codes in the contract against the deployed clients.
provisions.statement: A wire code MUST stay unchanged once clients read it.
provisions.rationale: Wire codes travel to deployed clients, which branch on their exact values. Renaming a code that clients already read breaks each deployed reader that compares the old value, with no record the reader opens to learn the new one.

provisions.heading: Name a Boolean as a Predicate
provisions.evidence: Does every boolean field read as a predicate with no `is` or `has` prefix? Check the boolean fields the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every boolean field MUST read as a present-tense predicate that is true about the record when the value is true.
provisions.rationale: A boolean without a prefix is a fact about the record: `applies` says the constraint applies, and `recorded` says the entry is recorded. An `is` or `has` prefix adds a word that repeats what the value already says. The predicate form keeps each boolean readable in a sentence about its record.
provisions.example: Claimwick marks an applying constraint with `applies: true` instead of `isApplicable: true`.

provisions.heading: Name Commands as Verbs and Flags by What They Set
provisions.evidence: Does every subcommand read as a verb and every flag as its mode or value? Check the commands and flags the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every subcommand MUST read as a verb and every flag as the mode or value it sets.
provisions.rationale: A verb names what the command does, so `check` names an action without reading its arguments. A flag that names its mode or value reads the same way at each call site, and kebab-case keeps multiword flags writable without quotes. Stable exit codes let scripts distinguish a clean run, a blocking finding, and bad arguments.
provisions.example: The release check runs as `litespec model check --release` and exits 1 on a blocking finding.

provisions.heading: Name Each Date by What It Marks
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `FIELD_NAME_SHAPE` diagnostic for a date field.
provisions.statement: Every date field MUST end in `On` for a recorded date or carry a name that states what the date does.
provisions.rationale: A recorded date says when something happened or until when it holds: `readOn` says when an outside source was read, and `expiresOn` says when a waiver ends. `effectiveFrom` opens a validity span. The shape shows which dates record the world and which open a span.
provisions.example: A Claimwick constraint carries `readOn` on each source with the date the source was read, and a waiver carries `expiresOn` with the date it ends.

provisions.heading: Name Each Field by Its Word Class
provisions.evidence: Does every field use the name its word class gives it? Check the field names the change adds against the word-class table.
provisions.statement: Every record field MUST use the name its word class gives it in the word-class table.
provisions.rationale: One grammar means a reader who learned `serves` on a flow reads `serves` on a use case the same way. Each class answers one question about the field: whether it identifies, links, classifies, narrates, conditions, or reasons. Only names an outside standard fixes stand outside this grammar. Settled by [decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar](decision/0006-one-field-naming-grammar) on the evidence in [research/field-naming-evidence](research/field-naming-evidence) and [research/cross-layer-trace-evidence](research/cross-layer-trace-evidence).
provisions.example: The Claimwick flow `submit-an-expense` names its goal in `serves` and states each step in `statement`.

provisions.heading: Name Each Finding Code by Subject and Problem
provisions.evidence: Does every finding code read as subject-problem with a problem word from the table? Check the finding codes the change adds against the problem-word table.
provisions.statement: Every finding code MUST read as `<subject>-<problem>` with the problem drawn from the problem-word table.
provisions.rationale: A code in subject-problem form tells a reader what the finding is about and what is wrong with it without opening the message. A closed set of problem words, each with one meaning, keeps codes comparable across tools: one word for absent, one for expired, and no synonyms. The problem-word table lists each word with its meaning and an example.
provisions.example: A use case with no scenario takes the code `use-case-scenario-missing`.

provisions.heading: Read Each Field Name in Its Record Type
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` reports `FIELD_NAME_SHAPE` for a field named after a record type that holds anything but links to that type, for a link verb that holds no links, and for a date name that holds no date; reports strict camelCase, abbreviation, and American spelling breaks; reports `is*` and `has*` prefixes on booleans; reports `*When` and `*Because` fields holding non-strings, `*On`, `effectiveFrom`, and `effectiveTo` fields holding non-`isoDate` values, and `*Timeout`, `*Window`, `*Delay`, and `duration` fields holding non-durations; and reports a retired synonym (`coverage`, `displayStates`, `keyScope`, `valueType`, `basis`, `payload`, `rowShape`, `records`) and a field outside the contextual FieldCatalog registered per `(RecordType, FieldName)`.
provisions.statement: Every field name MUST use its canonical word for its structural role and read naturally in its record type's context, with the context-specific value shape the FieldCatalog states for its record type.
provisions.rationale: A reader meets a field inside one record, so each name reads naturally where it stands. The same canonical word carries context-specific values and shapes per record type: `states` holds lifecycle states on `aggregate` and UI states on `screen`, `scope` holds coverage on `constraint` and key scope on `idempotency`, and `fields` holds typed members on events, read models, and object shapes. The FieldCatalog registers every field per `(RecordType, FieldName)` with its word class, shape, and meaning, while retired synonyms such as `coverage`, `displayStates`, `keyScope`, `valueType`, `basis`, `payload`, `rowShape`, and `records` fail validation. A name that names a record type, such as `rules`, always holds links to that type. A Claimwick constraint states its legal rules in `obligations`, because `rules` holds links to rule records. This provision supersedes the global single-shape choice that locked one shape per name, settled by [decision/0123-name-fields-in-record-context](../intent/decisions/0123-name-fields-in-record-context/0123-name-fields-in-record-context.md).
provisions.example: A module states what its area covers in `covers` and what it does not cover in `excludes`. An actor states the acts the product holds it to in `responsibilities`, the one record type that carries that name. A setting names its configuration path in `configurationPath`, and a research source carries its label in `name`.

provisions.heading: Record the Project Vocabulary as Data
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `glossary-invalid` for a glossary that fails the glossary schema.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST record each term, its rejected synonyms, the scope of each rejection, and its mannered terms in the project glossary satisfying `schemas/glossary.schema.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: A glossary column headed "Avoid" helps a reader but gives a tool nothing to check. A rule held as data reaches the reader and the validator alike, so the same rejection appears in prose guidance and in diagnostics.
provisions.example:
A rejection carries the scope that binds it, because a word that is right in one module is wrong in another.

```json
{ "id": "term/customer", "term": "customer", "meaning": "A person or company that buys.",
  "rejected": [{ "word": "client", "scope": "^domain/modules/orders/",
    "reason": "client names the API consumer" }] }
```

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Identifier Citation
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a citation naming no written record.
provisions.statement: Every identifier citation MUST resolve to a written record.
provisions.rationale: A citation is a promise that a record exists at the other end. A citation that names nothing sends the reader searching for a record nobody wrote, so the model check fails it.

provisions.heading: Use Every Identifier Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-duplicate` for an identifier used twice.
provisions.statement: A record identifier MUST name exactly one record.
provisions.rationale: An identifier used twice names two records at once, so each citation of it points to both records. One use per identifier keeps each citation single-valued.
provisions.example: Two records named `use-case/spending.submit-expense` leave the model check reporting the duplicate on the second record.

provisions.heading: Use the Declared Record Identifier Grammar
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-invalid` for a record identifier outside the declared grammar.
provisions.statement: A consumer record identifier MUST use the form the Project Model states for its type, as `type/home.name` in kebab-case, with its name in the name form the record-name table gives its type and one to six lowercase hyphenated words.
provisions.rationale: The type names the record kind and `home.name` names the owning module or set, so an identifier resolves with no lookup table: a reader who sees `use-case/spending.submit-expense` knows it is a use case in the spending module without opening it. If two types shared one form, a citation needs its surrounding page to make sense, and search returns the wrong records. One grammar for each record kind keeps identifiers writable by hand and checkable by tool. The [Project Model](model.md) states the form each type uses, and the Identifier Forms section above states the name rules and checks. A name in the word class of what the record is shows the type without opening the record: a verb opens a use case, a noun phrase opens a goal, and a past participle opens a domain event. One name form per type keeps listings scannable and citations writable by hand. The record-name table lists the Intent, Behavior, and governance forms together. Settled by [decision/0077-use-the-standard-term-for-each-concept](decision/0077-use-the-standard-term-for-each-concept). A short hyphenated name is easy to read aloud in review and stays stable when the wording of the record changes. A long name gets shortened differently at each citation, and the shortcuts become competing names for one record.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` is a reaction owned by the spending module, and `step/submit-and-reimburse.attach-receipt` is the step where the employee attaches the receipt. Claimwick names the flow `submit-an-expense`, the use case `submit-expense`, and the setting `receipt-threshold`, each in one to six words. `decision/0001-receipt-threshold` counts its number as one word.

provisions.heading: Write Each Finding Message as a Fact
provisions.evidence: Does every finding message state one present-tense fact opening with the subject and identifier? Check the messages the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every finding message MUST state one present-tense fact that opens with the subject title and its quoted identifier.
provisions.rationale: A message that states a fact reads the same in the terminal and the book: both show what is true. Advice belongs in the finding table on the [model command page](../tools/model.md), where it is written once beside the code instead of repeated in each occurrence. Analyzer diagnostics keep their `LS` numbers and follow the same message rule.
provisions.example: A flow step with no serving use case reports `Flow step 'step/book-a-room.confirm-booking' is served by no use case.`

provisions.heading: Write Each Value in the Value Style
provisions.evidence: Does every statement, meaning, rationale, condition, failure, and title value use its row's style? Check the values the change adds against the value-style table.
provisions.statement: Every `statement`, `meaning`, `rationale`, `*Because`, `*When`, `condition`, `failure`, and `title` value MUST use the value style the value-style table states.
provisions.rationale: Values are read far more than they are written, in records, in the book, and in tool output. One written form per value means a period or a capital letter counts as part of the value, not a styling choice. The value-style table ends each row with the mechanical test the value meets. Settled by [decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values](decision/0011-one-grammar-for-names-and-values) on the evidence in [research/naming-grammar-evidence](research/naming-grammar-evidence).
provisions.example: A Claimwick flow step states "The traveller pays for the booking."

provisions.heading: Write in American English
provisions.evidence: Does any word use British spelling? Check the field names, enum values, and prose the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every field name and enum value MUST use American spelling.
provisions.rationale: One spelling per word keeps each term defined once and checked once: `license` in one record and `licence` in another splits each search and each listing. American spelling is the project spelling for field names and enum values; prose spelling follows the [Writing Standard](writing.md). Each British form is a rejected word beside its American spelling.
provisions.example: Claimwick writes `license` and `pseudonymize` in field names, values, and prose.

provisions.heading: Add Behavior Detail When Specifying Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `record-link-missing`, `step-use-case-missing`, `erasure-undeclared`, or `setting-requirement-missing` finding across Behavior records.
provisions.statement: Behavior that fulfills an Intent record MUST add the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, data classes with erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access that the Intent record implies but leaves unstated.
provisions.rationale: An Intent promise says what the product owes in product words, without saying how the system keeps it. Behavior turns each promise into the states, invariants, refusals, consistency, erasure positions, freshness, and tenant-scoped access that keep it. A detail counts as implied where every faithful fulfillment of the promise needs it and where no actor meets it as an outcome, limit, or figure the promise leaves unnamed. Without that detail, each implementer fills the gap with a guess, and two guesses about the same promise diverge. Settled by [decision/0047-cite-a-source-for-each-constraint-rule](decision/0047-cite-a-source-for-each-constraint-rule), world facts enter Intent as cited research or constraints before Specify adds detail.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimbursement promise gains an entity with Approved and Reimbursed states, a refusal for an expense that is already reimbursed, and atomic consistency over one aggregate.

provisions.heading: Implement Only Declared Behavior
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded`, `use-case-unrecorded`, `reaction-unrecorded`, `job-unrecorded`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, or `refusal-unimplemented` finding across the implementation.
provisions.statement: Implementation MUST add only the code shapes its stack pages fix and no observable outcome, edge, write, or access grant its Behavior records leave undeclared.
provisions.rationale: Stack pages fix the code shapes: the handler, the repository call, and the published domain event each have one prescribed form. An extra outcome, edge, write, or access grant splits the project into a specification saying one thing and code doing another. A record sentence describing a possible future specifies nothing: code builds no interface, provider list, or hook for a feature no record specifies.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense handler returns a code no result declares. The run fails `result-undeclared`, and the fix declares the result or removes the code. A record sentence saying a country pack adds a national audit file specifies no feature: the code builds no audit file provider for it, and the national audit file arrives as its own specified feature.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario Through the Public Boundary
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `use-case-scenario-missing` or `proves-unreached` finding across scenarios and tests.
provisions.statement: At large size or with the `bdd` extension, each scenario MUST be proved by one test through the public boundary.
provisions.rationale: Small projects carry no scenarios unless the `bdd` extension enables them, so the rule binds large projects and small projects with the extension. A scenario is the leaf of the record tree, so one test through the public boundary joins each leaf to running behavior.
provisions.example: Claimwick, a large project, carries a scenario for its missing-receipt refusal, and one test proves it by submitting an expense without a receipt through the endpoint.

provisions.heading: Raise Open Needs as Owner Questions or Backlog Items
provisions.evidence: Does every need the upper layer neither states nor implies have a question to the owner with a recommendation or a backlog item? Check the added records from a lower record layer beside the owner questions and the backlog.
provisions.statement: Where the upper record layer neither states nor implies a need, such as a refusal, eligibility condition, limit, or a figure the owner sets, travel up as a question to the owner with a recommendation or as a backlog item, never as a record or code.
provisions.rationale: The lower layer decides nothing the upper layer leaves unstated and unexpressed, so the need travels up with its context instead of turning into a guess. A question carries product choices to the person answering for them. A backlog item keeps the rest where it stays visible until specified. The specification is closed: an agent builds what it states and nothing more. A figure the owner sets is one such need: the [Project Model](model.md) carries the one list of owner-set figures, and each one binds the product to buyers, markets, or law, so an accountable person decides it. A figure the business changes while the system runs is aggregate data, not a setting: its range is a rule with a refusal, and its change is a use case with access and audit. A setting is operator configuration the running system reads. A question carries a recommendation with each figure: a figure without one asks the owner to research from nothing, while a recommendation gives a default to accept or correct. Grouping figures by subject lets the owner answer one set at a time.
provisions.example: Claimwick meets a need for a refusal of expenses with a future date, which the receipt promise leaves unstated and unexpressed. The need becomes a question to the owner instead of a rule an agent writes. A receipt threshold the promise leaves unnamed travels up as a question with a recommended figure the same way.

provisions.heading: Write Each Layer from the Layer Above It
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `behavior-unrecorded` finding for a refusal literal or a screen that calls no endpoint, and reports `mark-missing` for a code element that carries no mark.
provisions.statement: Each record below Intent MUST be written from a record in the record layer above it.
provisions.rationale: Without a parent above it, a lower record carries a promise from above or invents a new one, and reviewers tell the two apart poorly. Implementers then build from guesses, and two guesses about the same gap diverge. Writing each record from the layer above keeps one chain from promise to proof, so a gap shows as a missing parent instead of silent invention.
provisions.example: Claimwick's submit-expense handler carries a positivity guard with no rule above it. The agent writes the missing rule or reports the gap, and the guard stays until the record is written. Behavior with no parent is recorded or reported, not deleted for lacking one. A test with no record above it is a finding the team resolves by writing the missing record or reporting the gap. It is deleted only where a reviewer establishes that the behavior it protects is obsolete, redundant or wrong, and the pull request says so.

provisions.heading: Default to Hard Delete
provisions.evidence: Does every deletion with no retention or restore requirement remove the row in the delete transaction? Check the delete transaction code.
provisions.statement: A lifecycle implementation MUST use hard delete when no accepted retention or restore requirement applies.
provisions.rationale: Removing the row deletes the least and keeps the least: no hidden state, no filtered queries, and no purge job to watch. Rows kept without a duty still answer subject-access exports with data the product promised to delete.
provisions.example: A Claimwick expense deleted without a retention duty removes the expense row in the delete transaction.

provisions.heading: Preserve Legal-Hold Data
provisions.evidence: Does every retention run preserve held data past its retention date? Check the retention run code beside the hold records.
provisions.statement: A retention job MUST preserve data under legal hold.
provisions.rationale: A hold suspends the duty to delete, and the named data stays until the hold releases, even past its retention date. A job that ignores the hold destroys evidence the organization had a duty to keep.
provisions.example: Claimwick retention skips receipts under a tax hold and deletes them once the release record resumes their retention.

provisions.heading: Keep Stable Error Codes Locale-Neutral
provisions.evidence: Is every stable API error code identical across locales? Check the error code values in each locale's responses.
provisions.statement: A stable API error code MUST NOT change by locale.
provisions.rationale: Support tools and integrations match on the code. A code that varies per language forces each consumer to list every translation before handling one failure.
provisions.example: Claimwick returns the same code for a missing receipt in every locale, with the human-readable message translated beside it.

provisions.heading: Preserve Locale-Neutral Business Data
provisions.evidence: Is every domain value and API contract locale-neutral outside an explicitly localized exchange? Check the domain values and contracts.
provisions.statement: Domain values and API contracts MUST remain locale-neutral unless a use case explicitly exchanges localized content.
provisions.rationale: An expense state stored in Dutch breaks for an English reader, and a contract that shifts per language forces each consumer to handle wording before reading data. The interface translates for display, while the stored value and the wire contract stay in one form.
provisions.example: Claimwick stores the expense state as one code and renders the Dutch or English label from the catalog. A product description a merchant writes per language names its exchange explicitly.

provisions.heading: Derive a General Rule from a Consumer Need
provisions.evidence: Does a change prompted by one consumer name the general need and check the rule against products unlike that consumer? Check the change's wording, the products it tests, and any need left in the consumer as a convention or waiver.
provisions.statement: A change prompted by one consumer's need MUST state the general need behind it, design and check the rule against products unlike that consumer, apply the rule only where it makes sense across them, and leave a need that holds for one consumer alone in that consumer as a project convention or waiver rather than in LiteSpec.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec is a contract many unrelated products adopt. A rule shaped around one product's domain misfits each other product and teaches their readers a world they never meet. Checking the rule against an expense product, a library product, a consumer app with no organization, and a client-only app with no hosted sign-in, where the provision applies, keeps the rule sound for each.
provisions.example: A consumer asks for development seed data. LiteSpec adds a cast-based seeding default that works for an expense product and a library product alike, not a rule about one product's records, and a need that only that consumer has stays in its project as a convention or waiver.

provisions.heading: Keep Consumers Out of LiteSpec
provisions.evidence: Does the change name a consumer project or carry a consumer's domain vocabulary? Grep the change for consumer names and for vocabulary of a consumer's domain.
provisions.statement: Every page, provision, example, test fixture, template, decision, changelog entry, and tool message in LiteSpec MUST name no consumer project and carry no consumer domain vocabulary, records, flows, figures, people, or products, drawing examples only from the Claimwick expense product or the library product.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec serves many products in unrelated business areas. A reader who meets one consumer's name or domain vocabulary learns a world outside their own work, and a rule shaped around that domain misfits each product outside it. Claimwick and the library product are the shared examples, so each reader meets the same expenses and library holdings whatever product is built.
provisions.example: A page that explains a rule shows a Claimwick expense submitted by Ava, or a library patron borrowing a book, rather than an example lifted from a consumer's records.

provisions.heading: List Every Stack, Shape, and Extension in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `EXTENSION_UNLISTED` for an extension page no manifest entry lists, `LAYER_UNREACHABLE` for a page no stack selection reaches, and `MANIFEST_ANALYZER_PIN` for an analyzer pin that differs from the analyzer project version.
provisions.statement: The LiteSpec manifest MUST list every stack, shape, extension, and version pin the release carries.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the release record that tools read: stacks and shapes decide which pages apply, extensions decide which conditional bundles a project selects from, and pins decide which versions build. A stack, shape, extension, or pin the manifest omits is one no consumer selects and no tool resolves. Listing all of them in one file keeps the release reproducible from its tag.
provisions.example: The manifest lists the `delivery` extension with its page path `docs/ext/delivery.md` and its `project` activation scope.

provisions.heading: Mark the Tools with the Provisions They Follow
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits `MARK_MISSING` for a class with a method and no `follows` mark in a source project under `apps/`, and `MARK_UNRESOLVED` for a `follows` or `proves` mark in a .NET project under `apps/`, outside its `Fixtures/` folders, that names no provision in `docs/reference/provisions.md`.
provisions.statement: Every top-level class that declares a method in a .NET source project under `apps/`, and every test that verifies a provision, MUST name its provision in a mark: a `follows` mark on the class and a `proves` mark on the test.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec's own tools are technical classes: they serve no product record, and each exists because a provision requires a check, a reader, or a generator of its shape. A `follows` mark is the reverse index from that code to the provision, so a retired or renamed provision finds each class still built for it. A `proves` mark finds the tests that verify its check. LiteSpec keeps the research and decisions behind its provisions as records under `docs/intent/`, in the shapes a consumer uses; its provisions remain its specification, and the marks point at them directly. The site under `apps/site` is TypeScript with no mark form in the maintainer tool, so it carries no marks.
provisions.example: The .NET scenario reader carries `/// <follows>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</follows>`, and the test that confirms a scenario driven through a shared probe step carries `/// <proves>litespec/core/model#name-the-lowest-record-each-test-proves</proves>`.

provisions.heading: Model a Reported Spec Gap Before More Code
provisions.evidence: Does each reported spec gap have a LiteSpec model change that cites the gap before the consumer writes more code around it? Check the gap report beside the record type, field, or provision that answers it.
provisions.statement: When a consumer's agent reports a spec gap, a maintainer MUST model the missing concept in LiteSpec as a record type, a field, or a provision, with the change citing the gap, before the consumer writes more code around it.
provisions.rationale: An agent that meets a concept LiteSpec cannot express stops instead of bending the code, so the gap is a request for a contract change. Answering the question alone leaves the next agent to meet the same gap, and the consumer's substitutes grow. Modelling the concept in LiteSpec gives each consumer one decided shape, and citing the gap in the change shows which need the provision answers. The rule is checked against products unlike the consumer that reported it, as `litespec/core/maintaining#derive-a-general-rule-from-a-consumer-need` states.
provisions.example: An agent reports that Claimwick's per-diem rates have no home because the checks accept a rate table only as an external system. The maintainer adds the dated reference data and the rule that cites it, cites the gap in the change, and only then does the consumer replace the substitute.

provisions.heading: Publish a LiteSpec Release from a Tag
provisions.evidence: `dotnet test --solution LiteSpec.slnx` fails `ReleaseVersionTests` when the changelog, the template, or either package version differs from the manifest version, and `.github/workflows/release.yml` refuses a tag that does not name the manifest version, a release tag whose commit is not on `main`, and a candidate tag whose commit is not on `release/<version>`.
provisions.statement: A LiteSpec tag that publishes MUST be `v<version>` on `main`, or a release candidate `v<version>-rc.<n>` on `release/<version>`, and the changelog entry, the consumer template version, and the tool and analyzer package versions name the same manifest version.
provisions.rationale: A git tag is the single durable artifact naming a release: branches move and files change, but the tag stays. Reading the current release from the highest tag gives maintainers, consumers, and tools one shared answer. Writing that version into the manifest, the changelog, the template, and the tool package in the same release keeps the four consistent. A candidate lets a consumer test the packages a release publishes before the release branch merges. Its suffix keeps its packages apart from the release's, and the committed files keep the plain version, so a candidate changes nothing `main` names. Candidates publish from release branches by [decision/0059-publish-candidates-from-release-branches](decision/0059-publish-candidates-from-release-branches), so a consumer tests the release packages before the release branch merges. Each release publishes the CLI as one native executable per platform, in the tool packages and in standalone archives, so the version reaches a consumer with or without .NET, settled by [decision/0021-native-command-line](decision/0021-native-command-line) on the evidence in [research/native-command-line-evidence](research/native-command-line-evidence).

provisions.heading: Record the Reasoning Behind Each Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `RECORD_SCHEMA`, `RECORD_ID_MISMATCH`, `RECORD_SOURCE`, `RECORD_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE`, or `RECORD_DECISION_UNCITED` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A maintainer MUST keep the research and decisions behind each release as records under `docs/intent/`.
provisions.rationale: Provisions state obligations without the questions, sources, or conclusions behind them. Without that reasoning on record, a later change tells nothing about why a rule reads as it does. Settled by [decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records](decision/0001-keep-release-reasoning-as-records) on the evidence in [research/comparable-rationale-practice](research/comparable-rationale-practice).
provisions.example: Claimwick states its five-day reimbursement target in a provision, with the benchmark behind the number in a research record beside it.

provisions.heading: Replace Every Citation on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision rename MUST replace every citation of the old identifier in one change.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename changes the ID line, and no alias covers a missed citation. Every citation the rename misses names a provision that no longer exists, and readers following it find nothing. Replacing all of them in one change keeps the repository resolvable at each commit. A heading reword leaves the identifier unchanged, so it needs no citation changes.
provisions.example: A rename changes the ID line and every citation of it in the same change.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Fact to LiteSpec Before the Book Shows It
provisions.evidence: Does every fact the book shows come from LiteSpec? Look at the book beside the model output and the finding codes: each fact is a record field, a computed status, or a check.
provisions.statement: A fact the book needs that LiteSpec does not define MUST become a record field, a computed status, or a check in LiteSpec before the book shows it.
provisions.rationale: Rendering the book is a probe: what it cannot show is a gap in the specification. Closing the gap in LiteSpec gives every project the fact, checked; closing it in the book gives one view an unchecked fact. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md).
provisions.example: The book needs to say that a refusal has no scenario, so LiteSpec gains a check for it, and the book shows that check's findings.

provisions.heading: Cite Reference Data Instead of Literal Values
provisions.evidence: Does any rule statement state a value a reference-data table holds? Check the rule statements beside the reference-data tables.
provisions.statement: A rule SHOULD cite the reference-data table holding a value instead of stating the value in its statement.
provisions.rationale: A value written into prose drifts: each statement holding it needs its own edit when the value changes, and no check sees which statements hold it. One table with dated rows keeps each value once with its source, and the model checks that every cited table exists. Settled by [decision/0098-reference-data-tables](decision/0098-reference-data-tables).
provisions.example: The approval rule cites `reference-data/spending.decision-target` instead of stating five business days.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Specification File
provisions.evidence: a file under the documentation root that is neither a record file, an explanation beside its record file, nor a document, and sits under no declared unstructured path.
provisions.statement: Every file under the consumer documentation root MUST be a record file, an explanation file beside its record file, or a document, or sit under a declared unstructured path.
provisions.rationale: A file the validator leaves unclassified is skipped, and a skipped file looks sound: its errors stay hidden. Requiring every file to be a record file, an explanation, or a document, or to sit under a declared unstructured path, leaves no page unchecked. A directory index that owns no record uses the index style, and a `README.md` with no frontmatter is a document.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion in the Builder
provisions.evidence: Which features read below `verified`, and which children hold each one back? Look at `completion` on each feature in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST compute one completion stage for every requirement, use case, flow, feature and goal, and write it as `completion` with `stage`, `proof`, `heldBy`, `parkedBy` and `counts`, with a parent only as far as its weakest in-scope child, `heldBy` naming at most ten in-scope children at that stage, and `counts` holding `inScope`, `parked` and `total`.
provisions.rationale: Completion is a fact the builder counts from fulfillment, code, and proof, so no record carries a shorthand saying how far it is. One ladder reads the same everywhere: `unfulfilled` with no fulfilling Behavior record, `specified` with a fulfiller and no code, `coded` with code for every in-scope child, and `verified` with fresh proof for every in-scope child. With no test run, a coded record stays `coded` with proof `unknown`, with no failure reading. A requirement a waiver parks stays out of the stage and counts as parked: `heldBy` lists only in-scope records holding the stage back, and `parkedBy` lists parked records with the waiver that parks each and its `expiresOn`. The book shows "verified, 12 of 14; 2 parked", with a parked list naming each waiver and expiry. A goal's completion shows delivery only; its outcome reads `not measured` until the goal records `observations`.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, `feature/expense-submission` shows `coded` with proof `unknown` before any test run, held by the one requirement with no fulfiller; after a passing run proves every fulfiller, the same feature shows `verified` with no held-by entries.

provisions.heading: Compute Proof Statuses in the Builder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unimplemented`, `proves-unreached`, and `refusal-unimplemented` for a use case whose handler, proof, or refusal code is missing, and `proof-invalid` (level S) for a test that both passed and failed within the runs read.
provisions.statement: Coded, verified, tested, exercised, stale, flaky, and reachable MUST come from the builder, never from handwriting.
provisions.rationale: Handwritten state drifts: a record marked coded stays marked after its handler is deleted. Computed state cannot drift, because the builder re-derives it from handlers, routes, scenarios, and test runs on every run. A use case reads coded when a handler, reaction, job, or endpoint marked with it carries it out, verified when every scenario has a passing proof through the public boundary that is not stale, and stale when its run commit is behind HEAD with a changed path outside the record and documentation paths, or when its run commit is unknown. A run records its commit. A requirement reads verified when everything fulfilling it is verified and its measure's check passes. A record reads tested when a passing test that asserts something links to it. A flow step reads exercised when a passing proof of a use case, reaction, or job serves it. A proof reads flaky when its test both passed and failed within the runs read. Nothing above Implementation is computed from code: derivation from code into any other record is forbidden, and code-computed facts live in the book and the model output. Settled by [decision/0017-proof-that-holds](decision/0017-proof-that-holds) on the evidence in [research/lower-layers-practice](research/lower-layers-practice) and decision/0085-bind-proof-to-code-and-outcomes.
provisions.example: A use case reads coded when its handler exists.

provisions.heading: Connect Across Modules Only Through Declared Dependencies
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-locality-invalid` for a record under a module that is linked from another module with no declared dependency, module event, or integration event. A queries edge to a public query that lists the consuming module passes, and so does a commands edge to a public command that lists the sending module; a queries edge to a query use case whose `via` does not name the consuming module is reported as `query-target-invalid`, and a commands edge to a command use case whose `via` does not name the sending module is reported as `command-target-invalid`.
provisions.statement: Within one layer, a record under a module MUST be linked from another module only along a declared module dependency, through a module event, through an integration event, through a queries edge to a public query that lists the consuming module in `via`, or through a commands edge to a public command that lists the sending module in `via`.
provisions.rationale: A record linked from another module with no declared tie is not local: it belongs at product level. The declared dependency, the module event, or the integration event names the tie, so the seam where a monolith would split stays visible. A queries edge to a public query that lists the consuming module names its own tie: the consuming module's `queries` edge names the query, and the query's `via` names the consuming module back. A commands edge to a public command that lists the sending module names its own tie the same way. Links from one layer down to the next cross modules, because that is how one capability spans modules. This provision is the one rule for links across modules.
provisions.example: A spending rule resting on the finance module with no `dependsOn` tie and no module or integration event between them is reported; the rule moves to product level or the modules declare the tie. Reporting's reimbursement command declares a `queries` edge to spending's read-expense query, which lists `module/reporting` in `via`, so the edge passes with no `dependsOn` tie. Reporting's close-period command declares a `commands` edge to spending's close-expenses command, which lists `module/reporting` in `via`, so that edge passes the same way.

provisions.heading: Connect Every Behavior Record to Intent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-link-missing` for a use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting with neither `serves` nor `fulfills`, and `use-case-flow-missing` (level G) at large size for a use case that no reaction, job or other use case runs and that serves no flow step.
provisions.statement: A use case, reaction, job, notification, or setting MUST carry `serves`, `fulfills`, or both.
provisions.rationale: A behavior record with no served flow step and no fulfilled requirement answers to nothing above it: no promise explains why it exists. Pointing up with `serves` or `fulfills` ties every behavior to the Intent that asks for it. A use case is background-only when a reaction or job runs it, so `use-case-flow-missing` skips it.

provisions.heading: Declare Cross-Module References in DependsOn
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-reference-undeclared` (level G) for an `input`, `output`, or `steps` entry that names another module's record with no declared dependency. A field stating `held: opaque` passes unless the use case also reads or writes the named record or a step cites it.
provisions.statement: An `input`, `output`, or `steps` entry of a use case MUST name a record of another module only when the use case's module lists that module in `dependsOn` or when the entry is an input or output field stating `held: opaque` for an identifier the module stores and passes without loading, querying, or reasoning about the named aggregate.
provisions.rationale: The link checks read a use case's top-level links, but an entry inside `input`, `output`, or `steps` can name another module's record without appearing in any of them. Such a reference is a dependency the record graph leaves undeclared, so the module seam stays invisible to a reader and to a check. Naming the dependency in `dependsOn` states the tie where module ties belong. A module event, an integration event, or a public edge states the crossing when the two modules share no dependency. A module that only stores and passes an identifier needs no tie to the owning module: the value arrives through an event, a public query result, or the caller, and the module leaves the named aggregate unread. The field states `held: opaque` to record the carrying, and it still states how the value arrives: an input keeps its `origin`, and a query output group keeps its `reads`. A use case that also reads or writes the named aggregate, or whose step cites it, still declares the dependency.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, an input of `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` names `aggregate/reporting.reimbursed-expense` in `identifies`. Module `spending` does not list `module/reporting` in `dependsOn`, so the entry is reported; the modules either declare the tie or the use case reads the value through a public query. When a reporting use case takes the expense identifier its row came from as an input it only stores and passes, the input states `held: opaque` and needs no `dependsOn` tie to spending. When the same use case also reads the expense aggregate or a step cites it, the input is reported like any other cross-module reference.

provisions.heading: Declare One Mark Style
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-style-invalid` (level S) for a mark written in a form its language does not take.
provisions.statement: A project MUST write each C# mark in the one style that `marks` in `.litespec/project.yaml` declares, each TypeScript mark as a typed constant, and each operations mark as a comment.
provisions.rationale: Two styles in one language are two ways to do one job: a reader learns both, a check covers both, and a search for a record finds half its code. The C# style is a project choice made once, so every tool reads it from the project file and refuses the other style within C#. TypeScript and operations files have one form each, so a typed constant beside a C# documentation tag is two languages, not two styles. A code fix converts a mark to the form its language takes.
provisions.example: The Claimwick product declares `"marks": "xml"`, so its submit-expense handler carries a documentation tag naming `use-case/spending.submit-expense`, and an attribute naming the same use case is reported. Its use-case module carries the same identifier as a typed constant, and its deployment file carries its `follows` mark as a comment.

provisions.heading: Declare Size and Stacks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `size-type-missing` and `record-invalid` for a project missing its declaration or a required type.
provisions.statement: A project MUST declare its size and stacks.
provisions.rationale: Size decides which record types and test projects the checks require, while stacks decide which technology pages and checks apply. Without the declaration, the builder cannot tell a missing record from one the project never needed.
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example declares large with a server shape and two stacks.

provisions.heading: Derive a Computed Fact Instead of Restating It
provisions.evidence: Does every count, census, and membership list name its source or command? Look at the numbers the change adds.
provisions.statement: A specification MUST name the source or the command that produces any count, census, or membership list derived between records.
provisions.rationale: A restated number is right until the next unrelated edit changes the records it counts, and nothing reports when it goes stale. Naming the source or the command gives every reader the current figure instead of the figure from commit day. Derivation between records is allowed: generic refusals derive from `access`, `input`, and the knowledge the use case reads, and computed completion appears in the book and the model output only.
provisions.example:
A chapter states where its numbers come from rather than copying them.

```markdown
The figures below render from the retention schedule at build time.
```

provisions.heading: Explain Each Record Beside Its Record File
provisions.evidence: Does every Markdown file under a record root sit beside its record file or carry frontmatter? Look at the Markdown files beside the record files.
provisions.statement: An explanation file MUST sit beside its record file in the record's own folder, with the same name, and hold plain Markdown with no frontmatter.
provisions.rationale: The shared file name is the link: no field joins the two files, so a rename moves both and nothing else. Plain Markdown with no frontmatter stays readable in any reader and tells every check to read fields from the record file only. The file opens with the record title and uses H2 sections, so each explanation has one shape. One list of plain noun sections per record type, settled by [decision/0043-use-plain-noun-sections](../intent/decisions/0043-use-plain-noun-sections/0043-use-plain-noun-sections.md).
provisions.example: `submit-expense.yaml` explains its Example and Notes in `submit-expense.md` beside it.

provisions.heading: Explain the Book from LiteSpec Definitions
provisions.evidence: Does every book explanation come from a LiteSpec definition? Look at the book's explanations beside the glossary and the record type table.
provisions.statement: Every explanation the book shows MUST come from the glossary definition of the term or from the question its record type answers on this page.
provisions.rationale: The book explains itself so nobody needs a learning curve, and the explanation stays true only when it has one source. An explanation written for the book drifts from the definition the records follow. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md). Teaching text left the book pages, so the pages explain only from these definitions, as [decision/0090-make-the-book-an-explorer](../intent/decisions/0090-make-the-book-an-explorer/0090-make-the-book-an-explorer.yaml) chose.
provisions.example: The book explains a waiver with the glossary definition of Waiver.

provisions.heading: Follow the Authority Order
provisions.evidence: When records conflict, does the decision name the higher record that won? Look at the conflict decisions under `.litespec/intent/decisions/`, in the order this page states.
provisions.statement: A conflict MUST resolve toward the higher authority.
provisions.rationale: Intent records outrank Behavior records: constraint over product, product over requirement, requirement over rule, rule over use case, use case over result, and result over scenario. A use case asking for behavior its rule forbids loses to the rule, and the contradiction is reported and resolved by updating the inconsistent records.
