Where Intent has spoken, the specification wins over code; where the specification is silent, an agent builds nothing, as the Authority section states. Goals, problems, features, flows, actors, research, and prose carry no authority, so none outranks the ladder. Only an explicit product `excludes` overrides a requirement.

provisions.heading: Give Every Record One Parent
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` (level G) for a record whose required parent is missing.
provisions.statement: Every record except the product MUST have exactly one parent from the Placement Table on this page.
provisions.rationale: A record with no parent has no place in the book, and a record with two parents appears twice. One parent per record places every record exactly once: the container is the parent, so an entry sits under the record file that holds it, a scenario sits under its use case, reaction, or job, and a record file sits under its scope node. A feature requirement sits under its feature in its own folder, and types at product level, including a product-level requirement, sit under the product with no field written. The product is the root of the tree and stands above every record layer, settled by [decision/0091-place-the-product-above-layers](decision/0091-place-the-product-above-layers). One parent per record is settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `requirement/approval-reminders.receipt-over-threshold` sits under `feature/approval-reminders` in `intent/problems/expenses-wait-weeks/features/approval-reminders/requirements/receipt-over-threshold/`; `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits beside its aggregate; and `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds` sits in the file of `use-case/spending.submit-expense`.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Record File and Frontmatter Block to the Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for each record file and document frontmatter block that fails the record schema.
provisions.statement: Every record file and every document frontmatter block MUST satisfy the record schema for its declared type.
provisions.rationale: The record schema owns the field list of every record type and page style. A record file is one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`, holding no Markdown and no frontmatter fences. A document frontmatter block is YAML between two lines that hold only `---`, holding only the page style and its common fields. This page states the record types and their homes.
provisions.example:
A use-case record file opens with its identity fields.

```yaml
type: use-case
id: use-case/spending.submit-expense
title: Submit Expense
```

provisions.heading: Hold Module Rules in Rule Folders
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a rule in `module.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A module-level rule MUST live in its own folder under `behavior/modules/<m>/rules/<name>/`, never in `module.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The module record declares the module; rules are behavior and live with Behavior. A rule written into `module.yaml` hides behavior in a declaration no rule check scans.
provisions.example: A spending rule lives in its own folder under `behavior/modules/spending/rules/`, as `reimbursed-once/reimbursed-once.yaml`; the same rule written into `module.yaml` is reported.

provisions.heading: Implement Each Mapped Behavior Record Behind a Mark
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `aggregate-unimplemented`, `reaction-unimplemented`, `job-unimplemented`, `external-system-unimplemented`, and `use-case-endpoint-missing` (level S) for a record no mark names, where `aggregate-unimplemented` fires only for an entity aggregate, and `use-case-unreached` (level S) for a browser use case no screen calls; a request pipeline handler carrying the use case mark serves as its endpoint and needs no screen call.
provisions.statement: Every entity aggregate, every reaction, job, and external system, and every use case reached through a `browser` or `api` entry point, MUST be named by a mark on the code element the marks table gives it.
provisions.rationale: A mark points up, so a check reading marks alone finds code nobody recorded but misses a record nobody built. Checking each record that the marks table maps to code from the top closes the loop in the other direction: an entity aggregate with no root, a reaction with no event handler, a job with no host, an external system with no port, and a use case people reach with no endpoint. A use case with no screen calling it blocks at level S: the link between a use case and the screens that call it always blocks.
provisions.example: `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted` has no event handler carrying its mark, so the check reports `reaction-unimplemented` and blocks.

provisions.heading: Keep Code Out of Intent and Behavior Fields
provisions.evidence: Does any Intent or Behavior field copy a value from code? Look at the fields the change fills, beside the implementation.
provisions.statement: A project MUST fill no field on an Intent or Behavior record from code.
provisions.rationale: Code implements Behavior, so a field filled from an implementation restates what already ships instead of stating the promise under review. A fact learned from the world enters Intent as research or a constraint, cited and dated, and a need the upper record layer does not state becomes a backlog item outside the repository. Derivation between records stays allowed.
provisions.example: A positivity guard found in a handler becomes a backlog item for a rule, while the code stays untouched until the rule lands.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Name Unique in Its Record Type
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-key-duplicate` for a name that occurs twice in one record type, and for a use case, reaction or job name that occurs in another of the three types.
provisions.statement: Each name MUST stay unique in its record type.
provisions.rationale: Short identifiers resolve with no lookup table only when each name means one record of its type. Two records of one type with one name collide everywhere the identifier is read, while two records of different types with one name coexist: `actor/owner` and `role/owner` are different records. Folders do not narrow uniqueness within a type. Use case, reaction, and job names share one namespace, so a scenario cites its parent without ambiguity. Settled by decision/0087-keep-prose-checks-advisory-and-names-per-type.
provisions.example: Claimwick names one feature `approval-reminders`; a second feature with that name is reported even though the folders differ. An actor named `owner` and a role named `owner` coexist.

provisions.heading: Keep Module Dependencies Free of Cycles
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `module-dependency-invalid` for a module dependency cycle.
provisions.statement: Module dependencies MUST NOT form a cycle.
provisions.rationale: A dependency cycle says each module builds on the other, so neither has a seam to split along. The graph runs over Contracts project references, `queries` edges, `commands` edges, and reactions to another module's facts, beside the `dependsOn` links. A cycle means a concept is split across two modules, and the fix moves the concept into one module, never through a shared identifier. Settled by [decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag](decision/0110-module-dependencies-form-a-dag).
provisions.example: Spending depends on finance and finance depends on spending, so the cycle is reported naming both modules and the edges that close it.

provisions.heading: Keep Rules and Targets Out of Technical Decisions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-basis-missing` (level G) for a technical decision whose `basedOn` names nothing, and counts a quality requirement as fulfilled when a technical decision names it in `basedOn`.
provisions.statement: A technical decision MUST leave each rule the product obeys whatever its design to a constraint and each measurable target to a quality requirement, and name the ones it serves in `basedOn`.
provisions.rationale: A technical decision chooses one way among alternatives, and a better alternative may replace it tomorrow. A rule such as keeping personal data in the European Union, or a target such as answering checkout within two seconds, does not change when the library does: overriding it needs a business, legal, or organizational change. Written inside a decision, the rule disappears the day the decision is replaced, and nobody holds it as the promise it is. Kept in Intent, the rule and the target stand as the promises they are, the decision points up to them, and the chain runs unbroken from code through the decision to the constraint or requirement and the goal above it. A decision with no basis blocks at level G, like a product decision that no settled record names. A technical choice among equal options may serve no rule or target yet and still govern the code that follows it, but a product decision that settles no record governs nothing.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps each receipt for the tax file because `constraint/tax-receipt-retention` requires it, and answers submissions quickly because `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission` sets the target. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` names the constraint in `basedOn`, and `decision/0004-serve-receipts-behind-one-proxy` names the requirement in `basedOn`; neither the seven years nor the two seconds is written in a decision.

provisions.heading: Keep Shape Rules in the Schema
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record that breaks a shape rule and `record-key-duplicate` for two entries of one record that share a key, and the parity test `RecordSchemaParityTests` fails when the schema and the model check disagree on a rule both carry.
provisions.statement: Each rule on the shape of one record MUST be written in the record schema, and each rule on the graph between records stays in the model check.
provisions.rationale: An editor validates a record against the schema alone, so a shape rule the schema lacks lets a record pass in the editor and fail in the check. Graph rules, such as reference resolution, ownership, and consistency across records, need every record at once, which a schema cannot read. The schema holds required properties, minimum counts, conditional requirements, and allowed values. A list of objects does not use `uniqueItems`, since that compares whole objects, so the model check reports each key that two entries of one record share. Proposed by [decision/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema](../intent/decisions/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema/0058-keep-shape-rules-in-the-schema.md).
provisions.example: A Claimwick research record with an empty `sources` list fails the schema in an editor and the model check alike, and a research record that names source name `benchmark-report` twice is reported as `record-key-duplicate`.

provisions.heading: Keep the Whole Specification in the Records
provisions.evidence: Does every explanation section rest on filled backing fields, with no fact beyond the record and the records it cites? Compare each explanation file with its record file.
provisions.statement: Every fact an agent needs to build the product MUST stand in a record field, and no fact MAY stand only in an explanation file.
provisions.rationale: An agent builds from the records, and a check reads only fields. A fact written only in prose reaches neither: the agent builds without it, and no finding notices when it changes. Keeping every fact in a field makes the YAML a complete specification on its own, and leaves the explanation file free to restate and elaborate it for people. Settled by [decision/0095-keep-the-whole-specification-in-the-records](decision/0095-keep-the-whole-specification-in-the-records). Kept human-only for mirrors by [decision/0121-keep-explanation-mirrors-human-only](../intent/decisions/0121-keep-explanation-mirrors-human-only/0121-keep-explanation-mirrors-human-only.md): no check reads a `.md` mirror; `validate` and `model check` read YAML fields only.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `problem/expenses-wait-weeks` states its failure cases in `failureCases` and the condition that ends the problem in `resolutionCriteria`. Its explanation's Failure Cases section restates those cases and walks through one with the cast.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Check with Its Level
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) for a frontend whose reader is missing or failing, prints the level beside each finding, prints `inspection incomplete: reader for <frontend> missing, <N> findings not blocking` as its last line when any reader was missing with one clause per frontend, and exits with code 3 when no finding blocks but the inspection was incomplete. `litespec model check --release` blocks on `reader-missing` for a claimed layer. `litespec model review` reports the level R findings and exits zero.
provisions.statement: Every check MUST carry one of the levels G, S or R, where `litespec model check` blocks on G findings and on S findings whose reader is qualified, and only `litespec model review` reports R findings, without blocking.
provisions.rationale: The level tells a reader what a finding rests on: G rests on records only, S rests on code read through a stack reader, and R rests on prose quality a person weighs. `litespec model check` prints the level beside each finding, so a reader tells what each finding rests on at a glance. A missing required link is level G.

provisions.heading: Match Each Backend Mark to Its Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-folder-drift` (level S) for a handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root whose mark names a record outside its module and folder, and `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a code element, test, or folder outside the code folder its record's placement names.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, endpoint, reaction, job, aggregate
provisions.statement: A backend handler, endpoint, event handler, job host or aggregate root MUST carry a mark naming a use case, reaction, job, or aggregate in the module and folder it sits in.
provisions.rationale: Copying a handler and forgetting its mark is the most common agent mistake, and the folder already says what the mark should be. A handler that sits in one use-case folder while naming another sends readers and checks to the wrong record. An aggregate method and a technical class carry the mark of the use case that calls them, which may sit in another module, so their folder says nothing about their mark. The frontend mirror already compares each mark with its module; the backend check applies the same comparison to handlers, endpoints, and aggregates.
provisions.example: A handler in `Booking/Holds/HoldRoom/` marked `use-case/booking.release-hold` is reported, because the folder holds `use-case/booking.hold-room`.

provisions.heading: Move Each Identifier with Its Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder.
provisions.statement: A record that moves to another module MUST change the module segment of its identifier and every citation in the same change.
provisions.rationale: The folder decides: an identifier whose home segment disagrees with its folder names a home the record left. Only identifiers whose first segment names a module change with a module move. A rule identifier keeps its home segment, because the segment names the aggregate or module the rule is about rather than the folder that holds it. A move between product and module level changes no identifier, so no citation changes.
provisions.example: Claimwick moves `use-case/spending.submit-expense` from the spending module to the finance module, so the use case becomes `use-case/finance.submit-expense` and every citation changes in the same change.

provisions.heading: Name Book Labels with LiteSpec Terms
provisions.evidence: Does every book label use a LiteSpec term? Look at the book beside the glossary and the Links table: each label is a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, or a reads-as phrase.
provisions.statement: Every label in the book MUST be a record type, a field name, a computed state, a glossary term, or the reads-as phrase the Links table states for a connection.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec already names every concept once, for people and agents alike. A friendlier synonym in the book, such as promise for requirement, is a second word for one concept: the reader learns it, then meets the real word in the records and the checks, and has to translate. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md).
provisions.example: A use case page heads its results "Results" and its scenarios "Scenarios", with no "Endings" or "Examples" headings.

provisions.heading: Name Each Identifier from Its Title
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `identifier-title-invalid` for a page record whose identifier name is no word subsequence of its title, or whose record file is named for neither its identifier name nor the fixed file name of its type, and for a flow step whose act is no word subsequence of its title.
provisions.artifact: record:product, record:goal, record:direction, record:problem, record:feature, record:requirement, record:constraint, record:decision, record:research, record:flow, record:step, record:actor, record:role, record:module, record:aggregate, record:use-case, record:reaction, record:job, record:notification, record:reference-data, record:integration-event, record:entry-point, record:screen, record:external-system, record:runbook, record:waiver
provisions.statement: Every page record and every flow step MUST take its name from the words of its title in title order: a page record its identifier name, and so its folder and file names, and a flow step the act in its identifier.
provisions.rationale: Readers browse the folders before they open a record, so the folder name must say what the record says. A retitle that keeps the identifier leaves the folder and file saying the old name while the record says the new one, and no listing shows the gap. Taking the name from the title's words keeps the identifier, the file, and the folder on what the record says. A step lives in its flow's file, so only its act faces its title. Proposed by [decision/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title](../intent/decisions/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title/0061-name-each-identifier-from-its-title.md).
provisions.example: Claimwick titles a requirement "Nobody Approves Their Own Expense", so the requirement is `requirement/approval.nobody-approves-own-expense` in `nobody-approves-own-expense/nobody-approves-own-expense.yaml`. The name `no-self-approval` holds words the title does not hold, so it is reported. Claimwick titles a step "Submit Expense", so the step is `step/submit-and-reimburse.submit-expense`.

provisions.heading: Name Records in Prose by Their Identifiers
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a backticked identifier that names no written record and for a backticked provision the carried release does not ship.
provisions.statement: Prose in a record field, an explanation file, a document, or the `AGENTS.md` file at the consumer root MUST name every record by its identifier in backticks and every provision by the published identifier the carried release ships.
provisions.rationale: A name in plain words, such as a decision number without its identifier, cannot be resolved: nothing tells whether the record still exists after a rename or a move. The identifier in backticks is the one form every check reads, so a stale name fails the check at the line that names it instead of sending the reader after a record nobody wrote.
provisions.example: A waiver `exitWhen` reads "The gap closes when `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` lands." rather than "The gap closes when Decision 5 lands."

provisions.heading: Name the Field to Use Instead in Schema Errors
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` naming the field to use instead.
provisions.statement: A schema error on a rejected field or a link in the wrong field MUST name the field to use instead.
provisions.rationale: Some fields read naturally but belong elsewhere: `heldBy` on a permission, `required` on an output field, a notification under a step's `carries`. The record schema lists each rejected field with the field to use instead, and the link checks name the field for a misplaced link, so the error moves the author forward instead of leaving them to guess which of the many shapes they broke.
provisions.example: `heldBy` on a permission reports that the permission names its roles in `grantedTo`.

provisions.heading: Name the Lowest Record Each Test Proves
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` and `mark-unknown` (level S) for a test that names no record or a record of a kind a test does not take.
provisions.statement: Every test MUST name in a `proves` mark the lowest record it verifies, from the kinds the marks table on this page lists for a test.
provisions.rationale: A test outside the record tree is either proof of something the specification forgot to state or a test that verifies nothing anyone promised. Naming the lowest record it verifies places each test: a scenario or rule for behavior, a quality requirement for how well the product behaves, a technical decision for a technical choice, an external system or integration event for an agreement with the outside, a provision for a structural rule the code must keep, and a project convention for a standing rule the code must keep. A test that verifies a choice no record states shows a missing record, which is written at the level where the choice lives. A test with no record above it is a finding to resolve by writing the missing record or reporting the gap. It is deleted only when a reviewer establishes that the behavior it protects is obsolete, redundant or wrong, and the pull request says so. Proof stays layered: only scenario and rule proofs verify a use case, and a passing test that asserts something links to a quality requirement, a technical decision, an external system, an integration event, or a provision marks that record tested, so "the adapter is right" stays separate from "the promise is kept". A background use case is verified through the passing proofs of the use cases it serves. A browser success proof asserts the result sentence or the scenario Then text.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the submit-expense acceptance test proves `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds`; a load test of month-end submissions proves `requirement/approval-reminders.month-end-submission`; a receipt-rendering test proves `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf`; and the layering test that Domain references no persistence package proves `litespec/core/backend-architecture#point-dependencies-inward`.

provisions.heading: Name What Every Decision Decides
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-decides-missing` for a product decision that no settled record names in `basedOn`.
provisions.statement: Every product decision MUST be named in `basedOn` by at least one record it settles.
provisions.rationale: A decision that no settled record names governs nothing. Every link points from the lower or later record to the higher or earlier one, so the settled record names its decision in `basedOn` instead of the decision naming the record. A technical decision governs the code that follows it instead.

provisions.heading: Organize the Book by the Record Layers
provisions.evidence: Which book headings or groupings are not a record layer, a record type, or a record the identifier names? Look at the book's outline beside this page's record type table.
provisions.statement: The book MUST outline a project by the four record layers, with the governance records beside them, and place each record under the record its folder and links name, or at the top of its own layer when the product parents it.
provisions.rationale: The book is how people read the model, so it shows the model's own hierarchy. A reader who learns Intent, Behavior, Implementation, and Proof in the book reads the same structure in the docs folder, in the model output, and in every other LiteSpec project. An outline of the book's own invention is a second hierarchy to learn, and it drifts from the one the records keep. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md). The live server and the export share one data format in this outline, as [decision/0088-serve-the-book-live-and-export-it](../intent/decisions/0088-serve-the-book-live-and-export-it/0088-serve-the-book-live-and-export-it.yaml) chose.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` sits under Behavior, its module and its aggregate; its results under it; each scenario under the result it shows; and the handler that carries its mark under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Place a Record by Its Content and Link It by Its Reason
provisions.evidence: Does any record sit under a record that holds only part of its content, and does any record type in the Placement Table take a parent whose scope is narrower than its content? Compare each record's folder with the records it cites and the records that serve it.
provisions.statement: A record MUST nest under another record only when its whole content lies within that record, and otherwise sit at the lowest scope node that holds all of its content and name the record it exists for in a link field.
provisions.rationale: A folder states that everything inside it belongs to the record above it. Content is what a record states and what it changes; its links are its reasons, not its content. A record filed under one of several records its content spans claims a scope it does not hold. The reason a record exists can change while its content stays the same, so a link field keeps that change to one line where a folder would move the record. Settled by [decision/0078-place-each-record-by-its-content](decision/0078-place-each-record-by-its-content).
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, `flow/submit-and-reimburse` carries requirements of both `feature/approval` and `feature/approval-reminders`, so it sits in `intent/flows/` under the product and names its goal in `serves`. A reaction answering another module's integration event sits with the module whose records it changes, and names the event in `triggeredBy`.

provisions.heading: Place Child Records in Typed Folders
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a child record outside its typed folder, and for a module subfolder that names no typed folder.
provisions.statement: A project MUST hold each child record stored as its own file in a folder named for its type in the plural, inside its parent's folder, and each child stored as an entry in its parent's file.
provisions.rationale: A reader who opens a parent folder sees its own files with each kind of child kept apart, without opening each file. One rule for every parent replaces a placement sentence per type and gives every module one layout. A child stored as an entry has no file of its own, so a folder for it would hold nothing. Proposed by [decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders](decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders).
provisions.example: A feature's requirements sit in `features/approval/requirements/`, and an aggregate's use cases sit in `aggregates/expenses/use-cases/`, while a result stays in its use case file.

provisions.heading: Point Every Book Entry to Its Source
provisions.evidence: Does every book entry link to its file and line? Look at the book's record, code, test, and finding entries.
provisions.statement: Every record, code element, test and finding the book shows MUST link to the file and line it comes from.
provisions.rationale: The book is where a reader notices what to change, and the source is where the change is made. A link to the file and line makes the next step one click, and it shows that every entry comes from a written record or from code, not from the book. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md).
provisions.example: The submit-expense use case page links to `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/aggregates/expenses/use-cases/submit-expense/submit-expense.yaml` at its first line, and its handler to the handler file at the class.

provisions.heading: Point Every Link Up
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-direction-invalid` (level G) for a link from a higher layer to a lower one.
provisions.statement: Every link MUST point from the lower or later record to the higher or earlier one, with no exceptions.
provisions.rationale: A link from a higher layer to a lower one makes the layers depend both ways: an Intent record cannot be written or read before the Behavior records it names. Each permission names the roles that grant it in `grantedTo`, each settled record names its decision in `basedOn`, and each external system names the actor it represents in `represents`, so every record is written before the records above it read it. The reverse views are gathered for `model query` and the book, never stored. `holds` stays: actor and role are both Intent, so it is not a layer down-link.
provisions.example: `permission/request-expense` names `role/employee` in `grantedTo`, and the book gathers the employee role's permissions from the permissions naming it.

provisions.heading: Publish Each Integration Event from One Module
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `event-publisher-invalid` for an integration event with a second publishing module.
provisions.statement: An integration event MUST have exactly one publishing module.
provisions.rationale: An event with two publishers has two writers of one fact: readers cannot tell which module states it. One publishing module gives the fact one home, and every other module reads it through the event. The publishers follow from the records: the use cases whose `raises` holds the domain event the integration event `translates`.
provisions.example: `integration-event/expense-submitted` translates `domain-event/expense.submitted`, which only spending use cases raise, so the spending module publishes it.

provisions.heading: Record Each Screen's Captures from the Gallery
provisions.evidence: Which screens with a route have no capture? Look at `captureState` `route-not-captured` on screen records in the model.
provisions.statement: The builder MUST record each screen's captures from the gallery folders and file-name pattern the project file names, as `captures` with `path`, `theme`, `width` and `capturedOn`, and its `captureState` as `captured`, `route-not-captured` or `no-route`.
provisions.rationale: A reader judging a screen needs to see it, and a capture named by its route, theme, and width is the copy the built screen makes. The route slug names the file the same way everywhere: the leading slash dropped, segments joined with a hyphen, a parameter reduced to its name, and the root route named `home`. A missing gallery folder captures nothing and fails nothing, so a project with no photography yet still builds its model.
provisions.example: The Claimwick web gallery holds `expenses--light--1440.png`, so `screen/expenses.list` at `/expenses` shows that capture at theme `light` and width 1440 with `captureState` `captured`; a screen with no route shows `no-route`.

provisions.heading: Record Each Technical Choice as a Decision
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `decision-unimplemented` (level S) for a technical decision that no code element follows. It reports `decision-kind-missing` (level G) for a technical decision with no `kind`, `decision-scope-invalid` (level S) for a technical decision whose followers all sit in one module and each already carry an `implements` mark, and `decision-home-drift` (level S) for a technical decision kept at a level its followers do not match. The check runs in the CLI only, with no analyzer rule: whether any code follows a decision is known only across every project, and one compilation sees one project.
provisions.statement: A technical choice of one of the six kinds that code follows and no LiteSpec provision makes MUST be a decision under `.litespec/implementation/decisions/` that at least one code element follows.
provisions.rationale: Why a pattern, a library, or a configuration value was chosen is the first thing a maintainer asks before changing it. Written in a comment, the answer drifts and no tool finds it. Written as a decision, it carries its options, what speaks for and against each, and what would reopen it, and every code element shaped by it names it in a `follows` mark. A choice a LiteSpec provision already makes needs no decision, because the provision is the record. The six kinds are provider, package, format, boundary, topology, and replacement, as the [decision records page](../reference/decision-records.md) states: a choice of no kind is not a decision. A choice of no kind states its reason in the class documentation, and the mark on the class names the record the class serves. Technical decisions sit under Implementation because they name technologies and code, which Intent never holds, and they share the numbered sequence of product decisions, so all decisions share one identifier space. Settled by [decision/0040-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice](decision/0040-decisions-only-for-six-kinds-of-choice).
provisions.example: Claimwick renders each receipt as a PDF file. `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` weighs a PDF library against an HTML-to-PDF browser, chooses the PDF library, and names what reopens the choice: receipts no longer needing a downloadable file. The decision carries `kind: package`. The receipt PDF renderer carries `/// <follows>decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Render Generated Regions from the Model
provisions.evidence: Does any generated region outside an index region render code-computed facts? Look inside the generated fences beside the book and the model output.
provisions.statement: A generated region renders only facts derived from records, and a `decision-index` or `waiver-index` region also renders the computed follower facts its rows name.
provisions.rationale: A generated region sits inside a record page, so everything in it reads with record authority. Facts computed from code, such as coded and verified counts, describe the world rather than the promise, and rendering them beside records would lend them authority they do not hold. The book and the model output carry code-computed facts where readers meet them as computed. An index region is the exception: it lists the records beside it, so each row names the computed followers, concerns, and flags the reader needs to read the list. Settled by [decision/0072-generate-the-links-table-from-the-schema](decision/0072-generate-the-links-table-from-the-schema).

provisions.heading: Report One Shape in Schema Errors
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` naming only the errors of the selected shape, and the full shape list with `--verbose`.
provisions.statement: A schema error on a value matching no allowed shape MUST report only the errors of the one shape its discriminating field selects, falling back to the closest shape by error count, with the full list behind the `--verbose` flag.
provisions.rationale: A record declares its shape in `type`, so listing every shape the value is not wastes the reader's time: the cause sits in one shape's errors, buried under missing-property notes from shapes that never applied. Reporting only the selected shape's errors shows the cause first. The discriminating field is the `type` field, or the field the value carries that only one shape declares. The closest shape by error count is the best guess when neither selects one, and `--verbose` keeps the full list for the case the guess is wrong.
provisions.example: A rule record with a misspelled field reports that field under its rule shape, not under every other shape in the schema.

provisions.heading: Report Unverified Use Cases
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` (level S) for a use case whose scenarios are not all proved.
provisions.statement: A use case whose scenarios are not all proved MUST be reported as `use-case-unverified`.
provisions.rationale: An unverified use case is a promise with no proof, so the finding blocks until every scenario has a passing proof or a waiver parks the use case. The waiver keeps daily work loose where proof cannot land yet, and the release stays honest because no unverified use case passes the check unparked.
provisions.example: Claimwick adds `use-case/spending.export-expenses` with two scenarios and one passing proof: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-unverified` (level S) for it and exits 1, until a passing proof or a waiver covers it.

provisions.heading: Require Explanation Files on the Layers a Project Names
provisions.evidence: Does every record page carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections in order? Look at the record files beside their explanation files.
provisions.statement: A record page on a layer the project lists in `explanations.layers` MUST carry its explanation file with the required H2 sections.
provisions.rationale: On a complex product, every record needs explaining for people who did not write it. Listing a layer in `explanations.layers` makes the explanation a gate instead of a habit. The layers a project can list are `intent`, `behavior` and `governance`, and every record file on a listed layer carries its explanation file, requirements and waivers included. On a layer the project does not list, the explanation file is optional for every record type, including research and decision records.
provisions.example: Claimwick lists `intent` and `behavior` in `explanations.layers`, so its problem `problem/expenses-wait-weeks` carries `expenses-wait-weeks.md` with the sections Affected Users, Failure Cases, Current Workaround, Cost, Evidence and Resolution Criteria. A problem without that file, or without one of those sections, fails the check. When Claimwick lists `governance`, its waiver `waiver/export-expenses-unimplemented` carries its explanation file with Provision, Reason, Risk and Expiry.

provisions.heading: Resolve Every Page Link
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `link-unknown` for a link that resolves to no file and no written record identifier.
provisions.statement: Every Markdown link outside code in a record field, an explanation file, or a document MUST resolve to an existing file or to a written record identifier.
provisions.rationale: A link that points at a moved file or an unknown identifier reads as navigation and leads nowhere. A link whose target is a record identifier cites that record: link checks resolve it against the model's identifiers, citation checks count it, and the book links it to the record. Prose cites a record by its identifier, never by its file path.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipt rule is cited as `[the receipt rule](rule/expense.approver-is-not-submitter)`.

provisions.heading: Rewrite Every Link on a Rename
provisions.evidence: `litespec rename` leaves no citation of the old identifier, and `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `ID_UNKNOWN_REFERENCE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: An author MUST rename a record identifier with `litespec rename <old> <new>`, which rewrites every link and keeps the record at its level and in its owner's folder unless `--move` names another owner.
provisions.rationale: An identifier rename touches the record file, its explanation file, and every record that points at it. Rewriting every link in the same command leaves no citation pointing at the old name, so the repository stays resolvable at every commit. When the file name follows the identifier, both files move together. A plain rename changes no owner, so a record never changes level by accident, and a move to another owner is an explicit choice. Proposed by [decision/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders](../intent/decisions/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders/0060-put-child-records-in-typed-folders.md).
provisions.example: `litespec rename use-case/spending.close-run use-case/spending.complete-run` updates the page and every citation together.

provisions.heading: Scaffold Pages and Reserve Identifiers
provisions.evidence: Does every new page carry a reserved identifier? Look for pages created without `litespec new`.
provisions.statement: An author MUST scaffold a new page with `litespec new <type> <id>`, which reserves its identifier.
provisions.rationale: Two agents working in parallel mint the same identifier when each writes a file by hand, and the collision surfaces only at merge time. Scaffolding reserves the identifier before any prose exists, so the second author learns the clash at creation and picks another name. For an article type the command also writes the explanation file, and for a document style it writes the document.
provisions.example: `litespec new reaction spending.send-receipt-reminder-on-expense-submitted` creates the reaction record file with its reserved identifier.

provisions.heading: Serve Every Flow Step
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `step-use-case-missing` for a flow step with no serving use case, reaction, or job, beside `step-screen-missing` for a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves, and beside `step-implementation-missing` (level S) for a step whose serving use cases have no implementing code.
provisions.statement: Every flow step MUST have a serving use case, reaction, or job.
provisions.rationale: A step no use case, reaction, or job serves promises a moment the product never builds. Use cases, reactions, and jobs point up with `serves`, so each step id collects the behaviors that carry the actor through it. Three findings cover the three gaps: `step-use-case-missing` names a step no use case, reaction, or job serves, `step-screen-missing` names a step a browser or device use case serves that no screen serves, and `step-implementation-missing` names a step whose serving use cases have no implementing code. Reworded by [decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences](decision/0049-literal-flow-words-concrete-consequences).

provisions.heading: Show Only Computed Judgments in the Book
provisions.evidence: Does every status, count, order, and finding in the book come from the builder or a check? Look at the book beside the model output.
provisions.statement: Every status, count, order and finding the book shows MUST be one the builder or a check computes.
provisions.rationale: The book is a view of the model, not a second authority. A judgment only the book makes, such as its own idea of what to do next, stays unchecked, fails no build, and stays invisible to an agent reading the model output. Settled by [decision/0008-book-follows-record-layers](../intent/decisions/0008-book-follows-record-layers/0008-book-follows-record-layers.md).
provisions.example: The book orders features by the completion the builder computes.

provisions.heading: Split Record Fields from Explanation
provisions.evidence: Does any explanation file state a fact a check reads, or any page carry field values outside the record file? Compare each explanation file with its record file.
provisions.statement: A fact a check reads MUST live as a field in the record file, the page's only metadata carrier.
provisions.rationale: Two metadata carriers on one page disagree sooner or later: source links, paths, and evidence drift between the record file and the explanation file. One record file keeps every field a check reads in one place: fields are checked and prose is not, so a check-read fact sitting in prose is invisible to its check. The page explanation cites entries by identifier, so entries need no file of their own. A generated region that `model render` writes from the record file is not a second carrier, because no person edits it and `model check` reports any drift from the record. The source-links region of a research or constraint explanation is one such region.
provisions.example: The submit-expense summary lives in the `summary` field of `submit-expense.yaml`, while why the flow reads well lives under Notes in `submit-expense.md`.

provisions.heading: State the Common Fields on Every Record
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record missing a common field.
provisions.statement: Every written record MUST carry its type, identifier, and title.
provisions.rationale: Type, identifier, and title are the fields every join needs. Without them on every record, the builder cannot connect decisions to requirements, scenarios to results, or records to terms, and the model falls apart into loose pages. A record adds `terms` when it uses glossary terms and `records` when it holds entries.

provisions.heading: State What a Reader Needs on the Record and Check Each Copy
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-governs-drift`, `classification-drift` and `data-class-fields-drift` for a stated copy that differs from its source.
provisions.statement: A record MUST state the links and facts a reader needs to read it alone, with every stated fact the model can also derive held by a check that reports a difference.
provisions.rationale: An isolated file reads whole by eye and by tool, without opening the files it links to. The copy stays honest because a check compares it with its source on every run: `governs` against the links naming the rule, `via` and `access` against the entry points and permissions the use case declares, a field `classification` against its data class, a data class `fields` list against the fields naming the class, and a screen `serves` against the steps its use cases serve. Judgments stay computed and are never typed: completion, scope, proof status, counts, and censuses. Settled by [decision/0070-keep-one-source-for-each-fact](decision/0070-keep-one-source-for-each-fact).
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense use case declares its entry points in `via`, and a check reports an entry point the explanation names that `via` lacks.

provisions.heading: State What Happens in Every Behavior Statement
provisions.evidence: Does any rule statement, scenario step, result meaning, or result sentence hide its behavior behind a vague word? Look at the statements the change adds.
provisions.statement: A rule statement, scenario step, result meaning, and result sentence SHOULD avoid words that hide behavior.
provisions.rationale: The vague words are handle, handles, handled, process, processes, manage, manages, various, etc., appropriate, appropriately, properly, as needed, and so on: each says that something happens without saying what. A reader cannot check a statement that hides its behavior, so each statement names the act in words a test could assert.
provisions.example: A scenario step reads "The member borrows the copy" rather than "The member handles the copy".

provisions.heading: Sync Record-Determined Code from the Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `sync-drift` for each file `litespec sync` writes that is missing or differs from what the records render now.
provisions.statement: Code that the records fully determine MUST come from `litespec sync`, written again in the same change as the record and never typed by hand.
provisions.rationale: A typed copy of a record fact drifts the first time the record changes and the copy does not: a refusal code typed into an exception and into the web, a permission name typed into a policy, an event decision typed into startup code. A generator removes the typing, and the drift check removes the drift. The records stay the one source, and the generated files carry no fact of their own. Split into two commands by [decision/0120-scaffold-explicit-files-and-sync-pure-data](../intent/decisions/0120-scaffold-explicit-files-and-sync-pure-data/0120-scaffold-explicit-files-and-sync-pure-data.md): `litespec scaffold` writes the explicit files a person owns, and `litespec sync` writes the pure data a tool rewrites.
provisions.example: The spending refusal codes live in a generated class, with one constant per refusal holding its code. When the receipt rule gains a refusal, the same change runs `litespec sync` and the exceptions read the new constant.

provisions.heading: Take Decision Numbers from One Sequence
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-key-duplicate` for two decisions sharing one number.
provisions.statement: A decision number MUST come from one sequence across every home, with each decision folder named `<four-digit number>-<name>/` holding its record file.
provisions.rationale: Product and technical decisions share one identifier space, so a number identifies one decision wherever it sits. `litespec new decision` takes the next free number, and no two decisions share it. Each decision folder is named `<four-digit number>-<name>/` and holds its record file `<four-digit number>-<name>.yaml`, with `decision/<four-digit number>-<name>` as its identifier. Numbers order decisions by when each choice was proposed, giving every record a short stable name a citation can carry. The number counts as a word, so digits never stand alone in the identifier.
provisions.example: `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` is the fifth decision, whether it sits under Intent or under Implementation.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record File in Canonical Form
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `format-drift` for a record file whose text differs from its canonical form.
provisions.statement: Every record file MUST match the canonical text the record writer produces for it.
provisions.rationale: One layout for every record keeps diffs small and readers on content: a change shows the moved fact, never reflowed prose or reordered keys. The tool owns the layout, so `litespec model format` rewrites every record file into canonical form and the check reports any file that differs.
provisions.example: A use-case file opens with `type`, `id`, and `title`, holds its own fields in schema order, and closes with `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Home
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-placement-invalid` for a folder outside the closed set of its layer and level, `record-placement-invalid` for a `modules` folder naming no declared module, and `record-placement-invalid` for a record outside its home.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every record in the home its type names.
provisions.rationale: A fixed home tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. A record kept anywhere else misses the checks that scan its home, so it looks sound while nothing validates it. Settled by [decision/0042-record-named-folders](../intent/decisions/0042-record-named-folders/0042-record-named-folders.md), which puts each named record in its own folder beside its explanation.
provisions.example: A decision lives at `.litespec/intent/decisions/0001-receipt-threshold/0001-receipt-threshold.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Write Every Record in Its Record File
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a record file that does not parse or whose top level names no record type or container page style.
provisions.statement: Every record page MUST live in one record file holding one YAML mapping with its entries in `records`.
provisions.rationale: One file per page tells a reader where to open a record and tells the builder where to read it. The mapping holds exactly the fields the schema defines for its type, with entries in `records`, so every record has one shape and the checks read every record the same way. A record kept anywhere else misses the checks that scan its home. Settled by [decision/0020-records-in-yaml](decision/0020-records-in-yaml) on the evidence in [research/record-format-evidence](research/record-format-evidence).
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps `use-case/spending.submit-expense` in `.litespec/behavior/modules/spending/aggregates/expenses/use-cases/submit-expense/submit-expense.yaml`, with its results and scenarios in `records`.

provisions.heading: Write Links on the Record That Points
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a link whose target no record carries.
provisions.statement: A link MUST live as a field on the record it starts from, with an inverse stated only where a reader needs it and held by an agreement check.
provisions.rationale: One writing site keeps a link and its source in one edit: changing the source updates the link in the same change. Links written on the target instead would scatter each relationship across every page it touches. A record states the inverse only when a reader needs it there, and the agreement check holds the copy to its source, as `litespec/core/model#state-what-a-reader-needs-on-the-record-and-check-each-copy` states. The Links table states how each link reads in both directions. Settled by [decision/0002-parent-for-every-record](../intent/decisions/0002-parent-for-every-record/0002-parent-for-every-record.md).

provisions.heading: Accept Repeated Delivery
provisions.evidence: Does every event handler keep correct state when the same message arrives twice? Check the handler tests that deliver a message twice.
provisions.statement: An event handler that receives an outbox delivery MUST handle the same message more than once.
provisions.rationale: The target accepts a message while the Worker crashes before recording completion, and the requeued claim dispatches it again. Each handler absorbs the repeat without corrupting its state, since work assuming exactly-once delivery breaks on the first uncertain failure.

provisions.heading: Decide Every Domain Event Outcome
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `domain-event-outcome-missing` (level G) for a domain event no reaction or translating event consumes that states no `ignored`, `domain-event-outcome-drift` (level G) for a domain event stating `ignored` that a reaction or translation consumes, and `outbox-decision-drift` (level S) for a code decision contradicting the records and `outbox-decision-missing` (level S) for a domain event type with no outbox decision.
provisions.statement: Each domain event MUST reach exactly one decided outcome in both the records and the code's outbox decision: a reaction or a translating module or integration event consumes it, or its record states `ignored: true`.
provisions.rationale: A staged event with no handler fails each raising command at commit time. An event the code drops although the records consume it skips its reaction. Deciding each event once in the records, with matching code registration, keeps staging and handling one fact.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `domain-event/expense.submitted` is answered by the approver-reminder reaction and translated by the expense-submitted integration event, so it states no `ignored`; `domain-event/expense.approved` states `ignored: true` because nothing answers it. The outbox registration translates the submitted event and ignores the approved event.

provisions.heading: Deploy Readers Before Writers
provisions.evidence: Does every release plan deploy compatible readers before its additive writers? Check the deployment order in the release runbook.
provisions.statement: A release MUST deploy compatible readers before writers for additive event versions.
provisions.rationale: Old and new records share one store during rollout. Compatible readers deployed before the writers that emit new shapes keep every record dispatchable at each step, while the reverse order leaves new records without a reader until the readers catch up.

provisions.heading: Keep Published Events Available for Read Model Rebuilds
provisions.evidence: Is every module or integration event a read model names kept apart from delivery for as long as a rebuild may need it, with erased fields removed or the key shredded? Check the event log's retention beside the read models that read it.
provisions.statement: A project MUST keep every module or integration event a read model names in `from`, `erasedBy` or `removedBy` apart from the outbox's delivery records for as long as a read model may need rebuilding from it, with erased personal fields removed or the event key shredded.
provisions.rationale: A new or changed read model fills from the events the owner already published. An outbox that deletes delivered records after days leaves a new read model nothing to replay, forcing a hand-written backfill from the owner's tables.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the reporting module rebuilds its reimbursed-expense read model by replaying the kept expense-reimbursed module events, while the outbox deletes its delivery records after seven days. A retained event for an erased expense replays without the erased personal fields.

provisions.heading: Reject Independent Outbox Commits
provisions.evidence: Does any outbox writer use a separate connection or commit? Check each writer source and its path into the business session.
provisions.statement: An outbox writer MUST NOT use another connection or independent commit for required durable delivery.
provisions.rationale: Two commits on two connections split around a crash: the change persists without its message, or the message persists for a change that rolled back. Sharing one PostgreSQL database leaves separate transactions non-atomic, so the message joins the business transaction.

provisions.heading: Release Claim Transactions Before Calls
provisions.evidence: Does any claim transaction stay open across a network call? Check the Worker's dispatch path.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT hold an outbox claim transaction open during a network call.
provisions.rationale: A network call to a slow target lasts seconds or minutes. An open claim across that call pins locks and connection slots, starving the Workers behind it. Releasing the claim first lets the database serve other work while the call runs.

provisions.heading: Retry Delivery with Bounded Backoff and Jitter
provisions.evidence: Does every retry schedule use a bound, backoff, and jitter? Check the dispatcher's retry code.
provisions.statement: An outbox dispatcher MUST use bounded exponential backoff with jitter.
provisions.rationale: A failing target with ten thousand pending messages meets a retry storm when every message retries at once on a fixed interval. Bounded backoff with jitter spreads those retries over time and caps the total, so the target recovers instead of failing under the load.

provisions.heading: Stage Messages with Business Work
provisions.evidence: Does every pending durable message stage inside the scoped session of its aggregate changes? Check each command post-handler and its session.
provisions.statement: A command post-handler MUST stage pending durable messages in the same scoped business session as its aggregate changes.
provisions.rationale: The business change and its message persist together or not at all. Staging the message in the same scoped session as the aggregate changes puts both under one commit.

provisions.heading: Wait for Target Acceptance Before Completing
provisions.evidence: Does any outbox record mark completion before the target accepts the message? Check the Worker's completion code and the target's acceptance response.
provisions.statement: A Worker MUST NOT mark an outbox record complete before the target boundary accepts it.
provisions.rationale: A completion marked before acceptance declares a delivery with no acceptance behind it, and no retry follows a complete-looking record. The Worker records completion after the target boundary accepts.

provisions.heading: Add New Machinery Only for a Current Requirement
provisions.evidence: Does each added package, project, wrapper, process, cache, queue, or pattern cite a current use case, decision, or requirement? Check the added machinery beside the use cases, decisions, and requirements it cites.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST add packages, projects, wrappers, background processes, caches, queues, or distributed patterns only for a current documented requirement, and never for a direction alone.
provisions.rationale: Each package, project, wrapper, background process, cache, queue, or distributed pattern adds maintenance, failure modes, and concepts each later reader learns. A current use case, decision, or requirement justifies that cost by naming the activation criterion. Preference and possible future need justify nothing, so speculative machinery stays out. A direction justifies the shape of a record or a model, such as a field that keeps a later way of growing reachable, but it activates no machinery: that cost waits for the requirement that cites the direction. Unwired or unmeasured machinery leaves the repository instead of staying as guidance, by [decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker](decision/0029-delete-the-unwired-language-checker), [decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable](decision/0031-remove-only-the-timing-variable), and [decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating](decision/0034-measure-mutation-before-gating).

provisions.heading: Complete Work Before Merging
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` blocks on unreached records, such as `intent-unreached` and `constraint-unreached`, in every run, locally and in the pull-request check alike.
provisions.statement: What merges MUST be complete.
provisions.rationale: A branch stays incomplete, but what merges is complete. A record that stays unreached past a merge carries a gap waiver with `expiresOn` and `closedBy`, which parks reachability for that record until the waiver expires.
provisions.example: A Claimwick use case with no endpoint stays on its branch until the endpoint lands, or until a gap waiver with `expiresOn` and `closedBy` parks it.

provisions.heading: Compute Completion from Code and Tests
provisions.evidence: Does any record state its own completion? Compare the record fields with the completion the model computes.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST NOT write completion by hand, because the model computes it from code, tests, and passing scenarios.
provisions.rationale: A reader's first question is how much of a thing is coded and verified. Completion typed by hand answers with a report the next commit falsifies. The [model page](model.md) defines what the model computes.
provisions.example: Claimwick's book marks a use case complete when its handler exists and its scenarios pass, with the model deriving that from the runs.

provisions.heading: Confine Atomic Consistency to One Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every atomic use case rely only on its own writes, with every rule across use cases held by a state guard? Check the consistency field and the rules it cites beside the reactions that follow.
provisions.statement: Atomic consistency MUST cover only the writes of one use case, never an edge to another record.
provisions.rationale: Each edge crosses a commit boundary, so work past it fails after the caller succeeded. Atomic consistency promises one shared outcome, and that promise holds only inside the single commit a use case owns. A rule that spans two use cases is held by a state guard instead: the later act refuses until the earlier fact arrived.
provisions.example: The library's hold request waits for its copy in an awaiting-copy state, and lending the copy refuses until the hold fact arrives.

provisions.heading: End Every Effect Cycle in a Domain Event
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports no `effect-loop-invalid` finding on the changed records.
provisions.statement: An effect graph MUST NOT hold a cycle except through a domain event with a stated end condition.
provisions.rationale: A cycle with no end condition runs until something outside the records stops it, so no reader says when the work finishes. Routing each cycle through a domain event with a stated end condition names the loop and its exit in the records the graph checks.

provisions.heading: Keep One Authored Source
provisions.evidence: Does every fact on the changed pages trace to one authored source, with every stated copy equal to its source under its check? Check the changed pages against their sources and checks.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST author each fact once as its source and state it elsewhere only under a check that compares the copy with the source.
provisions.rationale: One source behind each fact lands each change in one place: the source changes once, and each stated copy follows under its check. A record repeats a fact from another record only when a reader needs it there, and the check reports a copy that drifts from its source. Judgments stay computed: completion derives from the model, and nobody types it by hand. Settled by [decision/0069-state-each-copy-under-a-check](decision/0069-state-each-copy-under-a-check).

provisions.heading: Locate Package Versions in the Manifest
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-version-drift` for a package whose version differs from its manifest pin, and `stack-invalid` for a named stack the manifest does not ship.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST resolve the standards-selected stack versions from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.
provisions.rationale: The manifest is the version authority for the stacks the standards select, so each consumer resolves the same tested combination. A version pinned in prose or remembered by an agent drifts from that authority with the next manifest change. Consumer dependencies still live in package manifests and lockfiles: only the standards-selected stack versions resolve from `litespec.manifest.yaml`.

provisions.heading: Share No Transaction Across an Edge
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an effect entry that names `sharesTransaction` or a use case that `runs` another use case; `dotnet build` reports `LS2021` for a command or event mediator held outside an endpoint, event handler, or job, and `LS2022` for an event published by user code.
provisions.statement: An edge between records MUST NOT share a transaction, so each use case commits only its own writes.
provisions.rationale: An edge that shares its caller's transaction makes two use cases one unit of work: the called use case depends on a commit it never owns, a failure in either rolls back both, and neither use-case record says what it commits anymore. Running each follow-on act from a reaction to the fact the first act raised gives each use case its own commit, its own failure handling, and its own record. The schema offers no field for transaction sharing, so a record declares no shared transaction. Settled by [decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers](decision/0064-raise-facts-and-send-nothing-from-handlers).
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimbursement commits the expense and raises its reimbursed fact, and a reaction in the reporting module answers the published fact in its own transaction.

provisions.heading: State the Strength of Every Provision
provisions.evidence: Does every added provision state its strength and scope? Check the provisions the change adds.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST state whether it is required, a default, or advisory, and where it applies.
provisions.rationale: Strength words work only when each one means exactly one thing. With the strength stated, an agent tells binding from advisory without a check existing, and a check stays an aid where one is cheap and sure, not the condition for a provision to exist.

provisions.heading: Take Every Name from the Intent Above It
provisions.evidence: Does every act carry the name the record above it states in its use case, method, event, permission, route, and screen label? Compare the names of one act across its record, its handler, its endpoint, and its screen.
provisions.statement: Every layer below a record MUST carry the name that record gives an act, a name chosen for what the act does in the business.
provisions.rationale: A name states what happens, so the right name comes from asking what the act really does, including how it ends. The record that states the act decides the name, and the use case, the aggregate method, the event, the permission, the route, and the screen label repeat it. A check that reports two names for one act reports drift, not the answer: the fix brings each layer to the name the intent states, and the intent changes first when its own word is wrong. A rename that only clears the check finding leaves one act with two names, as does a name kept in one layer while the others move. Settled by [decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept](decision/0026-one-name-for-each-concept).
provisions.example: In Claimwick, finance staff send an approved expense's payout to the bank, and the bank refuses it when the company account falls short. The act is a submission, not a payment, so the use case is `submit-payout`, the method `SubmitPayout`, the event `PayoutSubmitted`, the permission `submit-payout`, and the screen button reads "Submit payout". A later command records whether the bank paid or refused.

provisions.heading: Classify Every Aggregate Data Field
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `classification-drift` for a field whose `classification` differs from its data class.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST list its data fields with their meaning, classification, and data class in `data`.
provisions.rationale: Without a classification, personal facts sit beside public ones with nothing marking which is which. Each handler then guesses. A meaning with a classification of public, internal, personal, or sensitive tells each later reader how each field is handled, and the data class ties the field to its erasure position and its retention.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Data Class with Its Erasure Position
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `erasure-undeclared` for a personal or sensitive field with no declared position, `retention-enforcement-missing` for a class nothing enforces, and `data-class-fields-drift` for a data class `fields` list differing from the fields naming the class.
provisions.statement: Each data class MUST declare its classification, its `fields`, its purpose, its erasure position, its `basedOn` authority, its retention period with the date it counts from, and the enforcement that carries it out.
provisions.rationale: Erasure declared per field drifts: one field keeps a new position while another field in the same class keeps the old one. Declaring the position once per class, with per-field exceptions beside it, keeps one decision in one place. The `basedOn` names the authority behind the retention, and the enforcement names the job or use case carrying it out. Settled by decision/0016-typed-contracts-and-privacy.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, the submitter-contact class declares `personal` with `pseudonymize`, its purpose, and its accepting requirement. The expense-ledger class declares `internal` with `retain`, a statutory seven years from the financial year end, and the finance expiry job.

provisions.heading: Enforce a Data Class Through Its Aggregate
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `enforcement-job-unreached` (level G) for a data class whose `enforcedBy` names a job that runs or sends no use case writing the aggregate holding the class.
provisions.statement: When a data class names a job in `enforcedBy`, that job MUST run or send a use case writing the aggregate holding the data class.
provisions.rationale: An enforcement job reaching no aggregate leaves the retention promise unkept. The class states a period and an erasure position, and no command in the run path touches the rows the period covers. Following the job `runs` and `commands` effects to the use cases they send and those use cases `writes` shows whether the job reaches the class it enforces.
provisions.example: Claimwick expense-ledger data class names the finance expiry job. That job runs the erase-expired-expenses command, whose `writes` names `aggregate/spending.expense`, so the job reaches the class it enforces.

provisions.heading: Pause Deletion While a Hold Stands
provisions.evidence: Does every data class under audit, objection, or dispute carry its hold with its reason and start date, with deletion paused until the hold lifts? Check `retentionHolds` on each data class beside the enforcement runs.
provisions.statement: A data class MUST pause deletion while a retention hold stands, with each hold's reason and the date the hold starts on record.
provisions.rationale: A tax audit, an objection, or a dispute stops deletion. A product deleting records during an audit breaks the law even while following its retention period exactly. The hold carries its reason with its start date in `heldOn`, and deletion resumes with the lift date in `liftedOn`. This follows decision/0100-retention-holds-and-rounded-starts.
provisions.example: Claimwick finance team places a hold on the expense ledger while the tax office audits the year. The expiry job leaves held rows until the hold lifts.

provisions.heading: Purge Erased Data from Restored Backups
provisions.evidence: Does every restore runbook name its sweep job? Check the restore runbooks.
provisions.statement: A restore runbook MUST name the sweep job that re-applies erasure after the restore.
provisions.rationale: A backup holds data as it was, including rows erased since. Restoring it brings back rows the product promised to erase. The sweep job re-applies each erasure decided before the restore, so the restore brings the system back without bringing the erased data back with it.
provisions.example: The database restore runbook names `job/privacy.sweep-restored-erasure`. The job runs before traffic returns and deletes each row erased since the backup.

provisions.heading: Round an Event Start to a Calendar End
provisions.evidence: Does every retention period counted from a rounded event name its event and rounding? Check `periodStartsAt` on each data class.
provisions.statement: A retention period that rounds an event start up to a calendar end MUST name its event and its rounding in `periodStartsAt`.
provisions.rationale: The law starts counting where a record stops being current. The start then rounds up to the end of the year, so each record of one year shares one expiry. Naming the event with its rounding states both halves: the event starting the count and the calendar end it rounds to. This follows decision/0100-retention-holds-and-rounded-starts.
provisions.example: Claimwick keeps a receipt seven years from the end of the year its expense was reimbursed. `periodStartsAt` names `domain-event/expense.reimbursed` with `rounding: financial-year-end`.

provisions.heading: Scope Erasure to What the Subject Requested
provisions.evidence: Does every erasure use case cite the request it answers and touch only the data in it? Check the erasure use cases beside their requests.
provisions.statement: Erasure that answers a subject request MUST use `reach: requested` and touch only the data the request names.
provisions.rationale: A subject asking to delete one order asks nothing about the account. The requested reach ties the erasure to the request it answers. A narrow request thus stays narrow, and a broad request names everything.
provisions.example: A reader request naming one hold erases that hold. The reader other loans stay untouched.

provisions.heading: Boot the Production Configuration Before Release
provisions.evidence: `litespec verify production-smoke` reports `production-readiness-failed`, `path-failed` and `stub-adapter-shown` for the project that names a production block in `verify`.
provisions.statement: Before a release, a server project MUST boot its production containers from the committed configuration against an empty database and confirm that the readiness path answers, each public path answers behind the forwarded https scheme, and no stub adapter serves traffic.
provisions.rationale: A product that only ever ran with development settings fails in production on what development hides: a missing migration, a proxy that strips the scheme, or a stand-in adapter left bound. Booting the production configuration once before release finds those failures while they cost a rerun instead of an outage.
provisions.example: Before the Claimwick release, the team boots the production compose file with the example environment file, migrates the empty database, and sees the readiness path answer and the expense API answer behind the proxy, with no stub mail sender bound.

provisions.heading: Check Intent and Behavior Changes with the Book
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` exits zero when it reports no G finding, such as `record-invalid`, and the inspection was complete.
provisions.statement: An Intent or Behavior change MUST pass the G checks with the book.
provisions.rationale: G checks read records alone: shape, references, links, reachability, coverage, and the Behavior rules the check list names. Without them, a renamed record or a moved file silently breaks the references other pages rely on, and the book renders a graph that no longer holds. The command `litespec model check --since <ref>` blocks on findings about records and code changed since `<ref>` and reports the rest, so an adopting project clears new findings first.

provisions.heading: Qualify Each Stack Reader with Fixtures
provisions.evidence: Does every gating S reader show passing fixture runs? Check the fixture results beside the stack reader.
provisions.statement: A stack reader MUST pass its known good and known bad fixtures before it gates with S checks.
provisions.rationale: An unqualified reader blocks on noise or passes on silence, and each mistake trains the team to ignore its findings. Passing a known good tree and reporting each planted defect in a known bad tree proves the reader sees what it claims before it blocks any change.
provisions.example: The .NET reader passes the clean tree and reports the planted undeclared write before its S findings block.

provisions.heading: Record the Release Artifact
provisions.evidence: Does every release show one record naming its immutable artifact? Check the release records beside each artifact.
provisions.statement: A release MUST create one release record for its immutable artifact.
