provisions.rationale: Evidence scattered across builds and reports leaves no one place saying what one artifact proved. One release record per immutable artifact binds every result to the exact output it proves, so each artifact carries its own evidence.

provisions.heading: Regenerate Application Contracts
provisions.evidence: Does any committed contract differ from a fresh generation? Check the contract diff beside the source change.
provisions.statement: A source change MUST regenerate OpenAPI and frontend API types when it changes their source contract.
provisions.rationale: OpenAPI and frontend API types derive from a source contract, and clients build against the committed copies. A source change leaving those copies stale ships clients built against a contract the server no longer honors.

provisions.heading: Report Verification Exactly
provisions.evidence: Does every completion report name its commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, differences, limits, and covered use cases? Check the report beside the change.
provisions.statement: A completion report MUST name exact commands, outcomes, evidence scope, skipped checks, generated differences, scope limits, and covered use cases.
provisions.rationale: A vague report lets unrun checks hide among completed ones. Naming exact commands, outcomes, scope, omissions, differences, limits, and covered use cases tells a reviewer precisely what the evidence covers and what it leaves out.

provisions.heading: Run Boundary-Selected Checks
provisions.evidence: Does every change show a passing result for each check its boundaries select? Check the change report against the boundary table.
provisions.statement: A release change MUST run every check selected by its changed backend, frontend, flow, Intent, Behavior, and extension boundaries.
provisions.rationale: Each boundary carries failures the others miss: frontend checks say nothing about migrations, and backend suites say nothing about rendered screens. Running every check the changed boundaries select keeps each change evidenced where its failure lives. A narrow category passing alone certifies part of the change. The release build catches the conditional and optimization-gated breaks a debug build hides; frozen installation, lint, type checking, tests, and the production build each guard one failure class of a frontend; and an affected extension's stated verification is the written evidence for its surface.

provisions.heading: Run One LiteSpec Build
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `toolchain-drift` when any two of the three name different builds.
provisions.statement: A project MUST run one LiteSpec build at a time: the `LiteSpec.Cli` version the tool manifest pins, the `LiteSpec.Analyzers` version the build references, and the CLI running the checks name the same build.
provisions.rationale: Checks written against one build misread code written against another. An old tool reports findings the current build fixed, and a lagging analyzer runs its newest rules at no point, so the team fixes findings that apply nowhere and misses the ones that do. Moving the tool manifest, the analyzer reference, and the running CLI together keeps every finding about the build the code follows.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense product pins `LiteSpec.Cli` 7.0.0 in `.config/dotnet-tools.json`, references `LiteSpec.Analyzers` 7.0.0 from its central package file, and runs the checks with the 7.0.0 CLI.

provisions.heading: Verify Connected Flows
provisions.evidence: Does every completed flow show a passing test through the deployed boundary, and every flow change its passing flow tests? Check the flow tests beside each included flow.
provisions.statement: A completed flow MUST connect verified use cases to one observable outcome through a deployed public boundary, proved by its flow tests.
provisions.rationale: Use cases passing in isolation still fail together: wiring, permissions, and data cross boundaries the isolated tests touch not at all. A flow test running verified use cases to one observable outcome through the deployed public boundary proves the connected path customers actually take. A flow change alters the connected path, so a flow test through the deployed public boundary alone proves it still reaches its outcome; narrower suites keep passing while the flow itself breaks.

provisions.heading: Claim the Record Layers the Project Uses
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project file without `layers`, with a value other than those the table allows, or with a layer whose parent is not claimed.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST name each record layer it claims in `layers` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, with `litespec` or `own` for Implementation and Proof, leaving layers out only from the bottom.
provisions.rationale: Teams adopt LiteSpec in parts: the record model alone, records with marked code, records with acceptance tests, or all of it, with their own architecture or test practice where they have one. Naming each layer lets every tool check exactly the claimed part, so a missing test project is no finding for a team claiming no Proof, and a team keeping its own code layout still gets its marks checked. Leaving layers out from the bottom keeps every remaining link whole, since each layer points up to the one above it. See also decision/0027-projects-claim-record-layers.
provisions.example: The running Claimwick example claims all four layers with `litespec`. A product marking its code in its own layout and proving no scenarios yet claims `intent`, `behavior`, and `implementation: own`, and `model check` reports no `use-case-unverified` finding for it.

provisions.heading: Declare a Consumer That Has No Backend
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `stack-invalid` for a `client-only` project that names a backend stack.
provisions.statement: A consumer with no server of its own MUST declare the `client-only` shape and record a decision naming the surfaces left without coverage.
provisions.rationale: The shape decides which backend pages still apply. A `client-only` product keeps a domain model, so the backend architecture, domain, and application pages the manifest lists under `shapes` still apply to it. Persistence, the HTTP API, and API testing have no target without a server, and the decision names those uncovered surfaces.
provisions.example: A library catalog client declares `client-only` and records a decision naming persistence and the HTTP API as uncovered, while its domain model still follows the backend domain and application pages.

provisions.heading: Keep Every LiteSpec File Under One Folder
provisions.evidence: Does any LiteSpec record, document, explanation file, or generated file sit outside `.litespec/` or at the repository root? Look at the repository tree beside the project's `.litespec/` folder.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST hold every LiteSpec record, document, explanation file, and generated file under one folder, `.litespec/`, at the repository root.
provisions.rationale: LiteSpec material scattered across the repository sends readers and tools hunting the tree for it. One folder with one name in every consumer makes the material identifiable at a glance: a reader, a tool, or an agent finds the whole contract in one place, moves or deletes it without hunting, and keeps it apart from application code, tests, contracts, and `AGENTS.md`, which keep their own homes. Generated output inside it stays covered by its `.gitignore`, so a checkout holds committed records apart from built files. Every path in `.litespec/project.yaml` stays relative to the repository root. A command finds the consumer by walking up from the working folder to the first folder holding `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.example: Claimwick holds its project file, glossary, cast, and its Intent, Behavior, Implementation, Proof, and Governance folders under `.litespec/`, beside its application code, tests, contracts, and `AGENTS.md`, which keep their own homes. An agent asked to read the contract opens that one folder, instead of collecting a root project file, a documentation tree, a model folder, and a book folder from four places.

provisions.heading: Keep One Bounded Context
provisions.evidence: Does the project keep one business language and one deployment boundary? Check the module pages and `.litespec/project.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST keep one business language and deployment boundary.
provisions.rationale: One business language and one deployment boundary keep every module, record, and use case in a single consistent model. Modules organize related language, models, use cases, and code without becoming independent services or bounded contexts. A second language or boundary splits the project into systems the records, links, and checks no longer hold together.
provisions.example: A publishing product keeps Posts, Authors, and Comments as modules in one context, with one shared language.

provisions.heading: Point Behavior Docs at the Behavior Root
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project record without `paths.behaviorDocs`.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST set `paths.behaviorDocs` in `.litespec/project.yaml` to the folder that holds its Behavior records.
provisions.rationale: Tools see no Behavior tree the project record fails to name, so its records skip every check. The builder joins records, queries, diffs, and the book from one declared root. One declared folder keeps authors and tools on the same tree.
provisions.example:
```yaml
paths:
  behaviorDocs: .litespec/behavior
```

provisions.heading: Record Selected Extensions
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a selection without a criterion.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST list every selected extension in `selectedExtensions` in `.litespec/project.yaml`, each with its criterion.
provisions.rationale: Without a written selection, extensions drift in through dependencies and prose while the checks apply a different set. A later reader has no way to tell which condition justified each extension, or whether it still holds. Writing each selection with its criterion keeps the project record as the one place deciding which extension boundaries apply.

provisions.heading: Select a Size, a Shape and Stacks
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `stack-invalid`, when the project claims Implementation or Proof, for a shape whose backend stack count is wrong and a platform that names no frontend stack.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST select a size, a shape, one stack per frontend, and one backend stack unless the shape is client-only or the project claims neither `implementation` nor `proof` in `layers`.
provisions.rationale: Undeclared size and stacks leave each agent inferring the architecture from the directory tree, and two agents infer two architectures. Declared once, they tell every check which records and pages apply: the size decides which record types the project carries and which test projects prove them, and each stack decides which technology pages and checks apply. A project with no Implementation or Proof claim needs no code reader, so it leaves stacks empty or names them for information. Settled by decision/0122-isolate-three-stack-packs.
provisions.example:
A project with one web frontend and no flows selects small with the svelte stack. The running Claimwick example has flows, so it selects large. Claimwick declares large with a server shape and two stacks in `.litespec/project.yaml`:

```yaml
size: large
shape: server
stacks:
- dotnet
- svelte
layers:
  intent: litespec
  behavior: litespec
  implementation: litespec
  proof: litespec
```

Size selects the large record set, shape selects a backend stack, and each stack selects its technology pages, which satisfies this provision.

The diagram below shows what each choice decides.

![Size, shape and stacks and what each decides: size, small or large, decides the record types and the test projects, with large adding goals, problems, features, flows, and scenarios; shape, server or client-only, decides whether the project names a backend stack; stacks, one backend stack and one stack per frontend, decide the technology pages and the checks that apply.](../assets/diagrams/core-scope-selection.svg)

provisions.heading: Select Conditional Extensions Explicitly
provisions.evidence: Does `selectedExtensions` list exactly the extensions whose criteria hold? Check each entry against the extension catalog.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST select every extension whose activation criteria apply, and no extension whose criteria do not.
provisions.rationale: Conditional capabilities stay inactive until a documented product or engineering condition applies, so each project carries machinery a recorded condition justifies. Selecting exactly the extensions whose criteria hold keeps the active rule set minimal and reviewable. The manifest's extension list is the closed set to select from, so no informal extension slips in. See also decision/0030-limit-the-jobs-extension and decision/0126-consolidate-everyday-capabilities-into-core.
provisions.example: Caching, durable messaging, and multitenancy are extensions. The extension index lists each with its activation criteria.

provisions.heading: Write Every Hand-Written LiteSpec File in YAML
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` for a project file that is not `.litespec/project.yaml` or lacks `schemaVersion`; scope: the project file.
provisions.statement: A consumer MUST write every structured LiteSpec file a person edits, the project file, the records, the glossary, and the pattern catalog, in YAML that states its `schemaVersion` and names its schema in a first-line `# yaml-language-server: $schema=<url>` comment.
provisions.rationale: Without one syntax, readers learn a new format per file, and edits hide in brace noise. People write these files and review them in pull requests, so one syntax with comments keeps every edit readable, and one syntax across the folder means a reader learns it once. The schema comment gives an editor completion and validation without a key in the data, and `schemaVersion` tells a tool which shape the file holds. See also decision/0023-every-handwritten-file-in-yaml. Files programs exchange, such as check results, the model, and `--format json` output, stay JSON, which every tool reads without a parser of its own.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `.litespec/project.yaml` starts with the comment naming `https://litespec.dev/<version>/schemas/litespec-project.schema.yaml`, then `schemaVersion: 1`, and lists its layers, size, shape, and stacks as YAML keys. Its explanation files beside the records are Markdown. Its check results under `.litespec/proof/checks/` stay JSON, written by its harness.

provisions.heading: Declare the Page Scope
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_BLOCK` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: Each page that owns provisions MUST declare its stack and concern in a `**Stack:**` line and a `**Concern:**` line directly under its title.
provisions.rationale: Without the block, the page's provisions stay unfiled. Retrieval has no way to tell which change they govern, so it shows them everywhere or nowhere. One block under the title tells every reader and tool which situation the page governs, with no need to read further. Declaring both fields once keeps the page, rather than each provision, as the home of the shared scope.

provisions.heading: Give Every Provision Its Layer and Trace
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_VALUE` diagnostic for a `layer` or `trace` value.
provisions.statement: Every provision MUST carry the record layer of its page, or state its own layer as a `layer` field on its Applies to line when that layer differs from its page layer; a provision that ties its layer to the records states `trace: yes` on that line.
provisions.rationale: A tool reporting the part of the record model a project claims reads each provision's layer and trace from the provision index. A provision with no layer, or with a layer copied from its page, gives the tool no exact part to report. The page gives the default, one field states the exception, and the index carries the result beside the artifact, so no reader composes the layer by hand.
provisions.example: A provision about expense records on a page under `docs/core/` carries `any` from its page and states no field. A provision requiring code marks on the same page states `**Applies to:** layer: implementation; trace: yes`. Its index row carries `implementation` and `yes`.

provisions.heading: Name the Artifact of Every Provision on a Page That Names One
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_ARTIFACT` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: On a page where one provision names an `artifact`, every provision MUST name the kinds of file it governs, or `artifact: any` when it governs every file of its layer.
provisions.rationale: The `litespec rules` command matches a provision to a file by the kind of file the provision names. A provision naming none on a page of named kinds matches every file of the layer. A handler receives the validator and port provisions beside its own, and an agent reads provisions outside the file in front of it.
provisions.example: On the application page, the provision for validators names `artifact: validator`. The provision for the whole application concern names `artifact: any`. Running `litespec rules` on a command handler returns the second and leaves out the first.

provisions.heading: Record Each Replaced Default
provisions.evidence: Is every choice against a default recorded where its provision's Replacement names? Check each replaced default's recording place.
provisions.statement: A project that chooses otherwise than a provision of Strength default MUST record its choice where the provision names.
provisions.rationale: Without the record, a reader cannot tell a deliberate choice from a provision nobody read. A default holds until the project says otherwise in writing. The provision names the recording place in its Replacement, so each choice sits where its provision points. An advisory provision asks for no record, which sets the two strengths apart.
provisions.example: A project keeps its pattern catalog outside the default path, and records the path in `paths.uiPatterns`, as the provision's Replacement names.

provisions.heading: Set a Rule Aside Only Through a Recorded Waiver
provisions.evidence: Does every waiver from a provision of Strength `required` name a provision, page, or finding code, and give a reason? Check each file under `.litespec/governance/waivers/`.
provisions.statement: A project that sets aside a provision of Strength `required` MUST record a waiver whose `waives` names the provision, with a reason.
provisions.rationale: A rule binds every project it reaches. A project quietly skipping a binding rule claims it follows the standard in records saying otherwise. The [waiver record](waivers.md) names the provision and the reason. A gap waiver's expiry date marks a gap the team means to close, so the waiver stays visible and ends instead of lingering.
provisions.example: Claimwick ships its weekend export without the review step. It records a waiver whose `waives` names the authorization provision and whose reason states the choice.

provisions.heading: State Applies to Only When Narrower
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_NARROW` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A provision MUST carry an Applies to line only when its scope is narrower than its page scope, its layer or trace differs from its page, or it marks its concern-wide scope with `artifact: any` on a page where another provision names a kind.
provisions.rationale: The page scope already governs every provision on the page. Repeating it on each provision gives one fact two homes, and the copies disagree at the next edit. Widening it misfiles the provision under situations outside the page. A line appearing only when narrower, at a different layer or trace, or marking concern-wide scope beside a named kind keeps retrieval exact.
provisions.example: On a page scoped to `concern: domain`, a provision for aggregates carries `**Applies to:** artifact: aggregate`. A provision for the whole domain concern carries no line. On an application page where a provision names `artifact: validator`, a provision for the whole application concern carries `**Applies to:** artifact: any`. On a record-model page, a provision about marks carries `**Applies to:** layer: implementation; trace: yes`.

provisions.heading: Use Only Declared Scope Values
provisions.evidence: `litespec-maintain validate` emits no `SCOPE_VALUE` diagnostic.
provisions.statement: A Scope block and an Applies to line MUST use only the stack, concern, artifact, layer, and trace values this page lists.
provisions.rationale: Retrieval matches situations to values. A value invented on one page matches nothing, and its provisions surface for no change they govern. One closed vocabulary keeps every value comparable across pages. A new situation earns its value on this page first, then uses it on its page.
provisions.example: A provision about the expense aggregate narrows with `artifact: aggregate` rather than inventing `artifact: receipt`. A provision about marks on a record-model page states `trace: yes` rather than inventing a trace value.

provisions.heading: Apply the Complete Stack
provisions.evidence: Does the project apply every page its stack selection brings in? Compare the files against the stack folders, the folders above them, and their stackless subfolders.
provisions.statement: A consumer selecting a stack MUST apply the pages in its folder, every folder above it, and their subfolders that hold no stack.
provisions.rationale: The stack is the unit of conformance: a consumer claims no stack while silently omitting an applicable page. Applying the folder, every folder above it, and their stackless subfolders keeps inherited principles in force without restating them. A deeper page replaces the provisions it names, so everything it leaves unnamed keeps applying. Settled by decision/0122-isolate-three-stack-packs.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Edge Between Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` emits no `effect-undeclared` or `effect-loop-invalid` finding across use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, and integration events, and reports `effect-unimplemented` (check level S) for a declared edge no code takes.
provisions.statement: Every edge between use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, integration events, and external systems MUST be declared in a record and checked.
provisions.rationale: The declared edges form the effect graph the checks verify, and an undeclared edge is the defect, not the mechanism carrying it. Cycles in the graph end in a domain event with a stated end condition. No edge shares a transaction: a use case commits its own writes, a reaction or job alone runs a use case, and an outbound integration event follows from the domain event it translates. The [behavior page](behavior.md) states the edge fields, and the [layers page](layers.md) states how Implementation is checked against them.

provisions.heading: Deliver One Complete Use Case
provisions.evidence: Does every use case page show behavior, persistence, entry points, tests, and operating records? Check the use case page against its records.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST complete with behavior, persistence, entry points, evidence, and operating impact.
provisions.rationale: A use case is done when a caller runs it and operations support it: behavior, storage, entry points, automated evidence, and operating impact together. Accepting a thinner slice leaves the missing parts for later, and later rarely itemizes what shipped half-built. Placeholder work leaves the use case unimplemented. Multi-step product outcomes belong to a flow rather than stretching one use case across several goals.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `use-case/spending.submit-expense` use case without its tests and operating records is not complete.

provisions.heading: Point Code and Tests up to Records
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing`, `mark-unknown`, and `mark-count-invalid` (check level S) for a code element with no mark, a mark naming no record of the type its element takes, or a handler marking other than one record.
provisions.statement: Every code element the marks table on the [model page](model.md) assigns a mark MUST carry one naming the record it serves, with each handler marking exactly one record.
provisions.rationale: A folder or a type name resembles its record, and a resemblance drifts with the next rename. The mark is the link from Implementation to Behavior and from Proof to the scenario it proves, in the two kinds the [model page](model.md) states: `implements` names the record served and `follows` names the choice followed. The mark holds the identifier, so the checks, the analyzers, and the editor follow the same link without guessing. One record per handler keeps each file answerable to one use case. Nothing above Implementation is computed from code, so the link points up and the records stay the authority.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense handler carries a mark naming `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense`, the `Reimburse` method on the expense root carries the same mark, and the reminder event handler carries a mark naming `reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted`.

provisions.heading: Point Every Technical Class up to Its Record or Choice
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` and `mark-unknown` (check level S), and `dotnet build` reports `LS5001` and `LS5002`, for a technical class with no mark, an `implements` mark naming no Behavior record, or a `follows` mark naming no provision of the carried release, no decision, waiver, or project convention, or a provision on a page the project's stacks do not apply.
provisions.statement: Every technical class the marks table on the [model page](model.md) names MUST carry at least one mark: an `implements` mark naming a Behavior record it serves, or a `follows` mark naming the LiteSpec provision, decision, waiver, or project convention that shapes it.
provisions.rationale: Every class in the outer layers exists for a record or for a reason. An input validator or a read model serves one use case, and a repository serves one aggregate, so each names that record in `implements` like the handler beside it. Code serving no record still exists for a reason: a provision requires it, a technical decision chose it, a waiver allows it, or a project convention states it, and a `follows` mark names that reason by identifier. The named target is the reason for the shape the class carries, so review judges a `follows` mark by whether its target requires that shape. A reader asking why the command pipeline commits once, or why the repository stores documents, follows the link instead of guessing, and a check finds the code still following a deleted decision. A class serves a record in a chosen way with both kinds.
provisions.example: The Claimwick submit-expense validator carries `/// <implements>use-case/spending.submit-expense</implements>`. The receipt PDF renderer carries `/// <follows>decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf</follows>`, and the command pipeline's commit step carries `/// <follows>litespec/core/backend-persistence#commit-each-command-pipeline-once</follows>`. The payout bank port carries `/// <follows>claimwick/conventions#confirm-large-payouts</follows>`.

provisions.heading: Update Records with Behavior
provisions.evidence: Does every behavior change update its use case page, tests, product records, decision, flow, and operating records? Check the behavior change against its records.
provisions.statement: An observable behavior change MUST update its use case page, implementation, tests, product records, decision, flow, and operating records together.
provisions.rationale: Records map to current names and paths when each behavior change carries them along. A change moving code but leaving the use case page, the tests, or the flow behind splits the project into stated fiction and unstated fact. Updating the records in the same change keeps the change to behavior and the change to its description in one place.

provisions.heading: Define Tenant Isolation
provisions.evidence: Does the adoption decision name its isolation model with its guarantee and operating trade-off? Check the adoption decision.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant decision MUST define shared-table, schema, or database isolation and state its guarantee and operating trade-off.
provisions.rationale: Shared tables, separate schemas, and separate databases isolate differently and operate differently. Each choice moves work between queries, migrations, backups, and scaling. Naming the model with its guarantee and its operating trade-off tells each later choice which isolation it relies on.

provisions.heading: Isolate Administrative Cross-Tenant Access
provisions.evidence: Does every administrative cross-tenant use case require a platform-scope permission, with an audit record for every run? Check the use case permissions beside the audit trail.
provisions.statement: An administrative cross-tenant operation MUST require a permission the actor holds through a role whose scope is platform, writing an audit record.
provisions.rationale: Support and operations sometimes reach across tenants. That reach takes exceptional control: a permission held through a role of `platform` scope, with an audit record for each use. Without both, one support login opens each customer data with no record of what it touched.

provisions.heading: Limit Every Delegation in Time
provisions.evidence: Does every delegation carry an expiry or a revocation path? Check each delegation record.
provisions.statement: A delegation MUST carry an expiry or a revocation path.
provisions.rationale: Without an end, a grant outlives its reason. The assistant keeps acting after the engagement ends, with no date prompting anyone to reopen the pairing. An expiry ends the pairing on its date, and a revocation path ends it on demand.

provisions.heading: Reject Unrestricted Tenant Input
provisions.evidence: Does any tenant resolver path accept a tenant identifier from request data? Check the tenant resolver code.
provisions.statement: A tenant resolver MUST NOT accept an unrestricted tenant ID from request data.
provisions.rationale: Any caller names any tenant where the tenant ID comes directly from request data. Rejecting unrestricted input keeps the request from choosing a data boundary outside its authenticated context.

provisions.heading: Resolve Tenant Identity from Trusted Context
provisions.evidence: Does every trusted host boundary resolve the tenant from an authenticated source? Check each boundary's tenant resolution.
provisions.statement: A trusted host boundary MUST resolve tenant identity from verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source.
provisions.rationale: The tenant decides which data the request touches. A trusted host boundary resolves it from verified claims, host mapping, or another authenticated source. A tenant identifier from request data is caller-chosen rather than authenticated.

provisions.heading: Scope Persistence Sessions to the Tenant
provisions.evidence: Does every session-creation path resolve the tenant through its provider's own tenancy support? Check each provider's session creation.
provisions.statement: A multi-tenant persistence implementation MUST resolve its tenant at session creation through the selected provider's own tenancy support.
provisions.rationale: A session opened without a tenant serves its next query without scope. Resolving the tenant at session creation scopes each query the session runs, so no query needs its own check. Filtering per query instead means any query omitting the filter reads across tenants.

provisions.heading: Scope Tenant-Owned Records
provisions.evidence: Does every tenant-owned document, query, constraint, cache key, outbox record, reaction, job, export, and storage path in code carry tenant scope? Check the code for each kind.
provisions.statement: Every tenant-owned document, query, unique constraint, cache key, outbox record, reaction, job, export, and object-storage path MUST include tenant scope.
provisions.rationale: Documents, queries, constraints, cache keys, outbox records, reactions, jobs, exports, and storage paths each carry one tenant data into reach of another where scope is absent. Leaving scope out of any one of them discloses or mixes customer data through exactly that gap. Each kind carries tenant scope in code.

provisions.heading: Verify Actor and Target Tenancy
provisions.evidence: Does every protected operation refuse when the actor and target tenants mismatch? Check the authorization tests.
provisions.statement: A protected multi-tenant operation MUST confirm actor and target tenancy, with the needed permission held at the resolved scope and the target belonging to it.
provisions.rationale: Checking the caller alone leaves the target unchecked. An authorized caller still names a resource from another tenant. The operation confirms both sides through one chain: the actor holds a role for the resolved tenant, the permission names the role, the use case declares that permission, and the target belongs to the same scope.

provisions.heading: Mirror Production Module Names
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` for a test folder under `{Module}/{Aggregates}/` naming no declared aggregate or use case, and `use-case-unimplemented` for a use case with scenarios and no `Application/` folder.
provisions.statement: Mirror the production module, aggregate, and use case folder names inside each test suite, so acceptance tests mirror `{Module}/{Aggregates}/{UseCase}/` with no layer segment.
provisions.rationale: When test folders mirror production folders, a reader finds the tests for a module without searching. Harness and flat files stay exempt: a `Support` folder and flat Architecture test files need no production counterpart. Adapter tests sit under the adapter's `Infrastructure/` path and are exempt by kind, since they prove a scenario through an adapter owning no use case folder.
provisions.example:
Each test tree mirrors the production module folders, with no layer segment:

```text
Unit tests/
  Posts/
    Posts/
      CreateDraft/
      GetPost/
Integration tests/
  Posts/
    Posts/
      CreateDraft/
  Support/
Architecture tests/
```

The same module names appear in every test tree, apart from the exempt harness files and adapter tests.

provisions.heading: Limit Each Non-Hub Screen to Four Offered Commands
provisions.evidence: Does every non-hub screen offer at most 4 commands, with only explicitly typed read-only lookups excluded? Check each screen record beside its route.
provisions.statement: A screen MUST offer at most 4 commands in `offers`, not counting read-only lookup queries explicitly typed as queries.
provisions.rationale: Each offered command is a job the page claims. A fifth offer shares the page with a second job, and the decomposition table applies again. Untyped reads count as offers until proven otherwise.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense detail offers open, approve, request changes, and reimburse: 4 offers. A fifth offer, such as editing workspace settings, moves to its own settings sub-route.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Route from One Locked Archetype
provisions.evidence: Does every route compose exactly one archetype and fill only its declared slots? Check each route against its archetype row.
provisions.statement: A route MUST compose exactly one of the six locked archetypes using only its declared slots.
provisions.rationale: Open composition drifts: a list page grows a second form, a record page stacks drawers, a settings page buries a table. One archetype per route fixes the slots up front, and the declared slots keep each job in its approved shape.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense list composes `ListPage` and fills `header`, `filterBar`, `table`, and `pagination`.

provisions.heading: Compose Each Screen from Its Owners Queries
provisions.evidence: Does every screen join each owner's query, with no query that only shows another module's data? Check each screen beside the owning modules.
provisions.statement: A screen that shows data owned by several modules MUST join each owner's query, and a query that only shows another module's data belongs to that module.
provisions.rationale: A screen that copies another module's data into its own query answers one question twice, and the copies drift apart. Joining each owner's query keeps one owner per fact.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense detail joins the spending query for the expense with the payouts query for its reimbursements.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Screen Job and Archetype
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a screen without `route`, `archetype`, `job`, `offers`, `primaryAction`, `states`, or `leadsTo`, and for an `archetype` outside the six locked archetypes.
provisions.statement: Each screen MUST declare `route`, its optional sub-nav parent in `section`, its `archetype` from the six locked archetypes, its `job` as one plain sentence naming the single user job, its `offers`, its `primaryAction`, its `states`, and its `leadsTo`.
provisions.rationale: A screen without a stated job and archetype is reviewed by feel. One sentence forces the one-job decision up front, and the archetype fixes which slots and guardrails the review checks. `primaryAction`, `states`, and `leadsTo` state what the person starts, what the page shows while busy or empty, and where each path continues. Organized jobs-first with six locked archetypes and rendered-page proof by [decision/0124-jobs-first-ui-verification](../intent/decisions/0124-jobs-first-ui-verification/0124-jobs-first-ui-verification.md).
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense list declares `route: /expenses`, `archetype: ListPage`, `job: "Find one expense among many and open it."`, `offers` with the list query and the new-expense command, `primaryAction: new-expense`, `states` for empty and loading, and `leadsTo` with the expense detail route.

provisions.heading: Declare Navigation on Each Browser Entry Point
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a browser entry point without `navigation`, and for a primary sidebar with more than 3 groups or more than 10 items.
provisions.statement: Each browser entry point MUST declare its `navigation` groups for daily work, periodic work, and settings, with `sections` for multi-facet areas carrying their ordered sub-nav items.
provisions.rationale: One reviewed list replaces one invented sidebar per route. Named groups keep daily and periodic work apart, and `sections` give multi-facet areas one ordered sub-nav.
provisions.example: The Claimwick employee app declares daily work (`Home`, `Expenses`, `Approvals`), periodic work (`Reports`, `Close`), and settings (`Settings`, opening `/settings/business` with its ordered sub-nav).

provisions.heading: Keep Route Files Small
provisions.evidence: Does every route file stay under 350 lines, or does a waiver decision record the reason? Check the route file sizes beside the waiver records.
provisions.statement: A route file MUST stay under 350 lines with an explicit waiver decision covering any file above that limit.
provisions.rationale: A route file of 500 to 1,500 lines holds several jobs, modes, or facets in one file. The count is the cheapest proxy for that defect, pushing modes into isolated parts and facets into sub-routes where the archetype guardrails check them. Teams treat 250 lines as the practical target, with the 350-line limit as the defect boundary.
provisions.example: Claimwick's flagged-expense review keeps each mode view under 250 lines by isolating `Match`, `Split`, and `Reject` behind route-backed mode tabs.

provisions.heading: Review Changed Routes with an Independent Visual Critic
provisions.evidence: `litespec ui review --since <base>` records the critic score per dimension for every changed route and files defect tickets for failing scores.
provisions.statement: Every new or changed route MUST be reviewed by an isolated vision-capable critic context that never built the route, scoring alignment, spacing rhythm, visual hierarchy, symmetry, golden archetype consistency, and single-job focus, with `litespec ui review --since <base>` capturing fresh screenshots beside the locked golden archetype screenshots.
provisions.rationale: The builder reads intent instead of pixels. An isolated critic sees the screenshots and the golden baseline, so it reports what a person sees. Six named dimensions keep the review on the product look. A failing score produces concrete defect tickets that agents fix before the owner reviews anything. Settled by [decision/0119-audit-the-rendered-page](decision/0119-audit-the-rendered-page).
provisions.example: The critic scores Claimwick's new mileage claim route against the locked expense form baseline and files "primary and cancel buttons differ in height by 4px."

provisions.heading: Run Geometry Sensors on Every Route
provisions.evidence: `litespec ui review` reports the failing sensor with its measured value for every route outside tolerance.
provisions.statement: Every route MUST pass the deterministic geometry and health sensor suite at `1440x900`, `1280x800`, and `390x844` in light and dark modes: column edges within 1px, control height with 0 variance and centers within 1px, balanced grids with no orphan cell, form containers within 720px, non-list screens within 2.2 viewport heights, at most 3 top-level sections with 0 nested surfaces, and the baseline health checks.
provisions.rationale: Alignment, uniform controls, symmetric grids, capped widths, bounded length, and flat surfaces are visible and measurable. Numeric tolerances turn each into a pass or fail, and the health checks ride in the same pass.
provisions.example: Claimwick's expense form passes with its `max-w-2xl` container, uniform 36px controls, and one `h1` at all three viewports in both modes.

provisions.heading: Bind Every Keyed Setting in One Marked Element
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-unimplemented` (level S) for a keyed setting no marked element implements, and `setting-key-drift` (level S) for a marked element whose name does not spell the setting's `configurationPath`.
provisions.statement: A setting with a `configurationPath` MUST be bound in code by one element that carries an `implements` mark naming the setting and whose name spells the path.
provisions.rationale: A setting reaches the running product through configuration, and the code reads it as a typed value. The code element holding that value is where the record and the configuration meet, so marking it with the setting it implements names the promise the element holds.
provisions.example: Claimwick's approval-reminder-delay setting carries `configurationPath` `Spending:ApprovalReminderDelay`. One element carries an `implements` mark naming `setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay`, and its name spells the path.

provisions.heading: Carry Every Key Placeholder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `idempotency-key-uncarried` (level G) for each key placeholder that no input of a use case, no field of a reaction's triggering event, and no input of a job's run use case carries.
provisions.statement: Each idempotency or deduplication key MUST name only placeholders that the record carries: an input of a use case, a field of an event a reaction answers, or an input of a use case a job runs.
provisions.rationale: A key template is evaluated where a repeat arrives. A placeholder without a value the record carries is left unfilled, so each call computes the same key or no key at all. Naming only carried fields keeps each key unique to the work it guards.
provisions.example: In Claimwick, `use-case/spending.submit-expense` keys repeats on `{expenseId}`, an input it carries. A key on `{attemptId}` is reported, because no input or triggering event supplies an attempt identifier.

provisions.heading: Change One Aggregate in Each Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-writes-invalid` for a command whose `writes` names more than one aggregate without a `boundBy` rule that governs the use case and names a decision in `basedOn`, and `record-placement-invalid` for a command use case at module level.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST name one aggregate in `writes`, live under that aggregate, and change one instance, unless a rule that governs the use case is named in its consistency `boundBy` and names in `basedOn` the decision recording the invariant needing more than one in one transaction, its record states `consistency: per-record` for independent instances, or it changes no aggregate and declares `writes: []`.
provisions.rationale: A command changing two aggregate types in one transaction couples their consistency boundaries: one failing part rolls back work with no reason to fail with it. One aggregate type per command keeps each transaction on one boundary. A command changing nothing, because it verifies or reports and raises a fact, declares `writes: []`.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command names `aggregate/spending.expense` in `writes` and lives under the expenses aggregate. The reporting reaction to its reimbursed fact answers in its own transaction instead of joining the write. The attach-receipt command names two aggregates with its atomicity rule in `boundBy` naming the decision recording the invariant.

provisions.heading: Cite the Invariants Most Writers Cite
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `rule-sibling-uncited` for a command writing an aggregate without citing an invariant most commands writing that aggregate cite.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST cite every invariant rule that governs an aggregate it writes when most commands writing that aggregate cite the rule.
provisions.rationale: A command writing an aggregate meets every invariant governing it, and the sibling commands writing the same aggregate show which invariants those writes meet. Where most of them cite an invariant, the outlier posts without the checks the others apply. Settled by decision/0101-check-rule-citations.
provisions.example: Three library commands write the loan aggregate. Two cite the one-hold-per-copy invariant, and the third is reported.

provisions.heading: Declare Consistency on Multi-Aggregate Commands
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `consistency-cites-missing` for an atomic multi-aggregate write with no `boundBy`, `atomicity-drift` for `writes` differing from the bound group, `atomicity-invalid` (level G) for a group above 4 aggregates, and `atomicity-duplicate` (level G) for a command saving more than one atomic write group; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a query carrying `consistency`.
provisions.statement: Each command writing two or more aggregates, or reading an aggregate whose rule guards its write, MUST declare its write consistency in `consistency`.
provisions.rationale: Consistency left unsaid reads as atomic until a multi-aggregate write fails halfway. Declaring the mode states the promise: `atomic` commits every write in `writes` as one group, and `per-record` commits each write on its own. A guarded command declares `atomic` with the guarding aggregates in `guards`.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares atomic consistency citing the reimbursed-once rule. The self-checkout scan declares per-record consistency across its attempts. The submit-expense command writes the expense and reads the report, so it declares atomic consistency citing the open-report rule with the report in `guards`.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Aggregate's Refusals Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a result refusal missing from its aggregate's refusal set, `record-invalid` for a refusal entry without `id` or `title`, and `code-placement-drift` or `record-placement-invalid` for a refusal and its exception declared under different homes: a refusal declared under an aggregate whose exception lives under another aggregate or outside `Domain/`, or an aggregate's exception whose refusal is declared at module level.
provisions.statement: Each aggregate MUST declare the refusals its rules raise once in `behavior/modules/<m>/aggregates/<aggregates>/refusals.yaml`, with each entry carrying its `id` and `title`.
provisions.rationale: Refusals declared per use case drift: one use case retires a code while its neighbor keeps it, and the same breach reports two refusals. Declaring each refusal once beside the aggregate whose rules raise it keeps one refusal and one meaning behind each result citing it. Settled by decision/0073-type-every-output-and-declare-refusal-sets.
provisions.example: The expense aggregate declares `refusal/spending.receipt-missing` with its meaning. The submit-expense refusal cites that id.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Module's Refusals Once
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a result refusal missing from its module's refusal set, `record-placement-invalid` for a module-level refusal raised by exactly one aggregate, and `code-placement-drift` for a module-level refusal carried outside `Domain/` or directly in `Domain/`.
provisions.statement: Each module MUST declare in `behavior/modules/<m>/refusals.yaml` only refusals no aggregate raises, with each code's meaning.
provisions.rationale: A refusal an aggregate rule raises is declared in that aggregate set. The module set keeps only the refusals no aggregate raises: a file refused before any aggregate exists, or a module-wide refusal. Settled by decision/0073-type-every-output-and-declare-refusal-sets.
provisions.example: The spending module declares a module-wide refusal with its meaning. With a `problemTypeBase` of `https://claimwick.example/problems/`, its problem type is the base followed by the code part after the module, and without a base it is the short name, the part after the module.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Effect with One Verb and Its Timing
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `effect-undeclared` for an edge the records never declared and `effect-timing-invalid` for a command `sends` or `calls` effect with `inline` timing; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for an effect entry without exactly one verb or its timing.
provisions.statement: Each effect entry MUST carry exactly one verb and its timing.
provisions.rationale: An edge no record declares stays hidden: calls between use cases, reactions, jobs, notifications, integration events, and external systems that no reader sees. Declaring each edge with exactly one verb, its timing, and its failure handling turns each coupling into data. The timing is `inline`, `after-commit`, or `async`, with timing on each use-case effect.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares no effect. It raises its reimbursed fact, the expense-reimbursed integration event translates that fact, and the reporting module's read model answers the published event.

provisions.heading: Declare Every Query Output
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `query-output-missing` for a query with no declared output.
provisions.statement: Each query MUST declare its output in named `include` groups.
provisions.rationale: A query without a declared output returns whatever its author fetched. Readers and screens guess the shape from code. Declaring the output in named groups with fields, classifications, the aggregates each group reads, and freshness states what readers receive.
provisions.example: The list-expenses query declares open and decided groups, each with `{ "mode": "immediate" }` freshness.

provisions.heading: Declare Paging on Every Collection Query
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `paging-undeclared` for a collection query with no paging.
provisions.statement: Each collection query MUST declare its paging with `mode` of `pages`, or `{ "mode": "none", "reason": "..." }` with its reason.
provisions.rationale: A collection without paging works until the data outgrows it: the first hundred rows return, and the next ten thousand time out. Declaring the order, the cursor or offset, and the default and maximum limits with mode `pages` states the paging beside the read.

provisions.heading: Declare the Result a Scenario Ends In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scenario-result-unknown` (level G) for a scenario ending in a result id that no result record declares and that is not a derived generic refusal.
provisions.statement: The result a scenario names MUST be declared by the use case: a written result, or one of the generic refusals the model derives.
provisions.rationale: A scenario whose ending no result declares asserts an outcome the use case promises nowhere, so its test proves a story nobody wrote down. Naming a declared ending ties each scenario to an outcome the use case owns.
provisions.example: A Claimwick scenario for `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` ending in `result/reimburse-expense.already-reimbursed` needs a written result with that id. Ending in `result/reimburse-expense.not-found` needs none, because the model derives that refusal.

provisions.heading: Derive Generic Refusals Instead of Writing Them
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-generic-written` for a use case writing a generic refusal as a record.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST NOT write a generic refusal as a record.
provisions.rationale: Hand-written generic refusals multiply: hundreds of pages each declare their own forbidden, and each drifts in wording and code. Deriving them keeps one of each per use case, current with the grant, the inputs, the target, the state, the knowledge, the caller, and the sign-in.
provisions.example: The library takes `rule/library.unknown-copy` on the id input of each use case loading a copy. Each use case derives `result/<use-case>.not-found` carrying `refusal/library.unknown-copy`, so a handler throwing `library.unknown-copy` is declared with no written result.

provisions.heading: Describe Every Use Case Input with Origin and Classification
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case input without name, meaning, or type, without `identifies` on an `id` field, without `items` on a `list` field, without `choices` on a `choice` field, or with `identifies`, `items`, or `choices` on another type, and `reference-unknown` for an `identifies` naming an aggregate part the aggregate does not declare with identity.
provisions.statement: Each use-case input MUST declare its name, meaning, type, origin, and classification.
provisions.rationale: An input without an origin is trusted on faith: caller-asserted values pass as verified claims, and money moves on an unchecked figure. Declaring the name, the meaning, the type, the origin, and the classification states what arrives, what it is, and how far to trust it. Settled by decision/0016-typed-contracts-and-privacy.
provisions.example:
```json
"inputs": [
  { "name": "expenseId", "type": "id", "identifies": "aggregate/spending.expense", "origin": "caller" },
  { "name": "amount", "type": "money", "rules": ["rule/spending.positive-amount"], "origin": "caller" },
  { "name": "lines", "type": "list", "items": { "type": "object", "fields": [{ "name": "amount", "type": "money", "required": true, "meaning": "The line amount." }], "minItems": 1 }, "origin": "caller" }
]
```

provisions.heading: End Every Use Case in Named Results
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-success-missing` for a use case with no success result; each refusal result on the use-case page carries its `refusal`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare its success result and, on every refusal result, its `refusal`.
provisions.rationale: Callers branch on named endings: success, or one refusal result with its stable code. Without a named success, readers guess what good looks like. Without a refusal id on a refusal result, each architecture layer reports the same breach another way.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares `reimbursed`, with the refusal results citing `refusal/spending.not-approved` and `refusal/spending.already-reimbursed`.

provisions.heading: Exercise Rules from Scenarios
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `scenario-rule-unexercised` for a refusal scenario whose result's rule is not in `exercises`, or an input rule no scenario of the use case exercises, and `exercises-uncited` (level G) for a scenario exercising a rule its use case cites nowhere in its steps, inputs, or results.
provisions.statement: A scenario MUST name the rules it shows in `exercises`.
provisions.rationale: A rule proved only through a test mark hides which example walks it: readers open the rule and find no scenario showing it. Naming the shown rules in `exercises` ties each example to the rules it walks, and each rule meets its scenarios. Settled by decision/0101-check-rule-citations.
provisions.example: In the library product, a scenario walking a second hold on one copy names `rule/lending.one-hold-per-copy` in `exercises`.

provisions.heading: Give Each Rule Boundary Its Own Scenario
provisions.evidence: Does every exercised rule boundary have its own scenario at the boundary? Look at `exercises` beside the scenarios of the use case.
provisions.statement: Each rule boundary a use case exercises MUST have its own scenario at the boundary.
provisions.rationale: A boundary shown only from the safe side proves nothing about the edge. Expiry, attempt limits, and one-time use each fail exactly at the line. Giving each boundary named in `exercises` its own scenario at the line pins the edge as a checked fact. Settled by decision/0071-give-every-stated-rule-a-field and decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing.
provisions.example: The hold expiry rule carries one scenario collecting on the last pickup day, and one collecting after the lapse.

provisions.heading: Give Each Use Case a Command or Query Kind
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case page without `kind` or with an unknown kind.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST declare one kind: command or query.
provisions.rationale: A use case with no kind reads as able to do anything, and the checks have no shape to confirm. The kind decides what the record touches: a command changes, and a query reads.

provisions.heading: Give Every Tenant Setting a Change Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `tenant-setting-change-missing` (level G) for a setting with `setBy: tenant` that no `change-*` use case names in `reads`.
provisions.statement: A setting with `setBy: tenant` MUST be changed by a `change-*` use case that names it in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A tenant setting holds configuration the tenant administrator changes while the system runs. Without a use case changing it, the value is fixed and the default turns into a permanent figure. Naming the setting in `reads` of the `change-*` use case states who changes it and under which access.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `setting/spending.claim-approval-limit` is set by the tenant, and `use-case/spending.change-claim-approval-limit` names it in `reads`. A tenant setting with no such use case is reported.

provisions.heading: Hold Every Cross-Aggregate Guard Until Commit
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `guard-undeclared` (level G) for a command whose `boundBy` rule governs an aggregate the command reads but does not write, and whose `consistency.guards` does not name that aggregate, and `guard-module-foreign` for a guard naming an aggregate of another module, or a bound rule over one the command reads but does not write.
provisions.statement: Each command whose `boundBy` rule governs an aggregate of its own module that the command reads but does not write MUST name that aggregate in `consistency.guards`.
provisions.rationale: A guard read at the start of a command shifts before the command commits: submit-expense reads the report as open, close-report closes it and commits, and submit-expense then commits an expense on a closed report. Naming the guarding aggregate in `guards` states that the rule holds when the command commits.
provisions.example: The submit-expense command reads the report and writes the expense, with the open-report rule in `boundBy`. It names the report in `guards`, so a racing close-report commit either waits or makes submit-expense refuse.

provisions.heading: Justify Every Wider Visibility
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `widening-cites-missing` for a widened include group with no cited requirement.
provisions.statement: Each include group visible to more roles than the aggregates it reads MUST cite the requirement widening it in `widenedBy`.
provisions.rationale: A read showing more than the aggregates it reads widens without a recorded choice: roles see figures their own grants disallow, and no requirement states the view. Citing the requirement in `widenedBy` keeps the widening a decided choice.

provisions.heading: Keep Each Scenario Inside Its Operation
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario assert only its own operation in `then`? Look at `then` beside the scenario's own operation.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST assert only its own operation's results, state, and raised events in `then`.
provisions.rationale: A scenario asserting a later operation effect ties two operations in one test. Where the first operation changes, the second breaks, and the failure points at the wrong record. Asserting only the scenario's own results, state, and raised events keeps each test on its record. Settled by decision/0081-own-scenarios-and-declare-outcomes and decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing.
provisions.example: The submit-expense scenario asserts the stored expense and its submitted fact. It leaves the approver payout to the flow test walking both operations.

provisions.heading: Keep One Kind per Verb
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-verb-invalid` for a use case opening with a verb of the other kind.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST open with a verb of its own kind, or with an either verb.
provisions.rationale: A query named `change-...` or a command named `read-...` mislabels what the use case touches in every listing. The first word is the first thing a reader trusts, and a mismatched first word teaches readers to trust no name. Settled by decision/0062-declare-project-verbs-in-the-glossary.
provisions.example: `use-case/lending.list-loans` is a query and passes. The name `use-case/lending.answer-inquiry` opens either kind on an either verb and passes. The name `use-case/lending.read-overdue-count` declared as a command is reported, and so is `use-case/lending.change-copy` declared as a query.

provisions.heading: List the Consumer Modules of a Public Query
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a `queries` edge naming no written use case, `query-target-invalid` for a `queries` edge to a use case that is not a query or whose `via` names no calling module, and `query-consumer-missing` for a public query no module queries.
provisions.statement: Each public query MUST list every consuming module in `via`.
provisions.rationale: A `queries` edge names the public query use case it reads, and the public query names the modules allowed to read it. Where the two lists disagree, the edge sits declared on one side only. A public query no module reads is published with no reader.
provisions.example: Spending's read-expense query lists `module/reporting` in `via`, and reporting's reimbursement command declares `effects.queries` naming `use-case/spending.read-expense`. A second consumer joins by adding its module to the list.

provisions.heading: List the Sending Modules of a Public Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reference-unknown` for a `commands` edge naming no written use case, `command-target-invalid` for a `commands` edge to a use case that is not a command or whose `via` names no sending module, and `command-consumer-missing` for a public command no module commands.
provisions.statement: Each public command MUST list every sending module in `via`.
provisions.rationale: A `commands` edge names the public command use case it sends, and the public command names the modules allowed to send it. Where the two lists disagree, the edge sits declared on one side only. A public command no module sends is published with no caller.
provisions.example: Spending's close-expenses command lists `module/reporting` in `via`, and reporting's close-period job declares `effects.commands` naming `use-case/spending.close-expenses`. A second sender joins by adding its module to the list.

provisions.heading: Mark Every Provider-Verified Input
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `input-claim-unverified` for a claim-shaped input with `origin: caller` on an entry point that authenticates through a provider.
provisions.statement: Each input carrying a claim a provider validated MUST declare `origin: verified-claim` with the entry point or external system that validated it in `verifiedBy`.
provisions.rationale: A provider claim filed as caller input is trusted on faith: a forged subject or email passes as verified, and access follows. Declaring the claim with the entry point or external system checking its issuer, audience, signature, and expiry ties each trusted value to the boundary earning the trust. Settled by decision/0079-cover-the-behavior-reviewers-found-missing.
provisions.example: The library sign-in command declares the provider subject with `origin: verified-claim`. Its `verifiedBy` names the provider sign-in entry point.

provisions.heading: Name Every Aggregate a Use Case Writes or Reads
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `write-undeclared` for a write outside `writes` and `reference-unknown` for an unknown aggregate.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name every aggregate it writes in `writes` and every aggregate it reads in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A write no record names stays invisible: the handler touches a second aggregate, the second aggregate changes, and no diff shows it. Naming each touched aggregate states the read and write footprint beside the behavior.

provisions.heading: Name Only a Provided Way Out in Each Refusal Sentence
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `refusal-next-step-unknown` (level G) for a refusal sentence naming a `use-case/`, `screen/`, or `setting/` id no record holds, or carrying `instead`, `alternatively`, `you can also`, or `or you can`.
provisions.statement: Each refusal sentence that names a next step SHOULD name a use case, screen, setting, or input that exists.
provisions.rationale: The refusal sentence is what the user reads. Where it promises a way out the product lacks, the user follows the advice into the same refusal. Naming only a use case, screen, setting, or input that exists keeps each promised step one the user takes.
provisions.example: Claimwick's closed-report refusal carries "This expense falls in a closed report. Reopen the report and submit again." only where the reopen use case exists; otherwise it carries "This expense falls in a closed report, so it cannot be submitted."

provisions.heading: Name the Configuration Key of Every Operator Setting
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-key-missing` (level G) for a setting with `setBy: operator` and no `configurationPath`.
provisions.statement: A setting the operator sets MUST name its configuration path in `configurationPath`.
provisions.rationale: An operator setting reaches the product through configuration. The record and the configuration meet at one path: the record states the default and the bounds, and the configuration names the value. Without the path, a renamed section silently falls back to a default nobody chose.
provisions.example: Claimwick's `setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay` is set by the operator. It carries `configurationPath` `Spending:ApprovalReminderDelay`.

provisions.heading: Name the Entry Points and Modules That Reach Each Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a live use case that names no entry point and that nothing runs, and `reference-unknown` for a `via` entry naming no entry point or module.
provisions.statement: Each use case a caller reaches from outside MUST name the entry points that reach it in `via`.
provisions.rationale: A use case with no named entry point reads as reachable from anywhere or nowhere. Naming the entry points shows how callers arrive at each behavior. A public query names the consuming modules beside or instead of entry points, and a public command names the sending modules.
provisions.example: The library `complete-sign-in` use case names the library app entry point in `via`. The provider redirects the browser to the host callback, where the ticket handler in the `Infrastructure/Pipeline/` folder runs the use case under its mark. No endpoint maps the callback route and no screen calls the use case.

provisions.heading: Name the Idempotency of Every Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a command without an idempotency mode or without the key, scope, or reason its mode needs; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a key with no `{field}` placeholder or a scope outside `tenant`, `account`, `login`, and `global`; `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a query carrying `idempotency`. `litespec model check` reports `idempotency-key-uncarried` for a key placeholder naming no carried field.
provisions.statement: Each command MUST declare its idempotency mode with the key, key scope, or reason that mode needs.
provisions.rationale: A retried call without a stated idempotency runs twice: a double payout, a double loan, a double notice. Declaring the mode states how repeats collapse. The mode is `key`, `state`, or `none`, with its key template and scope. Mode `none` carries the reason repeats are absent.

provisions.heading: Name the Result Each Scenario Ends In
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a scenario entry without `result`, and `reference-unknown` for a scenario ending in another use case's result. `litespec model check` reports `scenario-result-unknown` for a result id no record declares.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST name the result it ends in, written or derived.
provisions.rationale: A scenario without a named result reads well and proves nothing: it illustrates behavior without asserting an ending. Naming the result ties each example to the ending it walks toward, so each test knows what to assert.

provisions.heading: Name the Settings Each Use Case Reads
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `setting-unused` for a setting no record `reads`.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name the settings it reads in `reads`.
provisions.rationale: A setting a use case reads but no record names is a coupling nobody sees: the tunable moves, the use case reading it breaks, and no diff shows the pair. Naming the settings in `reads` beside the use case states the coupling beside the behavior reading it. Settled by decision/0012-use-cases-read-their-settings.
provisions.example: The send-approver-reminders reaction names `setting/spending.approval-reminder-delay` in `reads`. A move of the delay then meets the reaction reading it.

provisions.heading: Name the Use Case That Decides a Stale Figure
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `freshness-decider-invalid` (level G) for a `decidedBy` naming a query or a use case or aggregate outside the module that owns the figure's source, and `record-invalid` for a `decidedBy` with `immediate` freshness.
provisions.statement: Each query output group and each read model whose figure a command re-decides at write time MUST name in `decidedBy` that command use case or its aggregate, in the module that owns the figure's source.
provisions.rationale: A stale figure without a named decider leaves the reader guessing who settles it: the page shows seat availability, and nothing says the hold command re-decides it at write time. Naming the deciding command use case, or its aggregate, states the link beside the figure, so the reader follows it to the current truth.
provisions.example: The reimbursed-expenses list carries `snapshot` freshness and names `use-case/spending.reimburse-expense` in `decidedBy`. A reader seeing a stale row follows the link to the command deciding each reimbursement.

provisions.heading: Name What a Use Case Acts on from the Model
provisions.evidence: Does every use-case name carry an aggregate, a declared part, or a glossary term after its verb? Look at the words after the verb in each use-case name.
provisions.statement: Each use case MUST name, after its verb, an aggregate, a declared part, or a glossary term.
provisions.rationale: A free synonym after the verb hides which business record the use case acts on, and gives the concept a second word. The noun after the verb groups behavior by the record it acts on.
provisions.example: `use-case/lending.borrow-copy` names the copy aggregate, and `use-case/sales.add-line` names the declared line part. The name `use-case/lending.borrow-volume` carries no model word and is reported.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Guard Against a Competing Command
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `guard-race-scenario-missing` (level G) for a command with `consistency.guards` and no scenario carrying `competesWith`.
provisions.statement: At large size, each command carrying `consistency.guards` MUST be shown by at least one scenario naming the competing command in `competesWith`.
provisions.rationale: Each scenario running alone passes while the race stays unproven: each command meets the guard in its own state and commits. Running the guarded command against its competitor shows what the race brings. The scenario names the competing command in `competesWith`, and its `then` holds the refusal or the serialized outcome.
provisions.example: A submit-expense scenario carries `competesWith: use-case/spending.close-report`. Its `then` states that the expense is refused because the report closed, or that one command commits first and the other meets the new state.

provisions.heading: Prove Every Written Result with a Scenario
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `result-scenario-missing` (level G) for a written result no scenario shows.
provisions.statement: At large size or with the `bdd` extension, each written result MUST be shown by at least one scenario of its use case.
provisions.rationale: A written result no scenario shows is an ending nobody proved: it reads on the page and is asserted in no test, so it drifts from the code with the next change. One scenario per result pins each ending as a checked fact.
provisions.example: The reimburse-expense command declares the `already-reimbursed` refusal. A scenario walks an approved expense claimed twice to that refusal.

provisions.heading: Return Every Caller-Supplied Identifier from a Reachable Query
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `caller-identifier-unreachable` for a required caller-supplied identifier on a use case an entry point reaches that no query through the same entry point returns, and `module-identifier-unreachable` (level G) for one on a use case no entry point reaches that no query of its module returns.
provisions.statement: Each required input with `origin: caller` and type `id` that names no idempotency key placeholder MUST be returned as an `id` field identifying the same record, or the same identified part, by a query through the same entry point, or by a query of its module when no entry point reaches the use case.
provisions.rationale: A command needing an identifier no read hands to its caller fails when called: the screen offers the act, the caller holds no value to send, and the failure surfaces only at run time. Comparing the `identifies` links keeps the check exact, because names differ while the identified record stays the same.
provisions.example: Claimwick's approve-expense command takes `expense` identifying `aggregate/spending.expense` from the caller. The list-expenses query through the same entry point returns `expenseId` identifying the same aggregate, so the manager picks the expense from the list and approves it. A command taking an identifier no query through its entry point returns is reported.

provisions.heading: Run Follow-On Work Only from Reactions and Jobs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use-case effect that names `runs`, `emits`, or `commands`.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST NOT run another use case, so each follow-on act runs from a reaction to the fact the use case raised, or from a job.
provisions.rationale: A use case running another use case nests one command inside another. The inner command runs inside the outer commit. A reaction to the raised fact runs the follow-on act in its own transaction, with its own failure handling and retry, so each record states one unit of work.
provisions.example: In the library product, borrowing a copy raises the loan-borrowed fact. The send-due-notice reaction answers it in its own transaction, instead of the borrow command sending the notice.

provisions.heading: Keep Retired Background Out of Use Cases
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `record-invalid` for a use case carrying `background`.
provisions.statement: A use case MUST NOT carry `background`: each scenario carries its own `given`, `when`, and `then`, and shared narrative lives in the explanation file beside the record file.
provisions.rationale: `background` repeated one Given on each scenario and hid the step that differs, while the same setup lived in two places. Each scenario carrying its own situation, action, and assertion keeps one source of truth.
provisions.example: Each approval scenario states that the employee holds a session and one submitted expense awaits approval. No shared `background` holds it once.

provisions.heading: Start Every Use Case with a Declared Verb
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `use-case-verb-unknown` for a use-case name opening with a verb neither list declares and `term-verb-duplicate` for a glossary verb term restating a baseline verb, and `litespec model review` reports `verb-distinction-missing` (level R) for a declared verb retaking a retired synonym whose definition does not name the baseline verb it differs from.
