provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) for a named host folder that does not exist, and reads the handlers, endpoints and jobs of each named host that does.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST read every project that `stackConfig.dotnet.webapi` and `stackConfig.dotnet.worker` name, whether each field holds one glob string or a list of glob strings.
provisions.rationale: A backend serves its use cases from more than one web host and runs more than one worker host. Each host holds endpoints or jobs the others do not. Reading only the first host leaves the use cases that only the other hosts serve looking unimplemented. Each named host is therefore a source root of the read. A host that is not a WebApi or worker project, such as a command-line host, is not a stack root.
provisions.example: Claimwick serves member requests from one web host and partner requests from a second, so `webapi` lists both host projects and the reader reads the endpoints of each.

provisions.heading: Read .NET Code Through the Stack Reader
provisions.evidence: Does the .NET reader read every shape the statement names? Check the stack reader source for marks, injected repositories, returned codes, dispatch calls, aggregate method calls, raised events, and test results.
provisions.statement: The .NET stack reader MUST read marks in both styles, injected repositories, returned codes, dispatch calls, aggregate method calls, raised events, and test results.
provisions.rationale: Each check at level S reads one of those shapes. The mark links a code element to its record: a handler, an event handler, an endpoint, an aggregate root and its methods, a domain event, a refusal type, and a test each name what they serve. The reader reads a mark in either style and reports the style the project did not declare. Injected repositories prove `writes`: a repository serves the aggregate its implementing class names in an `implements` mark, or, with no such mark, the aggregate its interface names. Returned codes prove declared results and refusals, and dispatch calls prove declared effects. The reader reports `behavior-unrecorded`, `use-case-unimplemented`, `write-undeclared`, `result-undeclared`, `effect-undeclared`, and `refusal-unimplemented` from code. Test marks with the latest test run prove each scenario, and the reader reports `proves-unreached` and `use-case-scenario-missing` from tests. The reader also reads the options classes binding keyed settings, through each class's `SectionName` constant and properties. It reads the template store `stackConfig.dotnet.templateStore` names: one C# file whose top-level dictionary initializer keys are the template keys and whose texts write each parameter as `{{PascalCaseName}}`. Checks at level S block where this reader is qualified and report elsewhere.
provisions.example: Claimwick's reimburse-expense handler carries `/// <implements>use-case/spending.reimburse-expense</implements>`, and its approver-reminder event handler carries `/// <implements>reaction/spending.send-approver-reminder-on-expense-submitted</implements>`.

provisions.heading: Report a Stack Root That Matches No Folder
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `reader-missing` (level S) naming the field, the written pattern and the resolved folder that does not exist.
provisions.statement: The model builder MUST report `reader-missing` for a configured .NET stack root that matches no folder, and for the default modules root, when that default matches no folder in a project that selects the .NET reader.
provisions.rationale: A root matching no folder reads no source, so the records that source would implement are not gaps in the product. The tool read nothing where it expected code. Reporting the missing root beside the unimplemented findings lets a reader tell a reader gap from a product gap. The WebApi, worker, and shared kernel defaults name hosts and a kernel a valid project omits, so a missing default for those roots stays silent. Only a configured host or kernel path reports a finding.
provisions.example: A library project keeping its code under a product folder with no stack root configured reports `reader-missing` for the default modules root instead of reporting every aggregate and use case as unimplemented.

provisions.heading: Write Each Mark in the Declared Style
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-style-invalid` (level S), and `dotnet build` reports `LS5004`, for a mark written in the style the project did not declare.
provisions.statement: A .NET mark MUST be an `implements`, `proves`, or `follows` documentation tag when `marks` is `xml`, and an `Implements`, `Proves`, or `Follows` attribute when `marks` is `attribute`.
provisions.rationale: The `xml` style keeps business code free of attributes that are not of the business. The mark is a documentation tag read by the stack reader and the analyzers, which need the documentation file every LiteSpec project already generates. The `attribute` style carries the mark into metadata, so compilation keeps it and reflection reads it. Its attribute types are generated into each project as internal types by the analyzer package, so no runtime package is referenced. Domain stays free of outer-layer dependencies. A code element takes one mark per record, and a code fix converts a mark between the styles.
provisions.example:
In the `xml` style, Claimwick's reimbursement handler carries its marks as documentation tags:

```csharp
/// <summary>Reimburses an approved expense.</summary>
/// <implements>use-case/spending.reimburse-expense</implements>
/// <follows>litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage</follows>
internal sealed class ReimburseExpenseCommandHandler
```

In the `attribute` style, the same handler carries them as attributes:

```csharp
[Implements("use-case/spending.reimburse-expense")]
[Follows("litespec/core/backend-application#keep-command-handlers-to-load-call-and-stage")]
internal sealed class ReimburseExpenseCommandHandler
```

provisions.heading: Exclude Development Shortcuts from Release Builds
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5014` for a tagged type that a compilation without `DEBUG` declares, in every project that holds a shortcut. Review the host project file for the Debug-only `ProjectReference`, and `Program.cs` for the `#if DEBUG` registration, since no rule reads the project file.
provisions.statement: A .NET project that holds a development shortcut MUST stay out of release builds: referenced only in Debug builds, registered only behind `#if DEBUG`, with each shortcut type carrying its `development-shortcut` tag and refusing to run outside the Development environment.
provisions.rationale: A project referenced in every build puts its shortcut into the release artifact, where no deployment setting removes it. A `ProjectReference` with `Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Debug'"` keeps the project out of release builds, and the `#if DEBUG` registration keeps the host from naming a type a release build does not have. The types themselves stay outside the directive. The compiler drops a disabled region from the compilation, so `LS5014` reports no shortcut a release build compiles. The tag gives `LS5014` one way to find each shortcut, and the environment check stops a Debug build on a shared host from running the shortcut.

provisions.heading: Enforce Trusted Types on Raw Markup
provisions.evidence: Does every raw markup sink run inside the named policy, with the frontend sending the Trusted Types directive? Check the Content Security Policy header and the violation reports.
provisions.statement: A web frontend SHOULD send `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` in its Content Security Policy and pass every raw markup string through one named policy that calls the recorded sanitizer.
provisions.rationale: A recorded sanitizer protects only the calls that remember it. Trusted Types turns the browser into a second check: a raw string outside the named policy fails in testing instead of in a reader browser. A team ships report-only first, reads the reports, and enforces the policy once every reported sink passes through the named policy.

provisions.heading: Keep Component Boundaries Typed
provisions.evidence: `svelte-check` fails on an untyped Svelte prop, event, or snippet.
provisions.statement: A component MUST type its props, its events, and its snippets under strict mode.
provisions.rationale: An untyped prop fails at the call site the next author writes, after the code that uses it. Strict mode turns that failure into a build error at the author's own call. Typed events and snippets do the same for what the component reports and what callers fill in.

provisions.heading: Name Visual Files with the Stack Suffix
provisions.evidence: Does every file holding a custom drawing end with the stated suffix? Check the component folders.
provisions.statement: A file that holds a drawing no composite makes MUST end with `.visual.svelte`.
provisions.rationale: The suffix marks the one place outside the composites. A search over the suffix finds every custom drawing in one pass.
provisions.example: The Claimwick receipt sparkline lives in `ExpenseSparkline.visual.svelte`. The suffix tells review that the file draws outside the composites.

provisions.heading: Refuse Page Code Violations with ESLint
provisions.evidence: Does any refused element, binding, or layout utility show in the consumer's lint output outside visual files in route and module code? Check the lint output the consumer's configuration produces in CI.
provisions.statement: Route and module code MUST pass the ESLint rules that refuse raw layout and interactive elements, class and style bindings, and layout utilities outside visual files, with each refusal naming the composite to use.
provisions.rationale: A refusal without a replacement leaves the author searching the shared package. A refusal that names the composite tells the author the replacement inside the error itself. Visual files stay allowlisted because a drawing outside the composites has no composite to name.

provisions.heading: Render Raw HTML Through the Stack Sink
provisions.evidence: Does every raw HTML write go through the stated sink? Check for raw markup in the component files.
provisions.statement: A component MUST pass raw HTML to the page only through `{@html}`.
provisions.rationale: One named sink gives every raw HTML write a name a search finds, so review checks each use. Stored rich content renders under its recorded sanitization decision.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense note passes its sanitized HTML through `{@html}`, matching its recorded sanitization decision. Review finds the write by searching for the sink name.

provisions.heading: Use the Stack Class and Style Bindings
provisions.evidence: Does every class or style binding use the stated form? Check the component markup.
provisions.statement: A class or style binding MUST use `class`, `class:`, `style`, or `style:`.
provisions.rationale: Fixed forms keep styling in one vocabulary. The lint and a reviewer read the same four bindings on every component.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense status chip toggles its overdue tone with `class:overdue`. The binding reads as a class toggle beside the chip markup.

provisions.heading: Add the Stack Query Plugin to the Client Generator
provisions.evidence: Does the client generator configuration add the stated query plugin? Check the generator configuration of the Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: The client generator MUST add `@tanstack/svelte-query`.
provisions.rationale: The plugin gives every generated read a query key. One key shape lets loads prefetch and pages read back through the same cache entries.
provisions.example: The Claimwick client generator adds `@tanstack/svelte-query`, giving each generated read a query key. The expense list load and the expense page read share that key.

provisions.heading: Build a Web Form on the Shared Form Entry Point
provisions.evidence: Does every web form build on the stated form entry point? Check the form files under `src`.
provisions.statement: A web form MUST build on the shared form creator.
provisions.rationale: One entry point gives every form the same field setup. Refusal display on a field matches across forms because it comes from the same creator.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense form builds on the shared form creator, with no form library of its own. Its fields validate against the generated schema extended with app rules.

provisions.heading: Resolve Copy Through the Stack Dictionary Library
provisions.evidence: Does every copy call site use the dictionary library with fill, plural, typed keys, and a declared fallback? Check the copy call sites under `src`.
provisions.statement: The dictionary library MUST meet the locale-dictionary contract that the frontend data page states.
provisions.rationale: One contract keeps every sentence in one dictionary per language. Fill, plural, and fallback behave the same in every language the product ships.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console renders its receipt-required sentence through `svelte-i18n`, in every language it ships. Each copy call site uses fill, plural, typed keys, and a declared fallback.

provisions.heading: Declare Titles and Indexing Policy on Every Route
provisions.evidence: Does every public route define its title, description, canonical address, and indexing policy, with every private route carrying a `noindex` marker? Check the route metadata.
provisions.statement: A public route MUST define its title, its description, its canonical address, and its indexing policy, while a private route refuses indexing.
provisions.rationale: Link text and search results read the title, description, canonical address, and indexing policy. A bare address tells the reader nothing about the page behind it. An indexed console address puts a signed-in view in public search, so private routes carry `noindex`.
provisions.example: A channel route states `og:*` tags and one alternate per language. A console route carries a `noindex` meta tag in its document.

provisions.heading: Show Route Failure on the Error Surface
provisions.evidence: Does every route failure render on the stated error surface? Check the error handling of each route.
provisions.statement: A route failure MUST render on `+error.svelte`, which draws the shared problem state.
provisions.rationale: One error surface gives every route failure the same problem state and the same recovery. Readers learn one shape and follow one path back to working state.
provisions.example: When the Claimwick expense list fails, `+error.svelte` shows the shared problem state with its trace identifier. The reader copies the identifier for support and follows the recovery action on the page.

provisions.heading: Keep Route Group Names in Router Syntax
provisions.evidence: Does every folder under `src/routes` that shares a layout use a parenthesized name? Check the folder names under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A route group MUST keep its parenthesized folder name.
provisions.rationale: Parentheses form the router syntax for a shared layout. A group folder without them becomes an address the router serves.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console groups its expense pages under `(console)`, sharing one layout with no extra address. The address bar shows the page path without the group name.

provisions.heading: Resolve Imports Through the Lib Alias
provisions.evidence: Does every import into `src/lib` use the `#lib` alias? Check the import lines of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: Imports MUST resolve through the `#lib` alias that `package.json` declares in its `imports` field as `"#lib/*": "./src/lib/*"`.
provisions.rationale: One declared alias keeps every import of frame and module code readable. Relative steps break when folders move, while the alias stays stable.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console imports frame code through `#lib/app/words.ts`. The import reads the same from any route or module file.

provisions.heading: Write Components in Runes Mode
provisions.evidence: `svelte-check` fails on a legacy reactive statement or an untyped `$props` call.
provisions.statement: A component MUST hold its local state in runes, with props from `$props` and derived values from `$derived`.
provisions.rationale: Runes form the reactivity model the compiler understands. Legacy reactive statements and untyped prop access behave differently under the compiler. An effect covers what derivation expresses differently.

provisions.heading: Write the File Extension in Each Import
provisions.evidence: Does every import name its module file extension? Check the import lines in the `src` tree of each Svelte frontend.
provisions.statement: Each import MUST name its module file extension.
provisions.rationale: SvelteKit 3 resolves each import to its exact file. The extension removes the guess between a source file and its neighbor.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console imports `#lib/app/words.ts`, extension included. The path resolves to one file with no second guess.

provisions.heading: Generate the Records File into the Frame
provisions.evidence: `litespec model render` writes each frontend's file into its frame from its own entry points, and `litespec model check` reports `mark-unknown` (level S) for a mark naming a use case or screen outside its frontend's entry points.
provisions.statement: A frontend's generated `litespec-records.ts` MUST sit in its frame folder and hold only the use cases and screens of that frontend's own entry points.
provisions.rationale: The records file is a cross-route value, so it sits with the other cross-route values in the frame. A union per frontend turns a cross-frontend mark into a type error. The render writes the file before any screen exists, so a new web app runs the render once at creation.
provisions.example: `litespec model render` writes `apps/web/src/lib/app/litespec-records.ts` for the Claimwick web frontend. Its `UseCaseId` holds the use cases its entry point reaches and nothing else.

provisions.heading: Group the Web Frame by Capability
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `folder-ungrouped` for a frame folder past 20 files that holds none of its allowed groupings.
provisions.statement: A web frontend MUST group its frame folder into `session/`, `i18n/`, `api/`, and `ui/`, with no other folder.
provisions.rationale: One flat frame folder reads as one long listing. A reader finds a value by search alone, and review misses what the frame holds. Each grouping names the capability its values serve, so a reader finds a value by what it is for.
provisions.example: The Claimwick web frontend holds its session read and permissions in `session/`, its language dictionaries in `i18n/`, its API client setup in `api/`, and its formatting and shell data in `ui/`. Each value sits under the capability it serves.

provisions.heading: Keep Web Layouts, Error Surfaces, and Route Groups Unmarked
provisions.evidence: Do any layouts, error surfaces, or route groups carry a screen mark? Check the non-entry files under `src/routes`.
provisions.statement: A layout, an error surface, or a route group MUST NOT carry a screen mark.
provisions.rationale: A layout, an error surface, or a group draws no screen of its own. A mark belongs on the entry that draws the screen, so these files carry none.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `+layout.svelte` carries no screen mark. Its child route entries carry the marks for their screens.

provisions.heading: Locate the Frame in the App Folder
provisions.evidence: Do all cross-route values and browser uses sit in the frame folder their stack page names? Check the frame folder and the route and module sources.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST place cross-route values in the frame folder its stack page states: client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data.
provisions.rationale: Client configuration, session read, language choice, permissions, formatting, and shell data cross every route. A copy per route multiplies copies to keep equal. One frame folder gives each value one home, including browser uses reached from use-case modules.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Use-Case Module with Its Use Case
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `mark-missing` (level S) for a use-case folder exporting no `litespec` constant, `mark-unknown` (level S) for one naming no written use case, and `code-placement-drift` (level S) for a folder whose path does not mirror its marked use case.
provisions.statement: A frontend use-case folder MUST export one `litespec` constant whose `implements` names its use case, typed against the generated union of use-case identifiers.
provisions.rationale: A folder path shows a reader where to look, while a tool reads nothing from a path. A typed constant gives the tool the same link the reader sees. A mistyped identifier fails the type check against the generated union, and `litespec model check` reports it where no type check ran.

provisions.heading: Mark Each Web Route Entry with Its Screen
provisions.evidence: Does every route entry export its screen mark from the stated place? Check each route entry.
provisions.statement: A route entry MUST export its screen mark as the same typed constant a use-case module exports, from the `<script module>` of `+page.svelte`.
provisions.rationale: A mark where the address is declared ties the address to its use case in one link. The builder and the check read that one place. A wrong identifier fails the type check against the generated union.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list exports its mark from the `<script module>` of its `+page.svelte`. The constant matches the shape a use-case module exports.

provisions.heading: Refuse Stack-Specific Folder Names
provisions.evidence: Does any Svelte folder under `src/lib` take the name `stores`? Check the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A Svelte folder under `src/lib` MUST NOT be named `stores`.
provisions.rationale: A `stores` folder gathers shared state in one place outside the frame. The rules place shared state in the frame or beside its readers. Refusing the name keeps each value in the one place the rules give it.

provisions.heading: Use the Frontend Application Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every frontend tree follow the frame, routes, and modules layout its stack page states? Check the frontend tree.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST use the frame, routes, and modules layout its stack page states.
provisions.rationale: The frame, routes, and modules layout gives every file one predictable home. Cross-route values sit in the frame, each address maps to one route file or folder, and use-case code sits under the module that owns it. A reader moves from a use case to its code by path alone.
provisions.example: The Claimwick frontend follows the tree in the Concepts section above. Its frame holds shared values, its routes hold one page per address, and its modules mirror the backend use cases.

provisions.heading: Use the Generated Route Tree
provisions.evidence: Does every build and type-check script run the router's generate command, with no generated artifact staying tracked? Check the package scripts and the version control status.
provisions.statement: Generate the typed route artifacts from the files under `src/routes` with the router's own command, and keep them untracked.
provisions.rationale: The typed route artifacts derive from the files under `src/routes`. Generating them with the router command and leaving them untracked keeps one source of truth. Committed artifacts form a second copy that goes stale on rename.

provisions.heading: Use the Stack File Extension
provisions.evidence: Does every shared file use the stated extension? Check the `src` tree of the web frontend.
provisions.statement: A shared file MUST use the file extension `.svelte`.
provisions.rationale: One extension lets the compiler, the lint, and a search treat every shared file the same way. A second extension forces every tool to guess twice.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console holds its expense total as `ExpenseTotal.svelte`. The extension marks it as a shared file in the `src` tree.

provisions.heading: Keep Web Test Mocks to the Stack Libraries
provisions.evidence: Does any test replace a library the stack keeps? Check the mocks in each test file.
provisions.statement: A test MUST NOT replace Svelte, SvelteKit, the query library, or the form library.
provisions.rationale: Those libraries form the stack behavior the screen depends on. A stand-in for one of them tests the stand-in instead of the screen.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense page test runs against the real query library, replacing only the network call. The test proves the screen, not a copy of the stack.

provisions.heading: Refuse a Test Without an Assertion
provisions.evidence: `pnpm eslint` reports `vitest/expect-expect` for each test that contains no assertion.
provisions.statement: Lint MUST fail a Vitest or Playwright test that contains no `expect` assertion, through the `expect-expect` rule.
provisions.rationale: A test without an assertion passes unless something throws. It raises coverage while proving nothing about the code under test. The `expect-expect` rule of the Vitest ESLint plugin reports each such test in the lint output.

provisions.heading: Build Pages from Locked Primitives
provisions.evidence: Does any route or feature component build grid, bar, property, or metric geometry outside the four primitives? Check the route and module sources.
provisions.statement: Page geometry MUST come from `FieldGrid`, `ActionBar`, `PropertyList`, and `MetricGrid`, each used for its single job.
provisions.rationale: One primitive per job keeps geometry consistent without per-route tuning. A hand-built grid beside `FieldGrid` reimplements its alignment and drifts on the next edit.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense form lays its fields on `FieldGrid`, and its submit row uses `ActionBar` with primary and cancel in order. Geometry comes from the primitives on both parts.

provisions.heading: Compose One Archetype per Route
provisions.evidence: Does every route compose one archetype with only declared slots filled? Check each route entry.
provisions.statement: A route MUST compose exactly one page archetype and fill only its declared slots with primitives and feature components.
provisions.rationale: One archetype per route gives each address a single job and a fixed shape. A route mixing two archetypes serves two jobs. A slot filled with raw elements bypasses the primitives that keep geometry steady.
provisions.example: The Claimwick expense list composes the list archetype with header, filter bar, table, and pagination slots. Each slot holds primitives and feature components.

provisions.heading: Declare One Visual Reference
provisions.evidence: Does the product record name exactly one visual reference? Check the product record.
provisions.statement: A product MUST declare exactly one visual reference in its product record.
provisions.rationale: One reference gives every route the same density, navigation, tables, and hierarchy. Two references split the product into two looks. No check tells which route follows which once the product splits.
provisions.example: The Claimwick console declares one calm business reference, and every list and settings route follows it. A reader meets the same tables and hierarchy on each route.

provisions.heading: Keep `shadcn-svelte` Close to Upstream
provisions.evidence: Does any shared component rebuild an upstream primitive with different padding or height? Check the shared package beside the registry output.
provisions.statement: The shared package MUST build on shadcn-svelte near its upstream defaults, at the manifest pin, with no rebuilt wrapper that drifts in padding or height.
provisions.rationale: Near-upstream code merges cleanly on each release. Rebuilt wrappers with drifting padding and heights multiply upgrade cost and hide intent. Review tells drift from design only when local changes stay small. Settled by [decision/0024-keep-the-ui-source-lock](decision/0024-keep-the-ui-source-lock).
provisions.example: The Claimwick console uses the registry output as built, pinning `shadcn-svelte` from the manifest. Its shared components track upstream instead of rebuilding it.

provisions.heading: Keep Spacing on the 4px and 8px Scale
provisions.evidence: Does every gap and padding value sit on the stated scale? Check the shared primitives and the route sources.
provisions.statement: Gaps and padding MUST use the scale: 8px inside button and control groups, 16px inside sections and between fields, 20px or 24px card padding, and 24px between major regions.
provisions.rationale: One scale keeps rhythm steady across routes. Cards from different authors still line up. Ad-hoc values break alignment one route at a time.
provisions.example: The Claimwick record card pads 24px, its inner sections gap 16px, and its action row gaps 8px. Each value sits on the scale.

provisions.heading: Refuse Raw Layout Utilities in Routes
provisions.evidence: The route layout-class ESLint rule fails on any banned utility inside `apps/web/src/routes/**/+page.svelte`.
provisions.statement: Route files MUST NOT use raw layout or spacing utilities directly: `m-*`, `mt-*`, `mb-*`, `mx-*`, `my-*`, `p-*`, `px-*`, `py-*`, `gap-*`, `space-*`, `flex`, `flex-*`, `grid`, `grid-*`, `w-*`, and `h-*`.
provisions.rationale: Raw utilities in routes rebuild geometry per address. Two routes drift apart one class at a time. Primitives and feature components already carry the approved spacing and sizes.
provisions.example: A Claimwick route lays its filters through the list archetype filter slot, not through `flex` and `gap-4` classes in `+page.svelte`. Composition replaces styling in the route file.

provisions.heading: Check Documentation on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `project-invalid` (level G) for a page or configuration that breaks its contract, and `litespec model review` reports `page-section-missing`, `page-heading-invalid`, and `prose-missing` (level R) for a page missing a section or heading, or a record that lacks its prose field.
provisions.statement: The docs job MUST run on every pull request and fail on a page that breaks the page contract or configuration.
provisions.rationale: Documentation breaks come in small forms: a record with a missing field, a rejected term, a misconfigured path, a page outside its page contract. Each one is trivial to fix in the pull request that introduced it and hard to trace once later pages build on it. Running the docs job on each pull request catches each break where it started.

provisions.heading: Run Applicable Gates on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: Does the pull request show every selected job passing, with each skipped job recorded with its reason? Look at the pull request checks list.
provisions.statement: Every pull request MUST run the jobs the jobs table selects for its changed areas.
provisions.rationale: Each job guards one surface. A pull request that skips the job for a surface it changed merges work with no check on that surface. A skipped job carries the reason its surface stayed out, so the reviewer sees which surfaces stayed unchecked and why.

provisions.heading: Run Measured Checks on Every Pull Request
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `requirement-measure-missing` for a measured requirement with no check or no passing run.
provisions.statement: The measure job MUST run the check each measured requirement names for its kind.
provisions.rationale: Each kind of measure has one tool, and the measured-checks table maps them: k6 for API latency and errors, Lighthouse CI assert for frontend performance and weight, axe in the route suite for accessibility, OpenTelemetry signals for availability and latency objectives, and an ASVS 5.0 level with the ZAP baseline, free static analysis, OSV-Scanner, and Gitleaks for security. The tools write their result files under `TestResults/`, the builder reads them the way it reads test runs, and the check reports each measured requirement with no check or no passing run.

provisions.heading: Add a Missing Example Fact to the Cast, Not to the Seed
provisions.evidence: Does every name, amount, and date in the seed resolve to a cast entry, with no value invented in the seed? Look at the seed code against `.litespec/cast.yaml`.
provisions.statement: A seed step that needs a value the cast lacks adds the fact to the cast and reads it from there; the seed invents no name, amount, or date.
provisions.rationale: A value invented in the seed answers no example the specification states, so the seeded product shows a figure no reader traces. Adding the fact to the cast keeps the seed on the one source the [Writing](../core/writing.md) page requires of examples.
provisions.example: Claimwick seed needs a hotel night for the client visit that the cast lacks, so the night joins the cast as a figure and the seed reads it. The seed holds no amount of its own.

provisions.heading: Check Seeded Figures Against the Cast
provisions.evidence: Does each seed scenario read back what it seeded, compare totals, counts and states with the cast figures, and report each difference? Look at the seed scenarios and the cast figures they cite.
provisions.statement: A seed scenario reads back the state it seeded and compares the totals, counts and states with those the cast states, reporting each difference; a project whose proofs do not run yet checks its calculated results this way.
provisions.rationale: A seed that writes commands and stops shows only that the commands succeeded. A calculated total or an approval state goes wrong while each command succeeds, and a project with no running proofs learns that only at runtime. Reading the seeded state back and comparing it with the cast holds the results to the decided examples, and reporting each difference says which figure is wrong.
provisions.example: Claimwick approval scenario reads the seeded expense list back and checks Ava 48.90 EUR train fare for the approved state and the count of expenses in the open month against the cast. When a calculation writes 48.91 EUR, the seed reports the total difference instead of passing silently.

provisions.heading: Keep Development Shortcuts Out of Release Builds
provisions.evidence: `dotnet build` reports `LS5014` for a type carrying `<development-shortcut>` in a compilation without `DEBUG`; reviewers check the same exclusion on other stacks by reading the build configuration each stack page states. A project with no shortcuts has nothing to satisfy, and each stack page states how its builds exclude a shortcut.
provisions.statement: A development shortcut MUST be excluded from release builds at compile time, refuse to run outside the development environment, and carry the development-shortcut mark.
provisions.rationale: A runtime setting leaves the choice to whatever the deployment passes. A missing setting fails open, so the shortcut that makes local sign-in fast turns into the sign-in bypass in a release: a sign-in shortcut that issues a session without the real identity provider lets anyone in. Compile-time exclusion removes the shortcut from the release artifact, so no deployment setting brings it back. The development-shortcut mark gives a tool one way to find each shortcut and report the one that reached a release compilation. Settled by decision/0113-shortcuts-stay-out-of-release-builds.
provisions.example: Claimwick development sign-in lives in a project the solution references only when `$(Configuration)` is `Debug`, its registration sits behind `#if DEBUG`, and its type carries `/// <development-shortcut>Sign in as Ava locally</development-shortcut>`. A `Release` build has no sign-in shortcut in its output: Ava signs in through Claimwick own sign-in use case only in a development run.

provisions.heading: Run the API Walker After API Boundary Changes
provisions.evidence: Does the change report show `litespec api explore` run from a fixed seed against the seeded local stack after the last API boundary change? Look at the completion report and the walker output.
provisions.statement: When a change touches an API boundary, a workspace MUST run the [`litespec api explore` command](../tools/api-explore.md) from a fixed seed against the seeded local stack.
provisions.rationale: A walker reaches endpoints and payloads that hand-picked calls miss. A change to an API boundary adds an endpoint, alters a payload or leaves an event without a handler, and a build or one test walks only part of the surface. A fixed seed repeats the same route on each run, and running against the seeded local stack puts each call on real data, so a handler that needs an id no read returns shows up before release.
provisions.example: After Claimwick changes its submit-expense endpoint, the team runs `litespec api explore` from the fixed seed against the seeded local stack. The walker reaches the endpoint with Ava cast data and reports the response, so a payload the approval screen reads wrong shows up in that run.

provisions.heading: Seed Only Development and Test Environments
provisions.evidence: Do the seed and reset commands refuse to run in production, and does production reference data arrive only through migrations or startup data in the release? Look at the seed and reset commands and the migration and startup data.
provisions.statement: Seed and reset commands MUST refuse to run in production, with production reference data (charts, rates, country data) arriving only through migrations or startup data that is part of the release.
provisions.rationale: A seed that runs in production overwrites real data with example values, and a reset that runs there deletes it. Refusing outside development and test keeps example data where it belongs, while migrations and release startup data carry the reference rows production needs in a form the release controls and reviews.
provisions.example: Claimwick seed and reset commands check the environment first and stop with an error in production. The country rows and rates production needs arrive in a migration that ships with the release, so the cast values the development seed writes stay out of production.

provisions.heading: Show Failure Causes in Development
provisions.evidence: Does a development server failure name its exception type and message in the problem detail, and can every host's logs be read from a terminal without a browser dashboard? Look at the development problem-detail writer and the host log output.
provisions.statement: In development, a server failure names its cause in the problem detail with the exception type and message, and every host's logs are readable from a terminal without a browser dashboard.
provisions.rationale: A generic problem detail hides which handler or rule failed, so you read a missing record as a bad payload. Naming the exception type and message in the development problem detail shows the cause, and terminal-readable logs keep failures in the WebApi, the Worker and the frontends diagnosable without a browser dashboard.
provisions.example: Claimwick development WebApi returns a problem detail naming the exception type and message when an expense rule refuses a submit, and the WebApi, Worker and frontend logs print to the terminal that runs the AppHost, so Ben sees the cause without a browser dashboard.

provisions.heading: Start the Stack with One Local Command
provisions.evidence: Does one command named in the consumer `AGENTS.md` start WebApi, PostgreSQL, the frontends, and the Worker? Look at `AGENTS.md` and the AppHost project.
provisions.statement: A workspace MUST start WebApi, PostgreSQL, configured frontends, and its Worker where one exists, with one local command named in the consumer `AGENTS.md`.
provisions.rationale: A stack that needs several terminals and a wiki page starts differently for each developer, and the differences turn into bug reports nobody reproduces. One named command brings WebApi, PostgreSQL, the frontends, and the background Worker up together, so each developer and each agent starts from the same running system. The baseline command is the Aspire `AppHost`, with `ServiceDefaults` supplying the shared discovery, health, resilience, and telemetry defaults its resources rely on.

provisions.heading: Authorize Each Target Resource
provisions.evidence: Does each protected operation pass the application guard from its use case's declared permissions? Look at the guard decision for each protected operation in the authorization tests and the pipeline.
provisions.statement: The application guard MUST authorize every protected operation from its use case's declared permissions, as `litespec/core/backend-application#enforce-target-authorization-in-the-pipeline` states, with endpoints adding only coarse policies.
provisions.rationale: Two operations about the same record ask the same authorization question. The use case declares the permissions it needs, the guard resolves the actor roles at the scope of the target, and the decision follows from that declaration. A message whose target is the caller itself carries no target, and the guard decides while endpoints add coarse policies only.

provisions.heading: Bound Abuse at Exposed Endpoints
provisions.evidence: Does each public, authentication, webhook, search, and upload endpoint declare its setting with key and rejection response? Look at the setting records beside each endpoint.
provisions.statement: A public, authentication, webhook, search, or upload endpoint MUST declare its limit as a setting record with key and rejection response.
provisions.rationale: Public, authentication, webhook, search, and upload endpoints invite abuse: credential stuffing, scraping, flooding. Declaring the bound as a setting record names the key that isolates one caller from another and the rejection response the caller sees. The rejection is `429` with a stable code, so legitimate callers back off and retry.

provisions.heading: Derive the Actor from Claims
provisions.evidence: Does WebApi map verified claims through the one current-actor accessor, with no request data supplying the actor? Look at the actor resolution in WebApi.
provisions.statement: Actor resolution MUST map verified claims to identity, roles, and scopes through the one current-actor accessor in WebApi.
provisions.rationale: The actor comes from verified claims, not from the request. The WebApi boundary maps those claims to identity, roles, and scopes through the one current-actor accessor, and each operation reads the actor from there. Request data names anyone the caller wants, so it supplies the current actor nowhere.

provisions.heading: Keep Personal Data Out of Logs
provisions.evidence: Do logs, traces, and diagnostic records carry personal data in clear? Search the log sinks and a sample of recent log output for personal fields.
provisions.statement: A log, trace, or diagnostic record MUST NOT carry personal data in clear.
provisions.rationale: Once a log line leaves the process, it flows through collectors, dashboards, and long-term archives the product controls nowhere. Redaction at the sink is one pipeline stage that fails once, and by then the cleartext is downstream. A field that leaves the process in no log line stays out of that pipeline.

provisions.heading: Keep Secrets Out of Tracked and Observable Data
provisions.evidence: Does any source, log, trace, exception message, generated file, URL, snapshot, container layer, or browser storage hold a secret? Search the tree and a sample of log and trace output for key and token values.
provisions.statement: A secret MUST NOT appear in source, logs, traces, exception messages, generated files, URLs, snapshots, container layers, or browser storage.
provisions.rationale: Each place a secret lands is a place it leaks from: source reaches each clone, logs and traces reach each dashboard reader, URLs reach each proxy log, snapshots and container layers outlive the process, and browser storage reaches the user. Platform secret stores hold the values instead, and diagnostics redact sensitive configuration before emitting it, so the value enters the observable stream nowhere.

provisions.heading: Limit Public Error Detail
provisions.evidence: Does each public error carry the HTTP API error contract shape, with no stack trace, SQL, or provider body? Look at the error responses the endpoint tests assert.
provisions.statement: A public error MUST use the error contract `litespec/core/backend-api#return-stable-problem-details` defines.
provisions.rationale: The HTTP API rules own the error contract, so each public error carries the same stable shape with nothing extra. A stack trace, SQL, connection detail, provider body, uncontracted internal identifier, or authorization reason that reveals resource existence hands an attacker the structure of the system with each error.

provisions.heading: Parameterize Database Input
provisions.evidence: Does each external value reach the database through a query API call or a SQL parameter? Look at the repository code and each raw SQL file.
provisions.statement: An external value reaching the database MUST travel through a provider query API or a parameterized SQL parameter.
provisions.rationale: String concatenation or interpolation into raw command text makes the value part of the statement, so a crafted value rewrites the query. A provider query API or a parameterized SQL parameter keeps the value as data. Under the baseline, the provider query API is the Marten API, and it parameterizes.

provisions.heading: Protect Browser Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does each frontend ship framework escaping, a Content Security Policy, secure headers, redirect validation, forgery protection, and rich-content sanitization? Look at the frontend host configuration and the response headers it sends.
provisions.statement: A frontend MUST apply framework escaping, a documented Content Security Policy, secure headers, redirect validation, forgery protection, and sanitization of allowed rich content.
provisions.rationale: The browser renders each response as page content, so injected scripts, forged requests, malicious redirects, and hostile markup arrive as ordinary content. Each listed defense blocks one of those attacks. A route guard or hidden control only changes what the user sees, so it replaces API authorization at no point.

provisions.heading: Restrict a Protected Collection in the Database
provisions.evidence: Does each protected collection query apply its authorization scope as a database predicate before paging? Look at each query handler that returns a collection.
provisions.statement: A protected collection query MUST apply its authorization scope as a database predicate, before paging, rather than filter a materialized result.
provisions.rationale: A collection has no single target, so the per-target check has nothing to resolve against. The scope becomes part of the database query itself. Reading the unrestricted set exposes the rows to the process, and a page assembled from them leaks the total count even when each row drops.
provisions.example: A Claimwick query for the expenses of an organization adds the organization predicate to the database query. It loads no full set first.

provisions.heading: Use Deny-by-Default Policies
provisions.evidence: Does each new endpoint ask for authentication unless it carries `AllowAnonymous` on purpose? Look at the fallback policy and each endpoint marked `AllowAnonymous`.
provisions.statement: Set a fallback policy requiring an authenticated user, and mark each public endpoint with `AllowAnonymous` intentionally.
provisions.rationale: Without a fallback, a new endpoint nobody secured is public by accident. A fallback policy that asks for an authenticated user keeps each new endpoint protected until somebody marks it public on purpose with `AllowAnonymous`. Named role or scope policies add coarse checks while the guard keeps resource authorization.

provisions.heading: Validate at Trust Boundaries
provisions.evidence: Does each trust boundary validate transport shape and file metadata before use? Look at the endpoints, the upload handlers, and the provider response readers.
provisions.statement: A trust boundary MUST validate transport shape and file metadata before use, leaving message checks to application validators as `litespec/core/backend-application#separate-input-validation-from-invariants` states.
provisions.rationale: Each layer validates what it sees: the boundary checks transport shape and file metadata, the application validators check message shape, values, length, range, format, and pagination bounds, and Domain checks business invariants. Database content, provider responses, file contents, and generated text stay untrusted when they cross into a new output context, because validation for one context proves nothing about the next.

provisions.heading: Prove Each Scenario Through the Public Boundary
provisions.evidence: Does every scenario have a proving test with its mark, boundary call, and passing run? Look at the book beside the test bodies.
provisions.statement: Each scenario MUST be proved by a test carrying its proves mark, calling its use case through the public boundary, and asserting the result the scenario names.
provisions.rationale: A scenario states one behavior the product shows, and the proves mark is the test claim that it shows it. A test that drives the use case through its steps, its message, or its endpoint exercises the public boundary, while a test that constructs a handler, an aggregate, or a repository reaches past it and proves nothing. The assertion names the result: the success fields for a success, the refusal code inside an assertion for a refusal. A reaction or job scenario gets proved the same way: its test fires the trigger and asserts what the effects declare, the use case result, the sent notification, or the outside call.
provisions.example: An acceptance test for submitting an expense carries the mark for `scenario/submit-expense.submitting-with-a-receipt-succeeds`, drives the submit-expense steps, and asserts the submitted expense. An integration test for the same scenario builds the submit-expense message, sends it through the host, and asserts the same result. In both, the mark names the scenario, the call crosses the public boundary, and the model builder confirms the claim from the test body.

provisions.heading: Refuse Surviving Mutants on Changed Lines
provisions.evidence: Did any change land with survivors above the recorded threshold and no covering waiver? Look at the mutation report beside the waiver records.
provisions.statement: Gate each change on the project's recorded mutation threshold over its changed lines, starting at zero surviving mutants; each equivalent mutant is recorded as a lasting waiver covering the mutation finding.
provisions.rationale: Mutation testing seeds small faults into the changed lines and runs the suite against them. Each killed mutant is a fault the tests catch, and each survivor is a fault they miss. The gate counts survivors on changed lines only, so each change arrives proven.
provisions.example: A change touching the receipt check runs mutation over those lines with the scenario suite. Survivors at or below the recorded threshold let the change land, and the rest send the change back for a stronger assertion, or into a waiver when the mutant is equivalent.

provisions.heading: Use One Mock Rule for Every Stack
provisions.evidence: Does any test double replace the project's own repositories, handlers, modules, or generated contract types instead of an outside provider or a non-deterministic value? Look at each test double and the mocks each test file imports.
provisions.statement: A test MUST substitute only what the code under test does not own and what is not deterministic, and never the code's own repositories, handlers, or modules.
provisions.rationale: Each substitute replaces behavior the test runs nowhere with its author guess. A test that stubs its own repositories, handlers, or modules proves the guess instead of the code. A substitute belongs only where the code under test reaches nothing real: an outside provider it controls nowhere, another deployable it calls over the network such as the API a frontend calls, or a value that changes between runs such as the clock or randomness. Settled by decision/0032-one-mock-rule-for-every-stack.
provisions.example: To test payment, the test substitutes the card provider and a fixed clock, and runs the expense handler against the real expense repository. A Claimwick web component test answers its API calls with network mocks generated from the published API document.

provisions.heading: Approve New Packages Explicitly
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `dependency-undeclared` (level S) for a direct package in the bill of materials that the manifest does not pin and no decision admits, and `admission-invalid` (level G) for an `admits` entry missing any of its six facts.
provisions.statement: A package absent from the manifest MUST be admitted by a technical decision whose `admits` entry names the package with its owning layer, license, processing location, account owner, failure behavior, and operating cost.
provisions.rationale: Each package carries a cost nobody revisits: updates, advisories, license review, and migration work. A hosted one adds a place personal data travels and an account somebody owns. The decision answers those costs while the alternatives stay fresh: its options and choice give the use case and the alternatives, its `reopenedWhen` gives the removal condition, and its `admits` entry gives the facts a dependency gate asks per package.
provisions.example: The Claimwick `decision/0005-render-receipts-as-pdf` decision chooses a PDF library over an HTML-to-browser print and admits `nuget:PdfSharp` with layer `Infrastructure`, license `MIT`, location `in-process`, account owner `none`, failure behavior "the receipt download fails and the expense stays readable", and operating cost `none`.

provisions.heading: Pin Every Dependency Version Centrally
provisions.evidence: Does every version resolve through central management or the committed lockfile within the manifest major where one exists, with no version inline in a module file? Read the central version files and the module files.
provisions.statement: Every dependency version MUST resolve through central management or the committed lockfile, within the major `litespec.manifest.yaml` pins where it pins one.
provisions.rationale: An inline version in one module file stays invisible to the file that owns it, so two modules drift to two versions of the same package. Central management or the committed lockfile resolves each version in one owned place. The manifest pins the major of each baseline package, so a consumer takes a patch without waiting for a LiteSpec release, and it pins an exact version only where a check depends on exact output. Settled by decision/0036-pin-third-party-packages-to-their-major.
provisions.example: The Claimwick central version file holds Marten at 9.50.2 while the manifest pins `9.x`, so the project takes a patch without waiting for a LiteSpec release. Its receipt PDF library is pinned exact in the same file with a decision record, because the manifest names only the baseline stack.

provisions.heading: Declare Each Pipeline Concern in Its Own Class
provisions.evidence: Does any class declare two pipeline concerns? Read each pipeline declaration beside its message.
provisions.statement: Each pipeline declaration MUST sit in its own class, implementing exactly one pipeline contract.
provisions.rationale: Who sends a message and how the audit trail records it change for different reasons, and get read by different people: an access review reads the authorization declaration, and an audit review reads the audit declaration. One class per concern keeps each review to its own file. Settled by decision/0106-state-class-design-rules.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, the submit-expense authorization and audit declarations sit in two classes: `SubmitExpenseCommandAuthorizationDefinition` and `SubmitExpenseCommandAuditDefinition`. Each implements its own pipeline contract, and neither names the other concern.

provisions.heading: Give Each Class One Responsibility
provisions.evidence: Does every class have one responsibility, readable in one sentence without "and"? Read each class beside its callers.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A class MUST have one responsibility.
provisions.rationale: A class with one responsibility has one reason to change, so you review one job and a change risks one job. Without this rule, an author optimizes for fewer files and merges unrelated concerns wherever an interface allows it. The test stays plain: the job of the class reads in one sentence without "and". Settled by decision/0106-state-class-design-rules.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, an expense repository that also renders the spending report splits into the repository and a report renderer. Each gets read by different people and changes for different reasons.

provisions.heading: Implement One Capability per Class
provisions.evidence: Does any class implement interfaces for more than one capability? Read the interface list of each class.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A class MUST implement more than one interface only when the interfaces describe one capability.
provisions.rationale: Interfaces that describe one capability offer callers one thing, so they belong together. Interfaces for unrelated concerns, such as authorization, audit, idempotency, persistence, and rendering, change for different reasons and get read by different people. One class implementing two of them merges those concerns into one file, and a later reader reviews neither one alone. Settled by decision/0106-state-class-design-rules.
provisions.example: A class implementing `IReadOnlyList<T>` with `IEnumerable<T>` offers one capability. A class implementing an authorization contract with an audit contract merges two concerns, and splits into two classes.

provisions.heading: Name Each Definition After Its Message and Concern
provisions.evidence: Does every pipeline declaration class carry its message and concern in `{Message}{Concern}Definition` form? Read each declaration beside its message.
provisions.statement: Name each pipeline declaration class `{Message}{Concern}Definition`, such as `SubmitExpenseCommandAuthorizationDefinition`.
provisions.rationale: The message leads, so each declaration for one message lists beside it, and the concern trails, so each review finds its own file. One naming shape lets you move from the message to each of its declarations without searching. Settled by decision/0106-state-class-design-rules.

provisions.heading: Take Shared Behavior Through Composition
provisions.evidence: Does any class derive from a base that collects unrelated helpers? Read each base class beside its derived classes.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A class MUST take shared behavior through composition rather than through a base class that collects unrelated helpers.
provisions.rationale: A base class that collects unrelated helpers gives each derived class behavior most of them use nowhere, and each addition to the base reaches each derived class. Taking the behavior through a constructor parameter keeps each class beside only the behavior it uses. A base that defines one shared contract, such as the aggregate root base, is no helper collection. Settled by decision/0106-state-class-design-rules.
provisions.example: In the Claimwick product, an expense validator takes its receipt checker as a constructor parameter instead of deriving from a validation base that also formats currencies.

provisions.heading: Avoid Primary Constructors on Classes and Structs
provisions.evidence: Does any class or struct declare a primary constructor? Look at the type declarations in `apps/api/src`.
provisions.artifact: aggregate, state-record, value-object, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: A class or struct SHOULD NOT declare a primary constructor.
provisions.rationale: A primary constructor parameter is captured, mutable, and visible in the whole class body. Nothing marks it read-only, so a method reassigns it and each later call sees the new value. Inside the body, the parameter name reads the same as a local, so you lose the cue that something is class state. Copying a parameter into a property while using the parameter elsewhere stores it twice. Validation, guard clauses, and derived fields have no home: they need either field initializers with side effects or a second constructor that chains to the primary one. Documentation for the parameters moves to the type, where tools show it less well than on a constructor. A type with several dependencies puts them all on the type line, which wraps badly and hides the type name and role. Positional records look the same but behave differently, with generated read-only properties, which misleads readers who know records. An explicit constructor with private read-only fields avoids each one of these. Settled by decision/0106-state-class-design-rules.

provisions.heading: Name Repository Variables After Their Interface
provisions.evidence: Does each repository parameter, field, or local carry the name of its interface without the `I` prefix? Read the repository use sites.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, job
provisions.statement: Each repository parameter, field or local MUST be named after its interface without the `I` prefix, ending in `Repository`.
provisions.rationale: A short plural name hides which aggregate the variable guards. `orders` reads as a list, a query, or the repository, and each reader guesses. Naming the variable after its interface keeps one name per repository at each use site, so you read the dependency from the name alone.
provisions.example: A parameter of type `IExpenseRepository` is named `expenseRepository`, and a field of type `ILoanRepository` is named `loanRepository`. Each use site then names the same dependency the same way.

provisions.heading: Name Result Parts After Their Result
provisions.evidence: Does each type nested in a use-case result carry the full result name as its prefix? Read the result types.
provisions.statement: Each type nested in a use-case result MUST be named after the result it belongs to, as `{UseCase}QueryResult{Part}` or `{UseCase}CommandResult{Part}`.
provisions.rationale: A result part named for its own shape instead of its result collides with each other use case shaping the same thing: two summaries named `PostSummary` answer different queries with different fields. Leading with the full result name keeps each part beside the result it belongs to in each listing, and keeps command coordination apart from query projection without opening the file.
provisions.example: `ListPostsQueryResultItem` belongs to `ListPostsQueryResult`, and `ReadLoanQueryResultHold` belongs to `ReadLoanQueryResult`. Both read beside their results in each listing.

provisions.heading: Place Each Trigger with What It Runs
provisions.evidence: `litespec model check` reports `code-placement-drift` (level S) for an event handler or job class outside the folder its record's effects name.
provisions.statement: Each event handler and job class MUST live in the `Application/` folder of the use case its record runs, or, when it runs none, in the `Application/Notifications/` folder named for the notification it sends or the `Application/ExternalSystems/` folder named for the system it calls, with an event handler named `{Action}On{Fact}Handler`, and a handler whose record runs another module's use case stays in its own module, in the aggregate and use case folders of the use case it runs.
provisions.rationale: A reaction and a job are triggers, like an endpoint, and a trigger belongs to what it triggers. Placed with its use case, the handler names the command of that use case from inside the folder of the use case, so no command leaves its folder for a caller to reach it, and the folder shows each way the use case starts. A folder named for a fact gathers the commands of several use cases under one name instead, and those reactions span modules, so the question of what happens when a fact gets recorded gets answered by the model query on the event and by the handler names, which carry the fact.
provisions.example: `Lending/Application/Holds/ExpireHold/ExpireHoldOnLoanReturnedHandler` runs the expire-hold use case when a loan gets returned, and `Lending/Application/Notifications/LoanDue/SendDueNoticeOnLoanBorrowedHandler` only sends the due notice. The first lives in the folder of the use case it runs; the second lives in the folder named for the notification it sends.

provisions.heading: Reveal Asynchrony and Cancellation in Operation Names
provisions.evidence: Does each asynchronous operation name reveal asynchrony, with each cancelable operation signature taking cancellation explicitly? Read the public signatures in `apps/api/src`.
provisions.artifact: command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, port, repository, endpoint, migration, job
provisions.statement: An asynchronous operation MUST reveal its asynchrony in its name and accept cancellation explicitly when the operation is cancelable.
provisions.rationale: A caller decides from the signature whether to await and what to cancel, so both answers belong in the signature: the name reveals the asynchrony and a cancelable operation accepts cancellation explicitly. An operation is cancelable when it performs I/O or awaits, and anything else has nothing to cancel.

provisions.heading: Use Architectural Suffixes
provisions.evidence: Does each type name and each frontend file name carry the suffix its role assigns in the Role Suffixes table? Read the names beside the table.
provisions.artifact: state-record, domain-event, use-case, command-handler, query-handler, validator, reaction, repository, endpoint, job
provisions.statement: An architectural type MUST carry the suffix its role assigns in the Role Suffixes table.
provisions.rationale: A short name hides the role: `{UseCase}Handler` says nothing about coordination versus projection, and `{UseCase}Request` says nothing about passive boundary data. Full suffixes put the role in the name, so you sort types without opening files.
provisions.example:
An event handler names its act and the business fact without the kind suffix. `NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedHandler` answers `PostPublishedDomainEvent` and lives in the folder of the use case it runs. The name carries no technical suffix for the fact, so `NotifySubscribersOnPostPublishedDomainEventHandler` is wrong, while the event type keeps its kind suffix.

Application types keep their full suffix. The short forms `{UseCase}Result`, `{UseCase}Handler`, and `{UseCase}Validator` drop the command-or-query distinction the full name carries. A result part carries the full name of its result, not a bare summary name like `PostSummary`.

HTTP transport types keep their full suffix too. The short forms `{UseCase}Request` and `{UseCase}Response` drop the boundary marking. The `Model` suffix marks the type as passive boundary data instead of an operation or rich business object.

A polymorphic transport model mirrors a Domain discriminated union. Its abstract base names the concept and each sealed case names its case, with both ending in `Model`: `FulfillmentOutcomeModel` and `ShippedFulfillmentOutcomeModel`. The transport name drops the aggregate prefix of the Domain union, such as `OrderFulfillmentOutcome`, while its discriminator string keeps the stable case code of the Domain union unchanged.
